exp.15:4:
Paul asks that the church that meets in the house of Priscilla and Aquila be greeted. Then he greets Epenetus, whom he calls "my beloved." He says that he is the firstfruits of Achaia, that is, the first convert in that region. The phrase "Greet" is the same as "greet" in the verse above.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many people to show closeness and gratitude. At that time there were no Christian church buildings as there are today; believers gathered in homes. This version follows "Achaia."

God uses ordinary homes to build his church, and he values each person, even someone few remember. We can open our homes to pray or to share the Word, and encourage by name those who serve quietly.
exp.5:17:
It says that believers have already been set free from the power of sin and now belong to righteousness, that is, to living as God wants. "Being made free" means "set at liberty," and "servants" refers to those who serve a master completely, like slaves.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that no one lives without a master: either you serve sin, which leads to death, or you serve obedience, which leads to righteousness. He wants them to understand that their life changed by the grace of God and that this affects how they live each day. He uses the image of slavery because it was something they understood well.

For today: when temptation comes, remember that sin is no longer your master. Ask God for help and choose one concrete act of righteousness, such as telling the truth or forgiving.
exp.0:14:
Paul says he is ready and eager to proclaim the gospel, that is, the good news about Jesus Christ, also to the believers who live in Rome. "As much as in me is" means "as far as it depends on me," and "I am ready" means "I am willing."

Paul is writing this letter to believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He explains that he had often wanted to visit them, but something kept him from doing so. He feels indebted to all kinds of people, whether educated or not, and for that reason he does not want to keep the message to himself. This eagerness leads him to say right away that he is not ashamed of the gospel.

For today: ask God who you can encourage or share the hope of Jesus with. Take on Paul's attitude: a simple and humble willingness, without waiting to feel perfect or fully prepared.
exp.14:14:
Paul tells the brothers in Rome that he has written to them in this letter with considerable frankness on some points. He did it to remind them of things they already knew. He explains that he can speak this way because of the grace, or favor, that God has given him.

Paul is the one writing. He has just praised the Christians in Rome, saying they are full of goodness and knowledge. Even so, he does not want them to think he is correcting them out of pride. He makes clear that his authority comes from the calling God gave him as a servant of Jesus Christ to the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jews.

We can correct or encourage others, but with humility, without pride, and with respect. Before speaking, it is good to acknowledge the good that is in the other person. In this way the truth is spoken with firmness, but also with love and grace.
exp.15:22:
Paul sends greetings from three people who were with him. Gaius is his host, that is, the one who lodged him in his home, and he also opened his house to the whole church. Erastus is the city treasurer, an official in charge of public finances. Quartus is simply called a brother. The phrase "saluteth you" means "sends greetings to you."

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, probably from Corinth, near the end of his letter. Before closing, he includes the greetings of his companions. Some scholars think this Gaius is the same man Paul baptized in Corinth, though this is not certain.

This list shows that the church is a varied family: a generous host, a public official, a brother with no known office. All of them matter. Today we can imitate Gaius: offering our home or our time to welcome others, without expecting recognition.
exp.15:5:
Paul sends greetings to a woman named Mary. "Greet" means to pass on his greetings or to say hello to her on his behalf. Paul acknowledges that she "bestowed much labour on us," meaning she worked hard and wore herself out serving. The phrase "on us" shows that her service benefited the Christians in Rome.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome. In chapter 16 he greets many people by name, both men and women, and recognizes their work. We do not know more about this Mary; the text does not say exactly what she did. We only see that Paul valued her and kept her in mind.

God sees and remembers quiet work. Today we can follow Paul's example by thanking those who serve in the church without drawing attention to themselves. A sincere word of gratitude can encourage someone who is tired.
exp.8:27:
This verse says that the Lord will carry out his word on the earth fully and quickly, with righteousness. The word "finish" means that he brings things through to their end, and "cut it short" means that he does it in a brief way, without delay. It is a quotation from Isaiah 10:22-23, and translators understand it in several ways, but the central idea is that God acts with determination.

Paul is speaking here about Israel. Although the people were very numerous, only a remnant would be saved. Paul quotes Isaiah to show that this does not mean God has failed. He keeps his word and follows his own plan of grace, which includes the Gentiles as well.

For today: do not take for granted that God will be slow to fulfill what he has said. Live with confidence and with humility, for salvation is a gift of his grace and not a right we inherit.
exp.7:17:
Paul says he is convinced of something: the sufferings of the present time cannot be compared with the glory that God will one day reveal in us. "I reckon" means "I am sure." "Suffers" means to endure pain, and "the glory which shall be revealed" is the glory that is coming.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we are children and heirs of God, and that whoever suffers with Christ will also be glorified with him. Then he speaks of all creation eagerly waiting for that day. His point is that present pain is real, but it is not the end of the story.

Today, when you go through an illness, a loss, or an injustice, you do not have to pretend it does not hurt. You can bring your pain to God and remember that he promises something greater. That hope does not remove sadness at once, but it helps you keep going with peace and patience.
exp.10:10:
Paul asks whether the people of Israel stumbled so that they would fall for good. He answers firmly: "God forbid." Rather, through their stumble, salvation came to the Gentiles, that is, to those who were not Jews. This was meant to stir up jealousy in Israel, a desire to return to God when they saw the blessings others were receiving.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, many of whom were Gentiles. He has just quoted David speaking of a hardening. Now he clarifies that this hardening is not the end of Israel. He wants the Gentiles not to think themselves superior and to see God's plan with hope.

For today: do not look down with pride on someone who is far from God right now. God can use even our falls to open paths of grace. Pray for that person and live in such a way that it awakens in them a hunger for God.
exp.7:29:
This verse describes a chain of actions that God takes on behalf of those who belong to him: he predestined them, he called them, he justified them (declared them righteous, forgiven), and he glorified them (he will give them a fullness of glory with Christ). The verse is written in the past tense, as if everything were already accomplished, to show that God is sure in his work.

Paul is writing to the believers in Rome. He has just said that God uses all things for the good of those who love him, even in suffering. Here he gives them a firm reason: their salvation begins and ends in God. Christians understand differently how predestination and human freedom relate to each other, but the emphasis of the text is on assurance.

For today: when you doubt or go through trials, remember that your salvation rests on God's faithfulness, not on your effort. It rests on the fact that he will finish what he began.
exp.14:29:
Paul asks the brothers and sisters in Rome, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the love that the Spirit gives, to join him in prayer. Here the word "but" in "but I beseech you" marks the transition from his earlier words to this request. "Love" in this verse means the love the Spirit gives.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He is about to bring a gift to the poor believers in Jerusalem, and afterward he hopes to visit Rome and continue on to Spain. In the verses that follow, he asks for prayer that he would be rescued from those in Judea who opposed him and that his service would be well received.

For today: do not be embarrassed to ask for prayer. Paul, though an apostle, leaned on others. Today you can choose a trusted person, tell them a specific need, and ask them to pray for you. And pray for them too.
exp.11:19:
Paul says that if someone who treats you as an enemy is hungry or thirsty, you should give him food and drink. "Hot coals" is a picture: by doing good, you place something like burning embers on that person. "Heap" means you keep piling them up little by little.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and quotes Proverbs 25:21-22. He asks them not to take revenge but to leave judgment to God. The "coals" are understood in several ways: that the person feels shame and repents, or that it is a judgment of God. The next verse, "Be not overcome of evil, but overcome evil with good," supports the first idea.

Today, if someone has offended you, look for a simple way to help him: a kind message, a meal, a favor. Do it not to humiliate him, but to overcome evil with good and leave the rest in God's hands.
exp.3:13:
It says that if God's inheritance were gained by keeping the law, then faith would be of no use and the promise would be left without value. Those who belong to the law are the people who trust in keeping Moses' rules. The heir is the one who receives what was promised. The word "vain" means empty, without meaning, and "made void" means cancelled.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. He shows them that Abraham received the promise before he was circumcised and before the law existed. For that reason the promise came through faith, not through works, and so it can reach all who trust in God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love with your effort. Trust his promise, rest in his grace, and obey him out of gratitude, not out of fear of losing your place.
exp.4:11:
The passage joins two ideas. Through one man, Adam, sin entered the world, and with sin came death, which reached all people, because all have sinned. The word "reconciliation" appears at the start of this section, and several scholars point out that the original text actually says "therefore," beginning a comparison that Paul completes in the verses that follow. The phrase "passed upon all men" means "reached all people."

Paul, the apostle, is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God reconciled us to himself through the death of Jesus. Now he wants to show how far that gift reaches by comparing Adam, through whom ruin came, with Christ, through whom salvation comes. Christians understand in different ways how Adam's guilt is passed on, but all agree that death is shared by everyone.

Today we can humbly recognize that no one is saved alone, and rest thankfully in the work of Christ, not in our own merits.
exp.7:28:
God, who knew his people beforehand, also appointed them in advance to be transformed so that they would resemble Jesus, his Son. In this way Jesus would be the firstborn, that is, the first and most honored, among a large family of brothers and sisters. Christians have understood the phrases about knowing beforehand and appointing in several ways, but all agree that the goal is for us to become like Christ.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He has just said that God works all things together for the good of those who love him, even in suffering. Here he explains what that final good is: being shaped into the image of Jesus. It is a promise that gives firmness.

For today: when you go through trials, remember that God can use them to shape your character. Ask him today to help you respond with the patience, humility, and love of Jesus.
exp.0:23:
Because they had rejected God, He gave them over to what their hearts desired. Their impurity was uncleanness. Their desires were strong and disordered. They dishonored their own bodies. The "foolish" people mentioned in the previous verse were those who lacked wisdom.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that all human beings need the gospel. Here he describes how people exchanged the worship of the Creator for idols. To "give over" does not mean that God causes evil, but that He allows people to suffer the consequences of their own path.

For today: when you feel your heart drifting away from God, do not ignore it. Bring it to prayer and return to Him soon, before evil desires carry you further away. God forgives those who repent.
exp.15:10:
Paul sends greetings to Herodion, whom he calls his kinsman, meaning a relative or a fellow Jew (the word can mean both). He also greets those of Narcissus's household, but only those who are in the Lord, that is, the believers in that household.

Paul is writing this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many people to show them affection and to strengthen the unity of the church. Who Narcissus was exactly is not known for certain; some think he may have been a well-known person in Rome, but this is only a guess. The household included family members and servants.

Today we can follow Paul's example: remember others by name, value believers who go unnoticed, and express appreciation to them through a greeting, a message, or a prayer.
exp.11:15:
The explanation says that believers should live in harmony and think alike about what matters. Having the same mind means sharing the same feeling and seeking the same good. Those who are proud are the ones who consider themselves superior. Joining with ordinary people, without looking down on them, is what it means to associate with the lowly. And being wise in your own opinion means believing that you are always the one who is right.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, where there were people of different backgrounds, Jews and non-Jews. In this passage he explains how faith is lived out in daily dealings: blessing those who persecute, sharing joys and sorrows, and seeking peace. The humility he asks for here helps keep the community from being divided by pride.

Today we can practice this by truly listening to someone who thinks differently, or by reaching out to someone who usually goes unnoticed, before insisting on being right.
exp.8:11:
It was said to her, Rebekah, the wife of Isaac, that God had told her her two twin sons would have different destinies: the older, Esau, would serve the younger, Jacob. This was contrary to the custom of that time, when the firstborn son held the place of privilege.

Paul speaks to believers in Rome, and quotes Genesis 25:23. He wants to show that God's promises do not depend on physical descent or on merit, but on his calling. He said this before the children were born or had done anything. Christians have understood in various ways how far this election reaches: whether it refers to nations, to individuals, or to both. Paul himself stresses that God is not unjust.

For today: we can rest in the fact that our relationship with God begins with his grace, not with our achievements. This leads us to humility and gratitude, instead of boasting or comparing ourselves with others.
exp.3:8:
Paul asks whether this blessedness, the happiness of being forgiven, belongs only to the circumcised, meaning the Jews, or also to the uncircumcised, meaning those who are not Jews. He recalls that, according to Scripture, faith was reckoned to Abraham for righteousness. Being reckoned means that God regarded him as righteous.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, a community of both Jews and non-Jews. He has just quoted King David (Psalm 32) about forgiveness. He will soon show that Abraham was declared righteous before he was circumcised, so the promise is for everyone who believes.

Today, no one needs to belong to a particular group, perform a rite, or have a good record to be forgiven. We can come to God with simple trust, believing in his promise, and also receive with respect those who come from other paths.
exp.12:0:
It says that every person must submit to the authorities who govern. "Soul" means person, and "higher powers" are those who have authority over us. "Ordained" means established or put in their place. Paul affirms that no authority exists unless God permits or arranges it.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, the capital of the empire. They lived under a powerful and at times unjust government. Paul wants them to live in an orderly way and that their faith not be confused with rebellion. The following verses describe the authorities as those who restrain evil. Scholars debate how far this obedience extends when an authority orders something contrary to God.

Today we can respect the laws, pay our taxes, and treat authorities with honor. If a serious conflict arises with our conscience, we pray and act with humility and respect.
exp.8:3:
Paul says that the Israelites received great privileges from God. They were adopted as his people, they saw his glory, they received the covenants, and the law was given to them. The phrase about the giving of the law is an old expression, and the rest of this comment has been removed because it explains a word not found in the verse above. They also received the service of God, that is, the way of worshiping him, and the promises.

Paul, a Jew who followed Christ, writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just expressed his deep sorrow because many of his people have not believed in Jesus. For that reason he lists what God gave them, to show how much his people are worth and how much their situation grieves him.

For today: value the blessings God has given you, but do not take them for granted. Use them to draw close to him, and pray with sincere love for those who do not yet know him.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that God shows his righteous anger from heaven against all the wickedness and wrongdoing of people. Those people hold back the truth, that is, they suppress it or restrain it, because they prefer to live in what is wrong. Ungodliness means living without reverence for God, and unrighteousness means treating others badly.

Paul speaks here, writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the gospel saves everyone who believes. Now he explains why all of us need that salvation: humanity has rejected the truth that God made known in creation, as the following verses say. Scholars debate how that anger is expressed, but the text indicates that God is not indifferent to evil.

For today: examine honestly whether there is some truth you are avoiding for the sake of comfort. Ask God for the courage to accept it and to live in line with it.
exp.3:22:
The explanation says that what Scripture records about Abraham was not written for his sake alone. The word "written" appears in the verse as "written," and "imputed" means "counted to him" or "reckoned to him." It refers to how God counted Abraham's faith to him as righteousness. The verse prepares the idea that this is also for others, as the next verse shows.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that God declares people righteous by faith, not by works. He uses Abraham as an example, because Abraham trusted God's promise even when it seemed impossible. Paul wants to show that this ancient story has a present purpose for those who believe in Jesus.

For today: read the stories of the Bible not only as accounts of the past, but as messages for you. Just as Abraham trusted God, you can trust what God has done in Christ. Today, tell God simply that you rest in Jesus, not in your own merits.
exp.6:0:
Paul asks the brothers whether they do not know something they already understand well: the law has authority over a person only as long as that person lives. Paul is speaking to those who know the law, that is, the law of Moses.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has been explaining that in Christ we are free from the rule of sin. Now he uses the example of marriage, which appears in the following verses: death ends the legal obligation. Scholars discuss some details of the comparison, but the central idea is that death changes our relationship to the law.

Today we can live without fear of condemnation, because in Christ we are no longer under that yoke. That freedom is not an excuse for sin, but an invitation to obey God out of love and gratitude.
exp.8:9:
This verse adds a second example. Paul says that this happened not only with Sarah and Isaac, but also with Rebecca, who conceived by one man, that is, became pregnant by one man, Isaac. He is referring to the twins Esau and Jacob, children of the same father and the same mother. The word "conceived" means to become pregnant.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that being a descendant of Abraham does not guarantee being a child of the promise. With Isaac, and then with Jacob, he shows that God works according to his purpose and his calling, not according to family origin. Christian interpreters disagree about how to understand election in this passage, but all of them recognize that God acts by grace.

For today: do not trust in your family, your church, or your merits to feel accepted by God. Receive his calling with humility and gratitude, and treat others with the same grace that you have received.
exp.2:15:
It says that wherever people who live apart from God go, they leave ruin and suffering behind. Destruction, damage or ruin is what the word for "destruction" means. Misery is the word for distress or hardship. "Ways" refers to the way they live. In other words, their manner of acting ends up hurting others and themselves too.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking. To show that everyone needs God, he joins several quotations from the Old Testament, mainly from the Psalms and from Isaiah (in this case, Isaiah 59:7). His purpose is to explain that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin, and that no one is saved by their own merits, but by the grace of God.

Today, this verse invites us to examine the effect of our words and decisions. We can ask ourselves: "Do I leave peace or harm around me?" With humility, let us ask God to transform us and teach us to be people who build up and do not destroy.
exp.5:18:
Paul says he will speak "in human terms," using an everyday example, because believers find spiritual things hard to grasp. He reminds them that they once gave their bodies, their parts, over to impurity and wickedness. Now they must give those same bodies, just as completely, to righteousness, so as to live a life set apart for God, in holiness.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has already explained that, by grace, believers stopped being slaves to sin. He uses the image of slavery, something very familiar in that time, to encourage them to live in line with their new freedom.

For today: think about what you use your hands, your mouth, your time, and your eyes for. Choose one of those areas today and deliberately dedicate it to doing something good, such as helping, speaking with respect, or serving others.
exp.8:1:
Paul says that he feels great sadness and a pain that does not leave him, and that this pain is in the deepest part of his being. The word "continual" means that it does not stop; it is constant. And "heart" refers to the innermost part of a person: their feelings and their will.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul. He has just affirmed that he is telling the truth, and that his conscience confirms it. He is speaking about his people, Israel, and about how many of them had not believed in Jesus. After the great verses of hope in chapter 8, Paul shows his personal burden for them. His words are neither cold nor critical, but full of love.

Today we can learn to feel sincere sorrow for those who do not yet know Christ, especially family members and friends. Instead of judging them, we can pray for them with constancy and treat them with love.
exp.8:25:
It says that in the very place where God had told them, "You are not my people," there they will be called "children of the living God." It is a promise of change: those who were far from God become his children.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and quotes the prophet Hosea (Hosea 1:10). Hosea originally spoke to the northern kingdom of Israel, which had turned away from God. Paul uses that text to show that God calls his people both from among the Jews and from among the Gentiles. Some scholars think Paul applies Hosea's words to the Gentiles by analogy; others think the text also speaks of a restored Israel. Both ideas fit his argument.

For today: no one is so far away that God cannot call them his child. If you feel rejected or out of place, remember this promise. And treat others with that same grace.
exp.0:19:
Although we cannot see God, this verse says that his eternal power and divine nature can be recognized when we look at what he has made. The words "clearly seen" mean that these things are plainly noticed and understood. The word "without excuse" means that no one has a reason to say they knew nothing about God.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of God's anger against those who hold back the truth, that is, who suppress it or reject it because of their wickedness. Here he explains that God has made himself known through creation, and that the problem is not a lack of signs, but that many did not respond with thankfulness or honor.

For today: when you see a sunrise, a tree, or the night sky, pause for a moment and give thanks to God. Let creation lead you to worship the Creator.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that Abraham is the father of the circumcised, but not of all of them simply by that fact alone. He is the father of those who, in addition to being circumcised, walk in the steps of the faith that Abraham had while he was still uncircumcised. The word "steps" is the key: they are the footprints left behind, living the way he lived, trusting God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. He explains that God declared Abraham righteous because of his faith, before he was circumcised. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, and circumcision on its own does not save.

Today, belonging to a church, a believing family, or a tradition is not enough. God looks at the trust of the heart. Ask yourself: am I following in the steps of faith, trusting God even when I do not see the outcome?
exp.0:20:
They knew God through creation, but they did not honor him as God or give him thanks. Instead, their reasoning became empty, and their foolish, senseless heart was filled with darkness. "Glorify" means to acknowledge and honor God for who he is.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that creation shows God's power and divinity, so no one has an excuse. Here he describes the source of the human problem: it is not a lack of information, but a heart that does not want to honor God or thank him. He then shows how this leads to idolatry.

For today: practice gratitude. Each day, thank God for something specific, and recognize that every good thing comes from him.
exp.11:4:
This verse says that although we are many different people, all who believe in Christ form one single body. Moreover, each one belongs to the others: we need one another and are united among ourselves.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. Before this verse, he asks them for humility: that no one think of himself more highly than he ought, because God gave each person a measure of faith. He uses the image of the body, with many parts and different functions. Afterward, he speaks of the different gifts God gives.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or feel useless. Today, look for a concrete way to serve someone in your church or community, and give thanks for the contribution of someone different from you.
exp.11:13:
Explains that we should wish and ask for good for those who harm us because of our faith. "Bless" means to speak well of someone and ask God to favor them. The verse repeats it for emphasis, and adds "and curse not": do not wish for or ask for harm against them. "Persecute" refers to those who treat us with hostility.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. After explaining what God has done for them in Christ, he shows them how to live that faith in practice. Earlier he speaks of hope, patience in suffering, prayer, and hospitality. Then he speaks of sharing joys and sorrows, and of living with humility. This verse joins both parts: love must reach even our enemies.

Today: if someone speaks badly of you or treats you with contempt, pray for that person by name and, if you can, answer with a kind word instead of revenge.
exp.14:4:
Paul prays that God, who gives patience and comfort, would grant believers to live in harmony with one another, following the example of Christ Jesus. "Likeminded" means having the same mind and purpose. "Grant you" is a request: this unity is a gift from God.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers from both Jewish and non-Jewish backgrounds who differed in customs and judged one another. Before this verse, he reminds them that Christ endured scorn out of love for others, and that the Scriptures encourage us to hope. Afterward, Paul says that this unity leads to glorifying God with one voice.

For today: if you have tension with a brother or sister in the faith, pray for that person and ask God for patience. Then take a concrete step, such as listening or forgiving, without waiting for them to agree with you on everything.
exp.1:6:
It says that God will give eternal life to those who do not grow weary of doing good and who seek for glory, honor, and immortality. "Patient continuance" means steady perseverance, staying firm without giving up.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he explains that God judges everyone fairly, Jews and Gentiles alike, according to their deeds. Earlier he speaks of those who harden their hearts and do not repent; here he shows the other path. Those who seek God steadily receive eternal life. Other passages in Romans make clear that salvation is by grace through faith, and that good works show that faith. Some scholars understand this in different ways, but the emphasis here is that God looks at the heart and the life.

For today: do not lose heart when doing good is costly. Choose one steady act of kindness, such as helping someone, forgiving, or being honest, and ask God for strength to keep going.
exp.14:24:
The explanation says that Paul is about to travel to Jerusalem to minister, that is, to serve or help, the saints, who are the believers in Jesus. The word "But" in the verse means "however," and the city is Jerusalem. His plan to go on to Spain will have to wait a little while.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He tells them of his plans to visit them on his way to Spain, but first he must deliver a gift. According to the verses that follow, the churches of Macedonia and Achaia collected money for the poorer believers in Jerusalem. Paul sees this as a debt of gratitude: the non-Jewish believers received spiritual blessings and now share material goods.

Today we can ask ourselves how we might concretely help others. Serving fellow believers with our time or resources is a real way to give thanks for what God has given us.
exp.8:7:
Here Paul says that physically descending from Abraham is not enough to be considered a child of God. Those who are born by natural bloodline are the "children of the flesh." Those who are born through what God promised and fulfilled are the "children of the promise." The phrase "counted for the seed" means that God counts them as true descendants.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. It grieved him that many of his own people did not accept Jesus, and some thought God had failed. Paul answers that God's word remains firm: from the beginning, God chose Isaac because of his promise, not because of ordinary family inheritance.

For today: do not rest on your family, your church, or your religious history. Trust God's promise and respond to it with sincere faith, for being part of his family is a gift of his grace.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that sin should not rule over our lives. "Reign" is like a king who gives orders. "Mortal body" is our present life, weak and temporary. "Lusts" are the disordered desires that push us to do wrong. "Obey" reminds us that we can choose whom we follow.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that, because the believer is joined to Christ in his death and resurrection, the believer no longer belongs to the realm of sin. That is why he tells them to consider themselves dead to sin and alive to God. His aim is to encourage, not to condemn: they live under grace.

For today: when temptation comes, remember who you are in Christ. Before you react, pray briefly and ask God for strength. Then choose one concrete action that honors God.
exp.7:38:
It says that nothing that exists can separate us from God's love. "Height" and "depth" speak of the extremes, above and below, and so they include the whole universe. "Creature" means anything that has been created. That love is not far away: it is given to us in Christ Jesus, that is, through him and joined to him.

The apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just mentioned suffering, persecution and danger. With this list, which comes from the verses before, he wants to give the believers assurance: no hardship or power, seen or unseen, can cancel the love that God showed in Christ. Some scholars debate exactly what "principalities" and "powers" mean, but in general they are understood as spiritual powers.

Today, when you feel alone, guilty or very weak, remember that your worth does not depend on your mood. Say it in prayer: "Lord, your love sustains me today."
exp.13:21:
It says that the conviction you have about what is permissible for you should be kept between you and God, without imposing it or showing it off. And happy is the one who does not feel guilty for what he decides to do. "Condemns himself" means that his conscience accuses him; "alloweth" means that he approves of it.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different consciences about foods and special days. Some ate everything; others, perhaps because of their Jewish background or to avoid meat offered to idols, abstained. Paul asks that the strong care for the weak and not make them stumble.

For today: in matters where the Bible leaves freedom, live with a clear conscience before God, without flaunting your freedom or judging the brother who thinks differently. Before acting, ask yourself: can I do this with faith and without doubts? Does this help my brother?
exp.2:27:
It says that a person is declared righteous before God by trusting in Jesus, not by keeping the commandments of the law. "Justified" means declared innocent and accepted by God. "Therefore we conclude" means that Paul draws a conclusion from what he has already explained. "The deeds of the law" refers to efforts to earn God's favor by obeying the law of Moses.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just shown that everyone has sinned and that God offers salvation through Christ. For that reason there is no room for boasting: no one is saved on the basis of their own merit. And since God is one, he justifies both Jews and non-Jews by faith.

For today: rest in God's grace and not in your performance. Obey out of gratitude, not to earn his love. And treat others with humility, for we all receive the same thing.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that people from other nations, the Gentiles, did not receive the law that God gave to Moses. Even so, they sometimes do by instinct what that law commands. "Naturally" means they do it by their own conscience, without anyone teaching them. So, although they do not have the written law, they are a law to themselves.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and Gentiles. He shows them that no one can boast before God. The Jews had the law, but hearing it is not enough; it must be obeyed. And the Gentiles, without having it, show that God placed in their conscience a sense of good and evil. Some understand this as a reference to Gentiles who do not believe, and others to believers; Paul does not clarify this here.

Today, do not compare yourself with others or boast that you know a great deal of the Bible. Ask God that your life shows what you say you believe.
exp.6:15:
Paul says that when he does something he does not really want to do, that very thing shows he agrees with God's law. If it bothers him that he does wrong, it is because he recognizes that the law is good. The word "consent" in the verse means "agree with" or "recognize."

Paul is explaining that God's law is not the one to blame for sin. He describes an inner struggle between what he desires and what he ends up doing. Christians have understood this passage in two ways: some think it speaks of his life before he knew Christ, and others see it as the struggle of the believer. In both cases, the law is good and the problem lies with sin.

For today: when you feel sorry for having failed, do not become completely discouraged. That pain can show that you love what is good. Bring it honestly to God and ask him for help to change.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that the power of the Holy Spirit, who gives life to those united with Jesus, has set us free from another force that held us captive: sin, which ends in death. Here the word "law" is understood as a principle or an active force. "Freed" means liberated.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of his struggle against sin (Romans 7). Now he explains why there is no condemnation: what the law of Moses could not accomplish because of human weakness, God did by sending his Son.

For today: when guilt or a bad habit tells you that there is no remedy, remember that you are no longer a slave. Ask the Spirit for help each day, and walk trusting in what Christ has already done for you.
exp.1:28:
He says that being a true Jew does not depend on what shows on the outside, but on what is within. The circumcision that really matters is the one of the heart, done by the Spirit, and not the one that only follows a written rule. The word "letter" refers to the law as a mere outward rule. And "praise" means approval or recognition: the one who lives this way does not seek the applause of people, but the approval of God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, among them Jews and non-Jews. He shows them that boasting of having the law or the sign of circumcision is not enough if life does not go with it. His point is that everyone needs God, and that He looks at the heart.

For today: before seeking for others to notice your faith, ask yourself what is really in your heart. Ask God for sincerity, and today do one act of kindness or obedience that no one else knows about.
exp.0:28:
It says that those who rejected God ended up filled with every kind of wickedness. The list includes unrighteousness (injustice), fornication (sexual immorality), malice (a desire to harm), greed (always wanting more), envy, murder, strife (quarreling), deceit, and malignity (hidden ill will).

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Before speaking of the gospel as salvation for everyone, he shows that humanity needs to be rescued. He explains that when people turn away from God, he gives them over to their own corrupt minds, and this shows in their actions. The list continues in the verses that follow.

Today we can examine our hearts with humility. It is easy to point out the sins of others, but this list includes envy, strife, and deceit, which also touch us. Ask God to cleanse you and change you.
exp.4:9:
Paul says that we were enemies of God, but God reconciled us to himself through the death of Jesus. The word "reconciled" means that the broken relationship was restored. If God did the hardest thing when we were his enemies, how much more will he keep us now that we are his friends. The phrase about being saved by his life refers to the risen Christ, who lives and sustains our salvation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, explaining that salvation is a gift from God received through faith. In the verses before this one he speaks of God's love, which was shown while we were still sinners. Here he states that this love gives us a firm hope for the future, including salvation from the wrath of God.

For today: if you doubt that God will sustain you because you feel weak or fail, remember that he loved you while you were far away. Rest in his love and speak with him with confidence, knowing that Christ lives for you.
exp.1:22:
Paul asks a piercing question: does someone who boasts of having God's law dishonor God by disobeying that same law? To boast means to take pride in something or show it off. To break the law means to violate one of its commands. To dishonor God means to bring disrespect upon him through your conduct, failing to honor his name.

Paul writes to the church in Rome. Here he addresses someone who is confident in knowing the law, and many understand this to refer to Jews who felt superior. His point is that having the law or being circumcised is not enough if one's life does not reflect it. Everyone needs the grace of God.

For today: knowing the Bible or speaking well of the faith is not enough. Examine whether there is anything you teach others that you yourself do not practice, and ask God for help to live it out with humility.
exp.7:14:
They say that those who belong to Christ did not receive a spirit of slavery that makes them live in fear again. They received the Spirit of adoption, that is, the Spirit who makes us children of God. Through Him we can cry out, "Abba, Father."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that those who are led by the Spirit of God are his children. The verses that follow say that the Spirit confirms this identity and that the children are also heirs with Christ. Paul contrasts living in fear, like a slave, with living secure, like a beloved child.

For today: when you feel afraid of not being enough before God, pray to him, "Father." Speak to him with confidence, without pretending or hiding, remembering that his love does not depend on your achievements, but on the fact that you are his child.
exp.10:3:
Paul quotes what God answered Elijah. The divine reply is the voice of God. God says he has kept for himself seven thousand men who never bowed the knee before Baal, that is, who did not worship that idol.

Paul speaks of Israel and asks whether God has rejected them. He answers that he has not. He recalls when Elijah, discouraged, thought he was the only faithful one left (1 Kings 19). God showed him that there were many more. Paul says that in his own time there was also a faithful remnant, preserved by God's grace, not by their merits.

When you feel alone in your faith, remember that God knows who belongs to him and always has other faithful people you cannot see. Take heart, remain faithful, and seek fellowship with other believers.
exp.8:26:
This verse says that Isaiah speaks with force about Israel. Even though the people are as numerous as the sand of the sea, only the remnant, that is, a small part that is left, will be saved. The word "crieth" means that he says it out loud and with seriousness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and quotes the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 10:22). He wants to explain why many Israelites did not believe in Jesus, even though God had made promises to them. Paul shows that God has always worked through a faithful remnant, and that his salvation depends on his grace, not on the size or the origin of the people.

For today: salvation is not inherited or earned by belonging to a group. Ask God to give you a sincere faith in Christ, and trust that his mercy reaches even those who seem few or far away.
exp.13:13:
Paul says that he is convinced, trusting in the Lord Jesus, that no food is unclean in itself. But if someone believes that something is unclean, then for that person it is unclean.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where there was tension between believers from a Jewish background, who kept the rules about food, and believers from a non-Jewish background, who ate everything. Paul does not order them to fight over this. He asks them not to judge one another and not to cause a brother to stumble, because each one will give an account to God.

Today, there are matters where sincere Christians think differently, and these are not sins in themselves. Before using your freedom, ask yourself whether it will help or wound a brother's conscience. Love first, and avoid arguing over secondary matters.
exp.0:9:
Paul says that when he prays, he asks God that, at last, if it is his will, the way may be opened for him to travel to Rome. "Making request" means asking or pleading. "A prosperous journey" means a journey that goes well, with the road open. The remaining quoted phrases in the source are simply the same idea in other words, "to you" and "to you all".

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He tells them that he remembers them always in his prayers and that he desires to see them so that they may encourage one another in the faith. He notes that he does not impose his own plan but leaves it in the hands of God's will. How that journey came about is another matter that the book of Acts narrates later.

For today: when you have a good desire, such as visiting someone or starting a project, bring it to God honestly and patiently. Ask that his will be done, trust his timing, and keep praying for the people you love.
exp.7:18:
It says that all creation waits with great eagerness, almost with its neck stretched out, for the day when it will be shown who the children of God truly are. "Creature" here refers to what has been created; "manifestation" means that something hidden is made visible.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of present suffering and the future glory of those who are children and heirs with Christ. Now he widens the view: creation also suffers because of the fall and waits to be set free. Some understand "creature" as all of nature; others take it in a more limited way, but the general sense is creation waiting for its restoration.

For today: when you suffer or grow tired of a broken world, remember that your pain is not the end. Wait with patience and hope, and care with respect for what God created.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that no one, by themselves, has true spiritual understanding or seeks God from the heart. The word "understandeth" refers to grasping who God is and what He wants. The old spelling "á" is an archaic way of writing "a".

Paul, the author of the letter, is speaking to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that Jews and non-Jews are equally under sin. To do this, he joins several quotations from the Old Testament, especially from Psalms 14 and 53. His aim is to prepare the way to explain that salvation is a gift of God through Jesus.

For today: if we depend on God to seek Him, we can live with humility and gratitude. If today you desire to know Him, it is a sign that He is already at work in you. Give thanks to Him and keep seeking Him with confidence.
exp.5:13:
It says that sin will not be the master of believers. The quoted phrase in the source, "Se enseñoreará," means it will rule or dominate over you as a lord over his servants. The reason is that they no longer live under the law, which only showed what is wrong, but under grace, the undeserved favor of God that gives forgiveness and strength to change.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just urged them not to let sin reign or give their bodies to it, but to give themselves to God. This verse is a promise that encourages them. Right away he makes clear that grace is not permission to sin, since whoever you give yourself to is the one you serve.

For today: when you feel trapped by a bad habit, do not give up thinking you cannot change. Ask God for help, each day surrender your decisions to him, and live confident that his grace sustains you.
exp.7:10:
It says that the same Spirit of God who raised Jesus lives in believers. Therefore, God, who raised Christ from the dead, will also give life to our mortal bodies, that is, bodies subject to death. The word "quicken" in the verse means to give life. To "dwell" means to live or to remain.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that, although the body suffers the consequences of sin and will die, the Spirit gives spiritual life. Here he adds a hope: the life God gives does not end in the inner person, but will also reach the body. Many understand this to refer to the future resurrection; some think it also includes strength to live now.

For today: when you feel weak, tired, or afraid of death, remember that the Spirit of God dwells in you. Ask him to give you strength to obey today, and trust in the promise of life that God will fulfill.
exp.2:30:
This verse raises a question: if we are saved by faith, do we then nullify God's law? Paul answers emphatically: "God forbid," that is, by no means. To "make void" means to leave without value, and to "establish" means to affirm or uphold. According to Paul, faith does not take away the law's value; rather, it confirms it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God justifies, that is, declares righteous, both Jews and non-Jews through faith. He anticipates the objection that this would throw contempt on the law. Interpreters explain in several ways how faith "establishes" the law: some say that faith recognizes what the law teaches about sin, others that it fulfills the law's purpose. Paul will develop this later.

For today: trusting in Christ is no excuse for living as we please. We can be thankful for grace and, with that same faith, want to obey God out of love.
exp.1:3:
Some people, the explanation says, look down on God's kindness without realizing it. "Kindness" here means gentle goodness, and "patience" and "longsuffering" mean that God holds back for a long time before punishing. To "despise" something is to treat it lightly. The verse states that this goodness aims to lead us to repentance, that is, to turn around and change direction.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke about those who judge others for their sins while doing the same things themselves. Here he asks them whether they think God's silence or delay means there will be no accounting. Then he warns that a hard heart that refuses to repent piles up judgment. Some believe he is addressing a moralistic Jew, but the text does not say this clearly at this point.

For today: when God gives you another chance, do not take it as permission to carry on as before. Ask yourself honestly what you need to correct, and take one concrete step today, such as asking forgiveness or letting go of a bad habit.
exp.15:8:
Paul tells the believers in Rome to greet Urbanus, whom he calls "our helper in Christ," and Stachys, whom he calls "my beloved." The word "helper" means a fellow worker, someone who labors alongside others in the work of the gospel, and the name Stachys is simply the name of this person, while "my beloved" expresses personal affection.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome and, at the end, sends greetings to many people by name. Beyond what this verse says, we know nothing more about Urbanus and Stachys. Urbanus seems to have worked with Paul and others, since Paul calls him "our." This list shows that Paul valued each person, not only the well-known leaders.

For today: notice those who serve without being seen and express your gratitude to them. A greeting, a message, or a word of affection can greatly encourage someone who faithfully helps in your church.
exp.4:10:
Paul says that believers have not only been saved from punishment, but also rejoice and take pride, in the good sense, in God. "We glory" here means we rejoice with confidence. This joy comes through Jesus Christ, who has caused us to receive the reconciliation, that is, the restored peace with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains how God makes people right with Himself through faith. Earlier he said that we were enemies of God and that Christ died for us. Now he concludes that this work produces more than relief: it produces joy. What follows shows Christ as the one who repairs what Adam damaged.

Today, when you feel far from God because of your failures, remember that your relationship with Him rests on what Christ has done, not on your performance. Thank Him today for that peace.
exp.2:5:
Paul responds firmly: "By no means" means "Certainly not!" Someone once argued that if our wickedness makes God's righteousness stand out, then God would be unjust to punish. Paul answers that if that were true, God could not judge the world, and the Bible teaches that he will.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and imagines the objections of someone who wants to excuse sin. He has already said that the Jews received God's words, but that this does not free them from judgment. Here he defends the fact that God is just and will judge everyone with truth. He himself makes clear that he is speaking "as a man," that is, using a human argument.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to sin. Trust that God is just, and live with humility, knowing that he will judge with truth.
exp.7:36:
It says that, in the midst of all the difficulties Paul has just named, believers do not merely endure but come out more than conquerors. This does not happen through their own strength, but "through him that loved us," that is, Christ. The word "Nay" here means "on the contrary." "More than conquerors" means that the victory is complete and certain.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just asked whether suffering (tribulation, hunger, danger, the sword) could separate us from the love of Christ. He quotes a psalm that describes the faithful as "sheep for the slaughter," and yet he affirms that God's love sustains the believer.

For today: when you face a trial, do not measure your victory by whether the problem disappears, but by who is with you. Repeat with confidence that Christ loves you and that no situation can separate you from that love. That assurance gives you strength to keep going.
exp.8:10:
Before Jacob and Esau were born, and before either of them had done anything good or bad, God had already declared his purpose. That purpose rests on God's choosing, not on what people do, but on the one who calls. The phrase about God's choice means "according to his choosing," and the word about standing firm means "would remain firm."

Paul is speaking to believers in Rome, many of them Jews and Gentiles together. He is explaining why not all of Abraham's descendants received the promise. He uses Isaac and Jacob as examples: God acts through his calling and his promise, not through human merit. Christians interpret in different ways how this relates to election and human freedom.

For today: you do not need to earn God's love through your performance. Rest in his grace, thank him for calling you, and respond with a life of trust and humble obedience.
exp.6:8:
Paul says there was a time when he lived "without the law," that is, without feeling the weight of the commandment. But when the commandment came to his conscience, sin came alive like something asleep that wakes up, and he died, that is, he felt condemned and cut off from God. The word "lust" here means disordered desire.

Paul speaks in the first person and argues that God's law is good, not bad. He explains that the law shows what sin is and awakens it in us. Scholars debate who this "I" refers to: Paul himself, Israel, or every person. Even so, the central point is clear.

For today: do not use God's law to feel righteous, but as a mirror that shows your need. When you see your weakness, do not despair; come to Christ, who gives forgiveness and new life.
exp.7:25:
What the passage says: Paul affirms that the Holy Spirit helps us in our weakness. "Infirmities" means weakness or limitation, so the verse is speaking of the ways we fall short. Sometimes we do not know what to ask God for or how to pray as we should. Then the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be put into words, that is, deep sighs that cannot be expressed in speech.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of waiting patiently for what we do not yet see, and of how all creation waits for its liberation. In the midst of that waiting, our prayer can feel weak. He then says that God, who knows hearts, understands the desire of the Spirit, because the Spirit prays according to the will of God.

For today: when you are so tired or confused that you do not know how to pray, do not keep silent out of shame. Speak to God honestly, even if your words are few or you offer only a sigh, and trust that the Spirit is with you.
exp.1:7:
Paragraph one describes people who are "contentious": quarrelsome, stubborn, and full of self-interest. They resist God's truth and would rather obey unrighteousness. The result is "indignation and wrath," which speaks of God's just judgment against evil.

Pablo writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God judges with impartiality, without favoritism, both the Jew and the Greek. Each person answers according to their attitude and their deeds. That is why this verse contrasts with the previous one, which speaks of those who persevere in doing good.

For today: examine with humility whether there are areas where you resist what you know to be true out of pride or stubbornness. Ask God for a heart willing to listen and obey, and take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.1:19:
He says that someone considers himself a teacher of those who do not know, and of "children," that is, of people with little knowledge. "The form of knowledge and of the truth" means that he has in the law a pattern or model of knowledge and of truth.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and speaks to a Jewish listener who feels secure because he knows God's law. Some think he is a Jew in general, and others think he is a believing Jew who is presumptuous. Paul does not mock the law, but shows that knowing is not enough if one does not obey, as the verses that follow make clear.

For today: if you teach or advise others, first examine your own life. Before correcting, ask yourself with humility: "Am I practicing what I preach?"
exp.2:19:
The explanation says that no one will be declared righteous before God by keeping the commands of the law. "No flesh" in the verse refers to no human being. Being "justified" means being declared innocent and accepted by God. The law serves to show us what sin is, not to remove it.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He has just quoted several passages from the Old Testament to show that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin. The law makes every mouth stop: no one can defend themselves or boast. With this, he prepares the next verse, where he presents the righteousness of God that comes through faith in Jesus Christ.

For today: stop trying to earn God's favor through your good behavior. Use the law as a mirror that shows you your need, and come to Christ with humility and confidence, resting in his grace.
exp.5:3:
Being baptized means we are joined to Christ in his death, as if we had been buried with him. But the story does not end in the grave: just as the Father raised Christ up by his glory, we too can live each day in a new life. The verse says we "should walk" in newness of life, meaning we are to live out our days this way.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that God gives grace abundantly, and someone might think, "Then let us keep on sinning." Paul answers, "By no means." Whoever belongs to Christ has already died to sin, so they cannot keep living in it as before. Some understand baptism here as the act of water, and others as spiritual union with Christ; many see both.

For today: if you belong to Christ, your past does not rule over you. Today, choose one old habit that harms you and ask God for strength to replace it with a new action that honors him.
exp.4:13:
Death ruled like a king from Adam until Moses. It reigned even over those who had not sinned by breaking a direct command, as Adam did. "In the likeness of Adam's transgression" means "in the same way as Adam's disobedience." And Adam is a pattern, a foreshadowing, of Christ, "who is to come."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that all of us need Christ. Death was already present before the law of Moses, which shows that sin affected everyone. He compares Adam with Christ: one brought death, the other brings grace. Interpreters debate how the effect of Adam's sin is passed on, but the central contrast is clear.

For today: do not carry your life as if it depended on your own record. If you are in Christ, your hope rests on his grace, which is greater than any failure. Today, thank him with a simple prayer.
exp.5:12:
It says that we should not hand over the parts of our body to sin so that they become tools of wickedness. Instead, we should give ourselves to God, as people who have passed from death to life, and use our members as tools for doing what is right.

Here the apostle Paul speaks to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that, through union with Christ, the believer is dead to sin and alive to God. Now he encourages them to live in line with that new reality. Afterward he clarifies that grace is not permission to sin, but the strength that frees us from sin's control.

For today: each day we can ask ourselves how we will use our hands, words, and eyes. This morning, offer them to God in prayer and use them to serve, to speak the truth, or to help someone.
exp.1:0:
It says that no one has an excuse before God if they judge others. "Inexcusable" means that a person cannot defend or justify themselves. Paul states that when you criticize another person for a sin, you condemn yourself, because you also do the same thing.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. In the previous chapter he described the sin of the pagans. Here he addresses the person who feels superior and points a finger at others. Many think he refers mainly to some Jews, although his words apply to anyone. His purpose is to show that all of us need the grace of God.

Before criticizing someone, examine your own heart honestly. Acknowledge your failures, and treat others with humility and compassion, remembering that you too depend on God's forgiveness.
exp.15:7:
Paul sends greetings to Amplias and calls him "my beloved in the Lord." Paul does not only name him; he expresses real affection for him, and he makes clear that this affection rests on the faith they share in Christ.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he sends greetings to many people by name. We know nothing more about Amplias; the Bible does not tell his story. It was a common name in that time, and yet Paul remembers him with warmth.

For today: set aside time to express appreciation to someone in your church or your close circle, even if that person is little known. A sincere message or phone call can encourage them greatly, because in Christ no brother or sister goes unnoticed.
exp.10:15:
It says that if the offering given to God is holy, the whole batch is holy too; and if the root is holy, the branches are holy as well. "Firstfruit" refers to the first portion set apart for God, the first of the harvest. "Holy" means set apart for God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, and he speaks of Israel, his people. He uses these two images to show that God has not forgotten Israel because of their relationship to the patriarchs. Scholars debate whether the firstfruit and the root are the patriarchs, the first Jewish believers, or both. Right after this, he warns the non-Jewish believers not to feel superior.

For today: remember that your faith rests on a root you did not plant, but on the grace of God. Treat with humility and respect those who think differently or do not yet believe, for God is still at work.
exp.4:2:
Paul says that believers not only rejoice in the hope of God's glory, but also boast in their troubles. "To boast" here means to rejoice with confidence. "Tribulation" means suffering or affliction, and "patience" means steady endurance, the perseverance to keep going forward.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and explaining what God does through faith. He has already said that we are justified, that is, accepted by God, and that we have peace with Him. Now he shows that suffering is not a sign of being abandoned, because God uses it to shape character and strengthen hope, a hope that does not disappoint because His love fills our hearts.

When you go through a difficulty, don't ask only "Why is this happening to me?" but also "What is God forming in me?" Ask Him for help to stay firm, without hiding your pain.
exp.6:23:
Paul says he feels like a wretched man and asks to be rescued from "this body of death." The word "wretched" means afflicted and without strength. "Deliver" means to rescue or set free. The expression "this body of death" is understood in several ways: our weak human nature, which is subject to sin, or the mortal body itself.

Paul writes in the first person and describes the struggle between wanting to obey God and feeling dragged toward sin. Scholars disagree about whether he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ or of his experience as a believer. What is clear is that his cry receives an answer right away: "I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord."

Today, when you are frustrated by your failures, do not hide or despair. Acknowledge your weakness honestly and turn to Jesus, who is the deliverer. He helps you day by day.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that in the gospel the righteousness of God is shown, or made visible. That righteousness is received through faith, and faith is the way from beginning to end. "Is revealed" is the same as the verse's "revealed." The phrase "from faith to faith" is understood in several ways: from one faith to a greater one, or from God's faithfulness to ours. Paul quotes Habakkuk 2:4: the just shall live by faith.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that he is not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God to save everyone who believes, Jew or Greek. Here he explains why: in the gospel God shows how he accepts us.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor by your good behavior. Trust in Christ every day, even in your doubts and failures, and let that trust shape the way you live.
exp.8:15:
This verse says that God's salvation and blessing are not obtained simply because a person wants them, nor through one's own effort. Everything depends on God, who shows mercy, that is, compassion we do not deserve.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just quoted what God said to Moses to answer a question: is God unjust when he chooses some people over others? Paul answers that he is not, because mercy is a gift from God and not a debt. Christians understand in different ways how this relates to human free choice, and among believers there is debate about this.

Today we can live with humility and gratitude, without boasting of our spiritual achievements. We can work hard and desire what is good, but rest in the fact that God sustains us by his mercy.
exp.8:32:
It says that God placed in Zion, that is, in Jerusalem and among his people, a stone that causes some to stumble and fall. But whoever believes in it will not be put to shame, that is, will not be let down.

Paul is speaking here about Israel. Many sought to please God through their works and not by faith, and that is why they stumbled. Paul joins two passages from the Old Testament (Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16). Almost all Christians understand the stone to be Christ, as Peter also shows in his letter.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we trust in Jesus or in our own merits. We can stop trying to earn God's favor and rest in what Christ has already done. Whoever trusts in him can have peace, even when others see it as something strange.
exp.7:33:
This verse asks a question: who will be able to condemn those whom God has chosen? The answer is Christ, who died for us, rose again, is at the right hand of God (that is, in the place of honor and authority), and intercedes for us, that is, he pleads on our behalf before the Father.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God gave up his own Son for us and that he is the one who justifies, that is, who declares the believer righteous. Paul uses questions like those in a courtroom to show that no one has the authority to condemn anyone who is in Christ. Afterward he speaks of the trials that cannot separate us from his love.

When guilt or the mistakes of the past speak loudly to you, remember that Christ has already died for you and today intercedes for you. Pray with confidence, without fear of being rejected.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that all people have sinned, that is, they have fallen short before God. "Falling short of the glory of God" means that no one reaches the level of goodness and perfection that God is and expects. Something is lacking; we are far from that standard.

The apostle Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God's righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ, because there is no difference: Jews and non-Jews are in the same need. For this reason, this verse explains why we all need to be justified freely, as the next verse says.

Today we can stop comparing ourselves with others to feel either better or worse. We all need the grace of God. That helps us to be humble, to treat others with mercy, and to trust in Christ, not in our own merits.
exp.15:0:
Paul introduces a woman named Phebe and commends her to the Christians in Rome. He calls her "our sister" and describes her as a servant of the church at Cenchrea. The verse uses the word "commend," which means to recommend her to them. The Greek word translated "servant" here means someone who serves or helps. Some believe it referred to an official role in the church; others think it describes her service in general.

Paul writes this letter from Corinth, and Cenchrea was the nearby port. Most likely Phebe carried the letter to Rome. That is why Paul asks that she be well received and helped in whatever she needs, since she has helped many people, including him.

Today we can notice those who serve quietly in our church and thank them. We can also welcome with affection and help the brothers and sisters who arrive from another place.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that Christ is the "end" of the law, meaning both its goal and its fulfillment. Through Him, righteousness, that is, being accepted by God, is offered to everyone who believes. The words for "to" and "for righteousness" simply mean "to" and "so that there may be righteousness." The word "end" can be understood as "termination" or as "purpose"; many believe Paul means both.

The apostle Paul speaks of his Jewish brothers. He acknowledges that they have great zeal for God, but they lack understanding that God himself gives righteousness. They tried to earn it by their own effort and did not submit to what God offered in Christ.

Today, you do not have to strive to deserve God's love. Trust in Christ, rest in what He has done, and let your obedience be born of gratitude, not of fear.
exp.8:2:
Paul says that he himself would wish to be "cut off from Christ," that is, separated from Him and under condemnation, if that could save his brothers. "Kinsmen according to the flesh" refers to his people, the Israelites, with whom he shares blood. The word "could wish" expresses a longing that he knows cannot be fulfilled.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken with great confidence about the love of God in chapter 8. Now he confesses his deep sorrow because many of his people have not believed in Jesus. He swears that he is telling the truth, and then he recalls the privileges that Israel received from God.

For today: truly loving those who do not know Christ means feeling sorrow for them, praying earnestly, and humbly seeking the opportunity to speak to them about Jesus, beginning with our own family.
exp.10:11:
The explanation says that Israel's failure brought blessing to the whole world. "Fall" and "loss" speak of their fall or spiritual loss in not accepting Christ. "Fullness" means completeness, that is, that Israel would one day be made whole again. If their stumbling allowed the Gentiles to receive spiritual riches, how much greater will the blessing be when they are restored!

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, especially the Gentiles. He is a Jew, and it grieves him that many of his people have rejected Jesus. Even so, he teaches that God has not cast them off. Some understand this fullness as a great future conversion of Israel; others see it as a process already underway. Christians debate this.

Today, we can trust that God can bring good even out of falls. And instead of looking down with pride on those who do not believe, let us pray for them with love and hope.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that the Gentiles, that is, the peoples who are not Jews, are invited to rejoice together with the people of God, Israel. "Rejoice" is a gentle command: "let them rejoice." The phrase "with his people" shows that there are not two separate groups, but one and the same feast.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where Jews and non-Jews had tensions. To show that the inclusion of the Gentiles was always part of God's plan, he quotes the Scriptures. This line comes from Deuteronomy 32:43, and scholars debate a little about the exact text that Paul follows, but his point is clear: the Gentiles also celebrate what God does.

Today, God calls us to rejoice with people who are different from us, of another culture or background. Try today to welcome someone different in your church and to celebrate with that person what God is doing.
exp.0:10:
Paul says he longs to see the Christians in Rome so that he can share with them some spiritual gift and so strengthen them.

Paul is writing this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. Earlier he told them that he prayed for them and asked God for the opportunity to visit them. He does not speak with pride: in the next verse he makes clear that he also wants to be encouraged by their faith. Scholars understand that "spiritual gift" in different ways, and the text does not say exactly what it was.

For today: do not see your Christian life only as receiving. Seek out someone in your church, pray for that person, and share with them a word of encouragement or a teaching from the Bible. God can strengthen both of you.
exp.14:11:
The explanation says that Isaiah announced that a descendant of Jesse, the father of King David, would come. That descendant will rise to rule over the Gentiles, that is, the nations that were not Jewish, and they will place their hope in him.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews, who had tensions between them. He quotes the Old Testament (Isaiah 11:10) to show that God always planned to include all peoples. Many understand that this descendant of Jesse is Jesus.

Today we can remember that hope in Christ is for everyone, regardless of origin or culture. This week, approach someone different from you with respect and kindness, and pray that Christ may be their hope too.
exp.14:17:
Paul says that he would not dare to speak of anything that Christ has not accomplished through him. He is referring to what Christ achieved in bringing the non-Jewish nations (the "Gentiles") to obey God, both by his words and by his deeds.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that he is a minister of Christ to the Gentiles and that he can boast about what God has done. Here he makes clear that he does not take pride in his own merits, but in the work of Christ through his ministry. The verses that follow mention miracles and the power of the Spirit.

For today: when God uses your life to bless others, give the credit to Christ and not to yourself. Serve with humility, with words and with deeds, and trust that it is He who gives the fruit.
exp.8:18:
Paul imagines someone raising an objection: "If God hardens whomever he wants, why does he still blame people? No one can oppose what he decides." The explanation of the word "resist" is removed, so the sentence about the word "se enoja" and the one about "Resistirá" are both deleted, since those quoted words do not appear in the reader's verse.

Paul is explaining that God is free and sovereign, using the example of Pharaoh. He anticipates the complaint of a reader who feels this is unjust. He does not answer with a theory; instead, in the following verse, he reminds the person who God is and who they are. Christians have understood in different ways how God's sovereignty and human responsibility relate, and the text does not fully resolve it.

For today: when you do not understand God's ways, do not silence your questions, but bring them to him with humility, trusting that his mercy is real and that he is just.
exp.5:10:
It says that believers should consider themselves dead to sin, but alive to God through Jesus Christ. Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that Christ died to sin once and now lives to God. Paul teaches that whoever trusts in Christ is united with him in his death and resurrection. That is why he asks them to see themselves this way, and from there he moves to practical commands: not to let sin rule over them.

For today: when temptation comes, remember who you are in Christ. Before you act, say in prayer: "Lord, sin is no longer my master; today I want to live for you." Then take one concrete step of obedience.
exp.15:21:
