Tertius says that he was the one who wrote the letter, and from there he sends his own greeting to the Christians in Rome. He does this "in the Lord," that is, as a brother in the faith. Old words: the "epistle" means letter, and "I salute you" is "I greet you."

Paul was dictating this letter, and Tertius was the secretary who was writing it down. This was a common practice in that time. For a moment, Tertius takes up the pen to speak in his own voice. We know nothing more about him; some consider him a Christian from Corinth, but that is a reasonable assumption, not a certain fact.

God values quiet service. Tertius did not preach or found churches, but his work helped this message reach us. Any task done with love "in the Lord" has value, even though almost no one notices it.
exp.10:2:
Paul is quoting the complaint of the prophet Elijah. He tells God that they have killed his prophets, that his altars have been torn down, and that he alone is left, and that now they are seeking his life.

Paul writes in a letter to the Romans and answers this question: Did God abandon Israel? He says no, and he offers himself as an example, since he is an Israelite. He recalls that Elijah (1 Kings 19) felt completely alone, but God answered him that he had kept seven thousand faithful people. In this way, Paul shows that God always preserves a remnant.

For today: when you feel alone in your faith or believe that everything is lost, remember that God sees what you cannot see. Speak with Him honestly, as Elijah did, and seek out other believers who will encourage you.
exp.7:16:
It says that if we are children of God, we are also heirs: we will receive what God has prepared, together with Christ. The condition is that we suffer with Christ, so that we may also be glorified with him.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the Spirit makes us adopted children and allows us to call God "Abba, Father." Now he explains that being a child brings an inheritance, but also the path of Christ, who went through suffering before glory. Later he will say that this suffering is not worth comparing with the glory to come.

For today: when you suffer for following Jesus, or for doing what is right, remember that you are not alone or forsaken. You are a beloved child, and your pain is not the end of the story.
exp.15:18:
Paul says that the obedience of the believers in Rome is known to everyone, and this gladdens him. But he wants them to be wise in what is good, that is, to understand and practice what is right, and innocent when it comes to evil, meaning untouched by it and not mixed up in it. Being known is what the word for "known" conveys here; being innocent, free of any cunning or wrongdoing, is the sense of the word "simple" in the verse.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome. Just before, he warned about people who were causing divisions and deceiving the naive with smooth words. For that reason he commends their faithfulness, but encourages them to stay alert so that no one leads them astray. Right after, he promises that the God of peace will crush Satan.

For today: learn to know the Bible well so you can tell what is true from what is false, and guard your heart against harmful curiosities. Be mature in discernment, but sincere and pure in your conduct.
exp.6:9:
It says that God's commandment was given so that people would live, that is, to guide them toward a good and full life. But Paul found that, in his experience, that same commandment ended up leading him to death.

Paul speaks in the first person about the relationship between the law and sin. Interpreters debate whether he is referring to his childhood, his life before Christ, Israel, or a general human experience. What is clear is his point: the law is not bad, but sin takes advantage of it to show its power, as the next verse says.

Today we can recognize that not even the best rules can change our hearts. We need the grace of Christ, not only our own effort.
exp.10:6:
Paul says that Israel, as a people, was earnestly seeking righteousness before God, but did not attain it. Instead, "the election," that is, the group of Israelites whom God chose by grace, did receive it. The phrase "the rest were blinded" means that their hearts closed and they could not recognize Christ. Some understand that God hardened them, and others that God confirmed the hardness they already had.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He asks whether God has abandoned Israel. He answers that he has not: there always remains a faithful remnant, saved by grace and not by works. He then cites the Scriptures to show that this blindness had been seen before.

For today: we cannot earn God's favor through religious effort. Receive his grace with humility, and ask him to keep your heart responsive to his voice.
exp.14:18:
Paul says that the gospel advanced through mighty signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit of God. Because of this, from Jerusalem and its surroundings all the way to Illyricum, he fully preached the gospel of Christ, that is, he proclaimed it completely in that region.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and wants them to know him before he visits them. He does not boast about himself, but about what Christ has done through him. Illyricum was northwest of Greece. We do not know for certain whether he reached it or only its borders.

For today: do your work for God with effort, but depend on the Spirit. When something good comes of it, do not keep the glory for yourself; give it to Christ, who truly gives the fruit.
exp.5:14:
Paul asks a question: if we no longer live under the law but under grace, can we sin without concern? His answer is firm: "God forbid," that is, by no means. To be "under the law" means to depend on keeping rules in order to be accepted; to be "under grace" means to live by God's undeserved favor.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has already explained that God's grace is abundant, and now he anticipates a misunderstanding: thinking that grace is permission to sin. He uses the image of serving a master. Whoever gives himself over to sin serves sin, but whoever obeys God lives in righteousness.

For today: grace is not an excuse but a new freedom. When you feel the temptation to justify something wrong by saying that God will forgive you, remember that his grace was given to you so that you might live for him.
exp.10:0:
Paul asks a question: Has God rejected his people, Israel? He answers with firm conviction: "God forbid," which means "by no means." As proof, he gives himself as an example: he is an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham and of the tribe of Benjamin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. In the earlier chapters he explained that many of Israel did not believe in Jesus. Now he makes clear that this does not mean God has abandoned his promise. Paul himself, once an opponent of the church, is a sign of God's faithfulness. He then mentions Elijah, who also thought he was alone.

For today: when you see someone far from God, or you feel far away yourself, remember that God is faithful and does not give up easily. Keep praying with hope.
exp.1:8:
It says there will be suffering and distress for every human being who practices evil. Its wording describes "tribulation" as a strong pain, and "anguish" as a grief that squeezes the soul. This applies first to the Jew, and also to the Greek, that is, to the one who is not Jewish. The word for "first" indicates that the Jews, having received the law, were the first to be judged, but not the only ones.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God judges with justice, without favoritism. The Jews could not feel safe simply because they were Jewish. The following verse sums it up: "there is no respect of persons with God," that is, God does not treat anyone with preference.

For today: let us not trust in our religion, family, or reputation as if they would protect us. Let us ask God to examine our heart and help us do good with humility.
exp.0:12:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome something he wants them to know: many times he planned to visit them, but something has kept him from coming until now. He wanted to have some fruit among them, meaning to see spiritual results in their lives, just as among the other non-Jewish peoples. "Gentiles" are those who are not Jews.

Paul writes this letter to a church he did not yet know in person. He makes clear that his absence is not a lack of interest. Although he does not say here what held him back, in Romans 15:22 he mentions that his work in other places kept him from coming.

For today: when you cannot be with someone you love, do not let them slip from your mind. Write to them, pray for that person, and look for them as soon as you can. And if your plans are delayed, trust that God is still guiding your path.
exp.3:1:
Paul says that if Abraham had been declared righteous by his works, he would have reason to feel proud. But before God he has nothing to boast about. To be declared righteous means to be accepted by God. To boast means to show pride in something.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs God's grace. Abraham was the great example for the Jews, so Paul asks what he found. Right away he answers from Scripture: Abraham believed God, and that was credited to him as righteousness.

Today we can remember that we do not win God's favor by our merits. If you feel inadequate today, trust in what God offers. If you feel superior, give thanks, because everything is his gift.
exp.3:9:
Paul asks a question and answers it right away. He wants to know when God counted Abraham's faith as righteousness: was it when Abraham was already circumcised, or when he was still uncircumcised? The answer is clear: it was before the circumcision.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. He explains that God declares a person righteous through faith, not through rituals. According to Genesis 15, Abraham believed long before he was circumcised (Genesis 17). So Abraham is an example for everyone who believes.

For today: you do not need to earn God's favor through rites, merits, or a good record. Trust in Jesus just as you are, and let that faith show in the way you live.
exp.6:11:
The explanation says that God's law, given through Moses, is holy, and that each commandment is also holy, just, and good. "Truly" means "certainly." "Commandment" refers to what God orders in his law.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking. He has just said that sin used the law to deceive him and lead him to death. So that no one thinks the law is bad, he makes clear that the problem is not in the law but in sin. The law shows what God wants and exposes our need for help.

For today: when one of God's commands costs you something or makes you uncomfortable, do not see it as an enemy. Recognize that it is good and that the fault lies in our heart. Ask God for his grace and his Spirit so that you can obey it with confidence.
exp.12:13:
We are told to clothe ourselves with Jesus Christ, that is, to live as he lived, and not to indulge the sinful desires of our human nature. The phrase "make not provision" means "do not give it attention" or "do not give it room." Here "the flesh" does not mean the body, but our tendency toward self-centeredness and sin.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Just before this, he speaks of the night being nearly over and the day arriving, and he urges them to put aside the works of darkness: drunkenness, debauchery, quarreling, and envy. This verse closes that appeal with an image: changing clothes, leaving the old behind and putting on Christ.

For today: when temptation comes, do not simply try to resist by your own strength. Ask yourself how Jesus would act in that situation, and decide to respond in that way. Begin the day by asking him to guide you, and avoid the places or habits that feed what you want to leave behind.
exp.8:12:
God says, as written in the Bible, that he loved Jacob and hated Esau. The word "hated" sounds very harsh. In biblical language it can mean "loved less" or "did not choose," as seen in Luke 14:26.

Paul speaks to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews, and explains why many from Israel did not accept Jesus. He quotes Malachi 1:2-3 and Genesis 25:23. His point is that God chose Jacob before the twins were born, without depending on their works. Christians understand in different ways how this choosing relates to human freedom, but Paul stresses that God acts with mercy.

Today we can receive salvation with humility, without boasting of our own merits. If God called us by his grace, let us live thankfully and treat others with that same mercy.
exp.10:4:
It says that, just as in the time of Elijah God kept a faithful group, so also now, in Paul's time, there remains a remnant of Israelites who believe in Christ. The word "remnant" means a small leftover group. "Election of grace" means that God chose them out of his undeserved favor, not because of their merits.

In his letter to the Romans, Paul asks whether God has rejected his people Israel. He answers that he has not: he himself, an Israelite, is proof of this. He recalls Elijah, who felt alone, yet God had seven thousand faithful people. The following verses stress that this comes by grace and not by works.

For today: if you feel alone in your faith, remember that God knows who belongs to him and works more than you can see. And rest in the fact that your relationship with him is sustained by his grace, not by your performance.
exp.4:20:
Here is how the explanation reads. It says that sin functioned like a king who ruled over humanity and led it toward death. But now grace, that is, God's undeserved favor, is the one that rules. It does this through righteousness, that is, by giving people a right standing before God, and its goal is eternal life. Everything happens through Jesus Christ, who is called Lord.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is comparing Adam, whose disobedience brought sin and death, with Christ, whose obedience brings righteousness and life. He closes this section by saying that grace has the final word.

For today: if you feel trapped by your failures or your past, remember that you no longer have to live under the rule of sin. Today you can ask Christ for help and trust that his grace is stronger than your weakness.
exp.3:10:
He says that Abraham received circumcision as a sign and a seal. That is, it was a mark that confirmed something already in place: the faith by which God had declared him righteous while he was still uncircumcised. In this way Abraham became the father of all who believe without being circumcised, so that God would also count their faith to them for righteousness. "Counting as righteousness" means that God regards them as righteous before him.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He wants to show that no one is saved by rituals or by keeping the law, but by faith. He uses Abraham, so respected by the Jews, as proof: God accepted him because he believed, before any ritual.

For today: do not trust in your rituals, your family history, or your good works to be right with God. Trust in him as Abraham did, and let your practices express that faith, not replace it.
exp.6:6:
Paul asks whether God's law is evil, and he answers firmly: "Certainly not!" He says that he would not have known what sin is if the law had not shown it to him. The explanation of "lust" as an unruly desire and "covet" as eagerly wanting what does not belong to us would be rewritten as: the law's words "you shall not covet" revealed the hidden desire in his heart.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we are no longer under the law as a way to become righteous, and someone might think that the law is therefore guilty of sin. Paul makes clear that the law is good; it only exposes the problem. Interpreters debate whether the "I" speaks of his past, of all humanity, or of Israel, but they all agree on the central teaching.

For today: when God's Word makes you uncomfortable, do not blame it. Use it as a mirror, confess what you see, and ask Christ for help to change.
exp.12:11:
This verse uses the image of night and day. The night is life without God, and the day is the new life that is drawing near with Christ. That is why Paul says we should cast off, or set aside, the works of darkness, meaning bad habits. Instead, we should put on the armor of light, that is, live with clean and steady conduct.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that love fulfills the law, and now he calls them to wake up from spiritual sleep. The salvation that is nearer is complete salvation, which will come when Christ returns. Interpreters debate how to understand that timing, but the call to live with urgency is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves which habit lulls us spiritually to sleep. This week, let us set aside one of them and practice something concrete of light: an act of love, honesty, or service.
exp.8:29:
What shall we say then? Paul asks what conclusion we draw from all this. He answers that the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, received it, and it is the righteousness that comes through faith. "Pursuing righteousness" means striving to be accepted before God; "that is" introduces the explanation that follows. "Gentiles" are those who were not part of the people of Israel.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where Jewish believers and non-Jewish believers lived side by side. He has been speaking about the faithfulness of God and about how not all of Israel responded to his promise, although a remnant always remained. Now he shows something surprising: people outside the law received righteousness by trusting in Christ, while many who sought it through works stumbled.

For today: we do not need to earn God's favor through effort or a good record. Trust in Christ, receive his forgiveness, and let that gratitude move your obedience.
exp.6:24:
Paul gives thanks to God through Jesus Christ, who answers his question about who will deliver him. Then he sums up his struggle: with the mind (his way of thinking and his deepest desire) he serves the law of God, but with the flesh, that is, his weak nature inclined to evil, he follows the law of sin.

Paul speaks in the first person and expresses great distress over the inner struggle between the good he wants and the sin that drags him down. Scholars disagree about whether he is describing his life before he knew Christ, his life as a believer, or a general experience. What is clear is that deliverance comes through Jesus.

Today, when you feel defeated by your own failures, do not stay stuck in guilt. Come before God honestly, give thanks for Jesus, and ask him for help with the next step.
exp.15:26:
Paul closes his letter with a note of praise: all the glory belongs to the only wise God, and it is given to him through Jesus Christ, forever. "Amen" means "so be it."

The closing note says the letter was written in Corinth and carried to Rome by Phoebe, a servant (deaconess) of the church at Cenchrea.

Paul speaks at the end of his longest and deepest letter, where he explains the gospel: salvation through faith in Christ for both Jews and non-Jews. That closing note is not found in the oldest manuscripts, and many scholars believe a later copyist added it, although what it says agrees with what Paul mentions about Phoebe in chapter 16.

Today we can end our days, our prayers, and our accomplishments by giving the glory to God and not to ourselves. Before going to sleep, try to thank him for one specific thing and say to him: "To you be the glory."
exp.13:9:
What the passage says: Paul asks two direct questions. "Judging" here means criticizing and condemning one's brother; "setting at nought" means looking down on him as inferior or worthless. Then he gives the reason: we will all stand before the judgment seat of Christ, that is, before his judgment.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements about food and special days (Romans 14:1-9). Some criticized those who were more strict, and others looked down on those who had more scruples. Paul reminds them that all belong to the Lord, and that only he is the Judge. The next verse says that each one will give an account to God for himself.

For today: When you feel the urge to criticize or look down on another believer for how they live out their faith in secondary matters, stop. Pray for that person and remember that you too will give an account to God. Focus on living sincerely before the Lord yourself.
exp.13:0:
He says we should welcome with kindness the one who is "weak in the faith," that is, someone whose faith is still fragile or who has doubts. "Receive ye" means to take in, to give a warm welcome. And he adds that we should not do it "but not to doubtful disputations," meaning not to start arguments about their opinions or uncertain thoughts.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. In that church there were believers who thought differently about what to eat and which days to observe. The verses that follow show that some ate everything and others only vegetables. Paul asks that no one despise or judge the other in these secondary matters. Scholars debate the exact details of the conflict, but the counsel is clear.

Today, if someone in your church is new or unsure in their faith, approach them with patience and kindness. Listen, respond with tenderness, and do not correct them over every small difference.
exp.7:26:
This verse says that God, who knows the deepest part of our heart, understands what the Holy Spirit means when he prays for us. "Searcheth" means to examine carefully. "Mind" means thought or desire. "Maketh intercession" here means asks or pleads on behalf of others. The Spirit pleads for believers ("the saints") according to what God wills.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we suffer and wait with patience, and that often we do not know how to pray. Then he encourages them: the Spirit helps us in our weakness. Some think the "groanings which cannot be uttered" are prayers without words; others think they are a deep cry of the Spirit within us.

When you are so tired or confused that you do not know what to ask for, do not be anxious. Pray sincerely, even with few words, and trust that God understands you and that the Spirit intercedes for you.
exp.13:12:
Paul says that we should no longer judge one another. Instead, we should firmly decide not to put a stumbling block or an occasion to fall in our brother's way. A stumbling block is something that makes another person fall; an occasion to fall is a trap that leads him to sin or to lose his faith.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different views about foods and special days. Earlier he reminded them that all of us will give account to God, so it is not our place to be judges of others. Then he explains that, although the food itself is not wrong, it can harm someone whose conscience has doubts.

For today: before criticizing someone for a questionable practice, ask yourself how you can care for his faith. Sometimes love means giving up something that seems permissible to you, so as not to wound a brother.
exp.12:1:
This verse says that whoever opposes the authority is, in fact, resisting what God has established, and that such people bring punishment upon themselves.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, who lived under the power of the Roman Empire. He teaches them that the order and justice of rulers serve the good of society. The verses that follow explain that authority should punish evil. This text does not say that every ruler is just; other passages in the Bible show believers who obeyed God rather than unjust orders (Acts 5:29).

Today we can respect the laws and those in authority, pay what is owed, and pray for them, without ceasing to obey God in conscience.
exp.3:16:
Paul quotes the promise God made to Abraham: he would become "father of many nations." That promise holds good before God, the one in whom Abraham believed. Paul describes God as the one who gives life to the dead and who "calls those things which be not as though they were": he speaks of what does not yet exist as if it already existed, because his word is certain to be fulfilled.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that Abraham is the father of all who believe, whether they are Jews or not, because the promise is received through faith and by grace, not by keeping the law. Abraham and Sarah were already very old, and even so he trusted in God.

Today, when something seems impossible or without a way out, we can keep trusting that God keeps what he promises, even when we cannot yet see it. Praying and waiting in faith is a good first step.
exp.1:27:
This verse says that being a true Jew does not depend on what can be seen on the outside. Circumcision, the physical sign on the body, is not the most important thing either.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. He shows them that both Jews and non-Jews need God. Some Jews trusted in their heritage and their rituals, but they did not obey God. Paul tells them that what counts is the heart, as the next verse explains.

For today: let us not confuse faith with outward appearances, such as going to church, using certain language, or belonging to a tradition. Let us ask God to transform our hearts, so that our lives are sincere before Him.
exp.6:22:
Paul says that inside him there are two forces in conflict. One is the desire to obey God, which lives in his mind and spirit. The other is a "law," that is, a power or principle that works in his body and pushes him toward sin. "Members" refers to his physical being. "Captivity" means being held prisoner, someone carried off by force.

Paul writes to believers in Rome and speaks in the first person about the struggle with sin. Scholars disagree: some believe he describes his life before he knew Christ, others that he describes the struggle of every believer. What follows, "I thank God through Jesus Christ," shows that salvation comes from Christ and not from one's own effort.

If you feel that you want to do good and sometimes fail, you are not alone. Recognize your weakness honestly and turn to Jesus, asking for his help every day.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that the law of Moses could not save us, because our human nature, called here "the flesh," was weak and unable to keep it. So God sent his Son in a body like sinful flesh, that is, with a real human body like ours, but without sin. And "for sin" means "to deal with sin." Thus God condemned sin in the flesh: he pronounced judgment against sin in the person of Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ. Now he explains why: what the law could not accomplish, God himself did through Jesus. Scholars understand the word "flesh" here in different ways, but in general it refers to human weakness apart from God.

For today: when you fail and feel guilty, do not try to earn forgiveness by your own efforts. Remember that Christ has already borne the condemnation, and ask him for his Spirit to live in a new way.
exp.2:21:
This verse says that God gives us his righteousness, meaning he accepts us as righteous before him, and that this comes through faith in Jesus Christ. It is for all who believe, no matter who they are. The phrase "there is no difference" means that no one has an advantage before God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that no one becomes righteous by keeping the law; the law only shows us our sin. Now he presents the good news: God offers another way, already announced in the law and the prophets. Jews and non-Jews alike need the same thing: all have sinned, and all are forgiven freely by his grace.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love or compare yourself with others. Trust in Jesus and rest in his forgiveness. And treat others with humility, because we all receive the same grace.
exp.3:2:
Paul asks what the Scripture says and answers by quoting Genesis 15:6: Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness. "Counted" means put to his account, recognized. Abraham did not earn that standing through effort; God declared him righteous because he trusted God's promise.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, among both Jews and non-Jews. He is explaining that no one is saved by their works. He puts Abraham, highly respected by the Jews, forward as an example. If Abraham could have boasted in his works, he would have, but before God he had nothing to glory in. What counts is his faith.

For today: do not try to earn God's love or acceptance through good behavior. Trust in Him and in what He has done for you in Christ. From that trust, good works flow as gratitude, not as payment.
exp.1:20:
He says that whoever teaches others must also teach themselves. Paul asks pointedly: if you preach that one should not steal, do you steal? The words for "steal" that appear in the original wording mean to take what belongs to someone else, which is the same act as stealing in the verse you read. The phrase "teachest another" is the same as "teachest another" in your verse, with its older form of spelling.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Here he speaks to a Jew who trusted in knowing God's law and saw himself as a guide to others. Paul does not deny that the law is good, but he shows that knowing it is not enough. It must be lived. With this he prepares his teaching that all of us, Jews and non-Jews alike, need the grace of God.

For today: before you correct or advise someone, examine your own life. Ask God to show you the areas where you still do not live what you say you believe, and take one concrete step of change today.
exp.6:16:
Paul says that when he does the wrong he does not want to do, it is not really his deepest desire that is acting, but the sin that lives inside him. "Doing" means "doing," and "dwells" means "lives in" or "stays in." He is not looking for excuses: he is describing an inner struggle.

Paul speaks in the first person about his fight with sin, and scholars debate whether he is describing his life before he knew Christ or his struggle as a believer. His central point is that God's law is good, because it shows him what is wrong. The problem is not the law, but the sin that dwells in weak human nature.

When you fall into something you do not want to do, do not sink into despair. Acknowledge your failure honestly, take responsibility for it, and turn to God, asking for his help and forgiveness. He sustains you in the struggle.
exp.12:2:
Paul says that rulers, here called "rulers" and "power," are usually not a terror to someone who does good, but to someone who does evil. If you want to live without fear of authority, do what is good, and you will receive its approval. The word "praise" here means recognition or approval.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city where the Roman Empire ruled. Earlier he has said that all authority exists under God's permission. Here he describes what government should do: promote order and restrain evil. It is a general description; Paul does not say that every ruler is just, and Christians understand this passage in different ways.

For today: try to live honestly in everyday life, such as paying what you owe and keeping just laws. In this way your good witness speaks for you.
exp.14:13:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome that he is sure they are full of goodness and knowledge. For that reason they are able to admonish one another, that is, to advise and correct one another with kindness.

Paul writes this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. After giving several instructions, he softens his tone and acknowledges the good that is among them. In the verses that follow he explains that he was direct in some parts because God entrusted him with serving the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jewish peoples.

For today: when you have to correct someone, begin by recognizing the good that God has already done in that person. A word spoken with respect and trust is received better, and it helps us grow together in faith.
exp.10:23:
Paul uses the picture of an olive tree. You, who were not Jewish, were like a branch of a wild olive tree, cut off from its natural tree and grafted into a good olive tree, which goes against what is normal. So if God could do that with you, how much more can He graft the Jews, who are the original branches, back into their own olive tree?

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, many of them of non-Jewish origin. He wants them not to feel superior to Israel, which had largely rejected Christ. He reminds them that they are grafted in by God's kindness, not by their own merit.

For today: let us live with humility and gratitude. Everything we have in God is grace, so let us not despise anyone or give up on any person.
exp.11:8:
What it says: Paul says that love must be sincere, without masks or pretense. "Without hypocrisy" is what it means. Someone who truly loves rejects evil and holds firmly to what is good. Here, "hold fast" is understood as joining firmly, clinging, staying close to what is good.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the gifts God gives to each person, such as serving, teaching, encouraging, and giving. Now he shows that all these gifts must operate with genuine love. Then he gives concrete examples: affection among brothers and sisters, mutual respect, diligence, and service to the Lord.

For today: This week, check whether any of your displays of affection are merely courtesy or appearance. Do an act of kindness without seeking recognition, and honestly step away from something bad that attracts you.
exp.10:34:
It says that no one has given something to God beforehand, so that God would be in debt and have to repay it. The verse uses the word "first," so the phrase "given to him first" is what the explanation is pointing to. The question expects the answer "no one": there is no one who can make God a debtor.

The apostle Paul writes this as he closes his long explanation of God's mercy toward Jews and non-Jews (Romans 9–11). With wonder, he praises God's wisdom and quotes ideas from the Old Testament, probably from Job 41:11 and Isaiah 40:13. His point is that salvation springs from God's grace, not from human merit.

For today: serve God without feeling that in this way you are paying him back or that he owes you anything. Everything you have, including your ability to give, comes from him. That frees us from pride and fear, and leads us to gratitude.
exp.14:30:
Paul asks the Romans to pray that God will deliver him from the unbelievers in Judea, that is, from those who did not believe and opposed him. He also asks that the gift he is bringing to Jerusalem will be well received. The "saints" are the believers.

Paul writes from Corinth, near the end of his third journey, before going to Jerusalem. He is carrying financial help that the churches of Macedonia and Achaia gathered for the poor believers there. He knows he is in danger, and he is also concerned that some Jewish believers may distrust him and not welcome the offering from non-Jewish churches. That is why he asks for prayer.

For today: do not face the hard things alone. Ask others to pray for you, and pray for them. Also, pray that your service will be done with humility and become a blessing.
exp.13:8:
Here is what it says: Christ died and came back to life with a clear purpose: to be Lord over everyone, both those who have already died and those who are still living.

Context: Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where some were judging one another over differences about food and special days. Just before this verse he says that we belong to the Lord, in life and in death. Here he gives the reason: Christ paid that price and has authority over all. So judging a brother or sister means taking a place that belongs only to Christ.

For today: When you find it hard to accept a fellow believer who thinks differently on secondary matters, remember that he also belongs to Christ. Before you criticize him, pray for him and treat him with respect, leaving the judgment in the Lord's hands.
exp.6:4:
He says that when we lived "in the flesh," that is, ruled by our old nature, sinful passions were stirred up through the law. Those passions acted in our members, that is, in our body and conduct. The phrase "bring forth fruit unto death" means that what we produced ended in separation from God and destruction.

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He has just used the example of marriage: death releases a person from the law, and so the believer, united to Christ, is free to bear fruit for God. Here he contrasts their past life with the new one.

For today: let us not trust in our own effort or in rules to make us good. Let us ask the Spirit to guide us, and remember that our life belongs to Christ.
exp.14:28:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome that he is sure of something: when he finally visits them, he will not arrive empty-handed. He will come full of the blessing of the gospel of Christ. The phrase "I shall come in the fulness" means that he will come with great spiritual riches.

Paul writes this letter from the end of his ministry in the East. Before he goes on to Rome and then to Spain, he must take a gift from the churches of Macedonia and Achaia to the poor of Jerusalem. He knows the road has dangers, but he trusts that God will be with him. Scholars debate whether he had in mind a blessing to give, a blessing to receive, or both.

For today: when you serve others, do not focus on what you lack. Go with confidence that Christ has given you something good to share.
exp.7:12:
This verse says there are two paths. If someone lives according to the flesh, that is, letting their desires and sinful nature rule them, they end in death. But if, with the help of the Spirit, they put to death the deeds of the body, they will live. Putting to death here means making sin lose its power over a person. The phrases about dying and living are commonly understood as separation from God versus full life with Him.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that the Spirit who raised Jesus lives in believers. That is why he says we owe nothing to the flesh. He will then show that those led by the Spirit are children of God.

For today: do not fight a bad habit alone. Ask the Spirit to strengthen you, and take concrete steps, such as staying away from what makes you fall and seeking brothers and sisters who can pray with you.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that God has no favorites. "Showing partiality" is an older expression that means treating someone better or worse because of their background, their position, or their appearance, rather than because of who they really are. God judges with complete impartiality.

The one speaking is Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome, where there were both Jews and non-Jews. Some Jews thought that, because they had the law of Moses, they were in a better position before God. Paul answers that God judges everyone by the same standard, both the Jew and the Greek (that is, the non-Jew). What counts is how each person lives before Him.

Today we can examine whether we treat others according to their nationality, their money, their church, or their culture. If God does not make distinctions like these, neither should we. Let us approach everyone with respect, with humility, and with the same love.
exp.1:24:
It says that circumcision does have value, but only if the person keeps God's law. If someone breaks the law, it is as though they were not circumcised. The explanation notes that "profiteth" means it is of benefit or useful, and that "breaker of the law" here means a transgressor, someone who violates the law.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, and at this point he is speaking to a Jew who boasts of having the law. Paul does not look down on circumcision, which was the sign of the covenant. What he corrects is the idea that an outward sign is enough, even when a person's life contradicts what they claim to believe.

Today we can think about our own outward signs: attending church, owning a Bible, or calling ourselves Christians. All of that is good, but it does not replace a life that obeys God. Let us ask him that our conduct match what we profess.
exp.4:15:
Paul says that God's gift does not work the same way as Adam's sin. One sin brought judgment and condemnation. But grace came after many offences, not just one, and it ended in justification, that is, in God declaring righteous the one who believes. "Gift" means a free present, and "offence" is a wrong or a transgression.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and comparing Adam with Christ. Adam is a pattern or model of Christ, because one man affected many. Paul wants to show that the work of Jesus is far more powerful than the damage caused by sin.

For today: if you carry guilt for your accumulated mistakes, remember that God's grace is not used up by the number of your failures. Confess your sin honestly and rest in Christ, who offers you forgiveness as a gift, not as a payment.
exp.10:22:
It says that the Israelites who were "cut off" because of unbelief can be grafted back in, that is, put back into the olive tree, if they stop persisting in their unbelief. The reason is that God has the power to do it. The word "graffed" in the verse is an older form of the word for grafting.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, among them believers of non-Jewish origin. He uses the image of an olive tree with branches cut off and a wild olive branch grafted in. He wants the non-Jewish believers not to feel superior to Israel. How and when this restoration will happen is interpreted differently by Christians.

Today, do not look with pride or with contempt on someone who does not yet believe. God can change any heart, and our attitude should be one of humility, gratitude, and prayer for those who are far away.
exp.11:6:
This verse says that each person should devote themselves faithfully to the gift God has given them. Whoever has the gift of serving others in practical tasks, let them give themselves to serving. Whoever has the gift of teaching, let them give themselves to teaching. The word "teaching" here refers to the teaching of the truth.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the church is a body with many members, and that each one has different gifts, given by the grace of God. Paul wants to prevent pride and envy, and to encourage everyone to help one another.

For today: do not compare yourself with others. Ask God in prayer how you can serve your church, and do it with steadiness and humility, knowing that your contribution is needed.
exp.14:12:
This verse is a prayer from Paul. He asks that God, who is the source of hope, fill believers with joy and peace as they trust in him. The result is that their hope will grow and overflow, and this happens through the power of the Holy Spirit. Here "power" is the meaning of the word that the verse renders as "power."

Paul writes to the church in Rome, made up of both Jewish and non-Jewish believers. He has just quoted the Scriptures to show that God always intended to include the Gentiles, that is, the peoples who were not Jewish. With this prayer he closes his teaching about living in unity and accepting one another, and hope in Christ is what unites them.

When you feel anxious or discouraged, pray with this verse. Ask God for joy and peace, and trust that he can give you hope through his Spirit.
exp.1:21:
Paul asks the one who thinks himself very religious: if you teach that no one should commit adultery, do you commit it yourself? If you say you hate idols, do you rob temples? This word, "rob temples," means taking or defiling what belongs to God or to his temple. There are several ways to understand the exact detail of this accusation, but the central point is clear: the conduct does not match what is taught.

Paul is writing to the church in Rome. Here he speaks to a Jewish teacher who trusted that he knew the law. His aim is to show that knowing the law is not enough, because everyone needs the grace of God. As the next verse says, this inconsistency was causing others to speak badly of God.

Today: before correcting others, examine your own life. Ask God to make what you say you believe match what you do, because your example can draw others closer to him or push them away.
exp.5:20:
Paul asks a question so that believers will think: what real benefit did they get from the life they lived before? Today they feel ashamed of those things, and the end of that path is death. "Fruit" means result or gain. "Ashamed" means they feel embarrassed to remember it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that, by believing in Christ, they stopped being slaves to sin and now serve God. He uses the image of slavery, and he says he does so "because of the weakness of your flesh," that is, so that they can understand it better. He invites them to compare their past life with the new one.

For today: when something from the past tempts you to go back, remember where it led and what it left behind. Then ask God for strength to live in his grace, where true life is found.
exp.9:20:
God says that all day long, that is, constantly and patiently, he stretched out his hands toward Israel. Stretching out the hands is a gesture of invitation and pleading, like someone calling another person to come back. But that people was disobedient (they did not want to obey) and gainsaying (they argued against him and answered back in opposition).

Paul quotes here from Isaiah 65:2. He has just explained that the gospel also reached non-Jews, something Moses and Isaiah had already announced. With this verse, Paul shows that most of Israel did not reject the message for lack of opportunity, but out of resistance. Even so, the image reveals the heart of God: he still keeps his arms open.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are answering God's invitation or arguing with it. Today is a good day to set aside pride, listen to his voice, and draw near to him with simplicity.
exp.3:18:
It says that Abraham did not grow weak in his trust in God. He looked honestly at his situation: his body was already dead in the sense of having no strength to have children, since he was almost a hundred years old, and Sarah's womb was also unable to bear. Even so, his faith did not go out. The word for "grew weak" means "became feeble."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that God makes a person righteous through faith, not through works. He uses Abraham as an example: he believed God's promise to give him a son, even though it seemed humanly impossible (Genesis 15 and 17).

For today: faith does not mean denying problems, but looking at them honestly and trusting God's promise more than what seems impossible. Today you can bring your difficult situation to God and decide to believe that He is faithful.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the one who has died is freed from the debt and the power of sin. The word "freed" here means being released from sin's claim. The verse's own wording, "he that is dead," is the same as saying "has died."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that when we are joined to Christ, our old way of living was crucified with him. Some were thinking that, since God forgives, they could go on sinning. Paul answers that the one who is united with Christ in his death no longer has to live as a slave to sin. Interpreters explain in different ways how this is lived out in practice, but they all agree that it is real freedom.

For today: when an old temptation comes, remember that you are no longer its slave. Say to God, "Your power has set me free," and take one concrete step to say no.
exp.5:19:
It says that when believers lived under the rule of sin, they had no relationship with righteousness. That is, they were free from it: it did not govern them, and they did not pursue it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the image of slavery, something very familiar in his time, to explain that no one lives without a master. He says he speaks in human terms so that they can understand him better. He reminds them that they once served sin, and now, through the work of Christ, they serve righteousness.

For today: ask yourself whom you are obeying in your daily habits. A freedom without God is often just another form of slavery. Today you can give God one concrete decision, such as your words or your time, and ask him for help to live in righteousness.
exp.14:2:
He says that Christ did not seek to please himself or take the easy path. Instead, he bore the rejection and insults that others hurled against God. The word translated as "reproaches" refers to insults or mockery, and "pleased not himself" means he did not seek his own comfort. The quotation comes from Psalm 69:9.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were tensions between believers from a Jewish background and those from a non-Jewish background, especially over matters of conscience such as food and special days. Paul asks the strong to be patient with the weak, that is, those whose faith or conscience is more sensitive. He sets Christ before them as an example of love that gives itself up.

Today, when someone thinks differently or grows more slowly in faith, do not despise or pressure them. Help them with patience, and ask yourself: "What would help build them up?"
exp.15:19:
It says that the God who gives peace will soon crush Satan under the feet of the believers in Rome. "Crush" means to destroy or grind down, and "soon" means quickly. Then Paul wishes them the grace, or undeserved favor, of Jesus Christ to be with them.

Paul writes to the church in Rome. He has just warned them against people who cause divisions and deceive the simple with smooth words. He asks them to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil. His promise recalls Genesis 3:15. Scholars discuss when and how it is fulfilled: whether in the history of the church, or fully at the end.

Today, facing deception and division, we are not alone. We can stand firm in the truth, pursue peace, and trust that God holds the final victory, relying on his grace each day.
exp.3:3:
The explanation says that when someone works, their pay is not given as a gift but as something owed to them. The sentences that explain the old-fashioned wording of the verse are removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that no one is declared righteous before God because of their efforts. He uses Abraham as an example: God counted him as righteous because he believed. With the image of wages, Paul shows that if salvation were earned through works, God would owe it to us. But it is received through faith, as a gift.

For today: do not try to win God's love through your good behavior. Do good as a grateful response to his gift, not as a payment so that God will accept you. Rest in his grace.
exp.13:5:
This verse says that the person who gives special importance to a certain day does so with the aim of honoring the Lord, and the person who does not observe it also acts before Him. The same goes for food: the one who eats gives thanks to God, and the one who abstains also gives thanks to God. To "regard the day" means to give a certain day special value.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were believers who held different views about holy days and foods. Many interpret that the differences were between believers of Jewish background and those of non-Jewish background, although the text does not give all the details. Paul asks that they not judge one another in matters where each acts with sincerity before God.

For today: when faced with differences in customs between fellow believers, on matters the Bible does not clearly command, ask yourself whether the other person is seeking to honor God. If so, replace criticism with respect and gratitude.
exp.2:1:
Paul answers that the Jews have an advantage "in every way," that is, in many respects. The first is that God entrusted them with "his words," his declarations or messages, which we today call the Scriptures of the Old Testament. Being given this trust means they were charged with guarding it with responsibility.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that being Jewish and being circumcised does not spare anyone from God's judgment if they do not live in obedience. Then he imagines an objection: is there no use at all in being Jewish? He answers that there is, because they received God's revelation. But receiving it is not the same as obeying it.

For today: if we have a Bible, we have a great privilege and also a responsibility. Having it at home is not enough; it is good to read it, believe it, and put it into practice with humility.
exp.7:3:
What it says: God sent his Son so that what the law required as righteous would be fulfilled in us. This is for those who do not live according to the flesh, that is, guided by their impulses and selfish desires, but according to the Spirit, guided by the Spirit of God. Since the verse reads "the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us," the phrase means that God's just requirement is carried out in those who live this way.

Context: Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that the law could not save because human weakness stood in the way, but Christ condemned sin and set us free. Next, Paul contrasts two ways of living: that of the flesh, which leads to death, and that of the Spirit, which gives life and peace.

For today: We need not struggle only with our own strength. Each morning, ask the Spirit to guide your decisions, words and reactions, and trust that Christ has already given you a new life.
exp.6:7:
The explanation says that sin took advantage of God's commandment to stir up in Paul all kinds of evil desires. "Covetousness" means disordered desire, such as greed. "Taking occasion" means that sin seized an opportunity. And "without the law sin was dead" means that, without the commandment, sin lay as if asleep, not showing its strength.

The apostle Paul is the one speaking. He explains that God's law is good, but that it cannot save, because sin uses it to expose and provoke our rebellion. Scholars debate whether the "I" is Paul himself, Israel, or human experience in general; perhaps it includes all of these.

For today: God's law shows us our need, not our solution. When a command awakens in us the desire to do the opposite, let us remember that we need the grace of Christ and the help of the Spirit, not just more of our own effort.
exp.5:21:
Paul says that now believers are no longer under the power of sin, but serve God. From that service comes a fruit: sanctification, which means being set apart for God and growing in a clean life that resembles Christ. At the end of this path is eternal life.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is comparing two ways of life: serving sin, which leaves shame and ends in death, or serving God, which bears good fruit and life. He wants to encourage them to live according to the freedom Christ gave them, without using it as an excuse to sin.

For today: each day we can ask ourselves whom we are serving with our decisions. Ask God for help to leave a habit that harms you and practice one that brings you closer to Him, trusting that His grace sustains you.
exp.10:16:
It says that some of the branches of the olive tree were broken off, and that you, being a wild olive tree (an uncultivated, wild olive), were grafted in among them in their place. In this way you came to share in the root and in the rich sap and abundance of the good olive tree.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were both Jewish believers and believers from the nations. The broken branches represent the Israelites who did not believe; the wild olive represents the believers from the nations. Paul wants to keep the non-Jewish believers from thinking they are superior. Interpreters debate some details of the image, but the emphasis is clear: the blessing comes from the root, which is God's promise to Israel.

For today: remember that your faith is a gift, not something you earned. Treat others with humility and gratitude, and pray for those who do not yet believe.
exp.10:1:
Paul affirms that God has not rejected his people, Israel, whom he chose and knew beforehand. Then he asks whether they do not know what the Scripture says about Elias. "Cast away" means rejected or set aside. "Foreknew" speaks of a relationship chosen in advance. "Saith" introduces what Elias said to God when he complained about Israel.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, made up of Jews and non-Jews. He asks whether God abandoned Israel, because many Jews had not believed in Jesus. He himself is proof that this is not so: he is an Israelite and a believer. He recalls the time of Elijah, when the prophet felt alone and thought everyone had turned away (1 Kings 19). God showed him that he still had a faithful remnant.

For today: when you feel alone in your faith or see everything falling apart, remember that God is faithful to his promises and keeps working, even where you cannot see it.
exp.7:4:
This verse says there are two ways of living, and that what occupies our minds shows which one we follow. "Living according to the flesh" means being guided by the desires and thoughts of human nature apart from God. Being "set on" something means giving one's attention and interests to it. Those who live according to the Spirit set their attention on the things of God.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God sent his Son to overcome sin, because the law did not have the power to change the heart. Now he shows the difference between the one who follows his own nature and the one who follows the Spirit. The verses that follow say the first leads to death and the second to life and peace.

For today: think about what you occupy your mind with most during the day. Today, set aside a few minutes to read the Bible or pray, and ask the Spirit to direct your thoughts.
exp.8:0:
Paul says that what he is about to say is entirely true. He affirms it "in Christ," that is, as someone who lives united with Him. He says "I lie not," and adds that his conscience, guided by the Holy Spirit, confirms that he speaks with sincerity. His conscience backs him up as a witness that stands beside him.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans. After celebrating God's love at the end of chapter 8, he begins a new theme: his deep sorrow for his fellow Israelites. The verses that follow say he suffers greatly for them. Paul stresses that he is not exaggerating, because he wants to be believed.

For today: when you speak about something that hurts you, do it with sincerity and without manipulation. Ask the Holy Spirit to form your conscience, so that your words and your love for others are genuine.
exp.7:35:
Those who follow Christ, it says, live constantly exposed to death. "For thy sake" means for God's sake. "We are killed all the day long" means we face the danger of death continually. "Sheep for the slaughter" are sheep destined to be sacrificed: they are seen as people without defense or worth.

Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, where God's people suffered even though they remained faithful. He uses it right after naming sufferings such as persecution, hunger, and the sword. With this he shows that pain is not a sign that God has abandoned us. The believers of his time did suffer persecution, and he knew it from his own experience.

For today: when you go through mockery, loss, or trials because of your faith, do not conclude that God has stopped loving you. Pray sincerely and remember that Christ intercedes for you and that his love remains firm.
exp.11:3:
It says that, just as our body has many parts, and each part does a different task, so it is with us. "Members" are the parts of the body, like the hand or the foot. "Office" means function or work. "Yet" means "but."

Paul is writing to the believers in Rome. He has just asked them not to live like the world and not to think they are better than others. He uses the image of the body to explain that the church forms one unity, yet each person has a different role. The verses that follow speak of the gifts God gives to each one.

For today: do not compare yourself with others or feel lesser for not having someone else's gift. Ask yourself how you can serve in your church or family, and do it with humility, also valuing what others contribute.
exp.0:22:
It says that people exchanged the glory of God, which never decays or ends, for images of things that do decay and end: mortal humans, birds, four-footed animals, and reptiles. The word "changed" in the verse means "exchanged." Being "uncorruptible" means something that does not rot or die. The phrase "made like" speaks of figures made to look like something.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that all of us need the gospel. Before this verse, he says that people came to know God through what He did in creation, but they did not give Him thanks or honor Him. The verses that follow show that this rejection brought painful consequences.

For today: few of us make statues of animals now, but we can still exchange God for money, fame, or pleasure. Ask yourself what thing today receives your greatest attention and gratitude, and give God first place again.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that when someone trusts God and believes in Jesus, God declares them righteous, that is, He treats them as someone with no guilt before Him. For that reason there is no longer hostility toward God, but peace. That peace comes through Jesus Christ, not through our own works. "Justified" is a courtroom word: it means declared righteous.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. Before this verse he explained that everyone has failed and that Abraham was accepted because he believed. Now he sums up what that brings: peace with God. He then says that this faith gives us access to grace, hope, and strength, even in trials.

For today: if you feel guilty or far from God, remember that your peace with Him does not depend on your performance, but on Christ. Pray today, thanking Him, and rest in that peace.
exp.0:8:
Paul says that God himself is his witness, meaning that God knows that what he affirms is true. He clarifies that he serves God "with my spirit," that is, with his whole heart and not only outwardly, in proclaiming the gospel of his Son. And he assures them that he remembers the believers in Rome in his prayers without stopping, that is, he mentions them constantly.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, a church he did not yet know in person. He has just thanked God because their faith was being talked about everywhere. By saying that God is his witness, he wants to show that his affection for them is sincere, and so he prepares the ground for asking them to receive him soon.

Today we can imitate Paul by praying steadily for specific people, even those we do not know well. Try writing down a few names today and praying for them regularly.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that, even when a person wants to do what is right, they discover a pattern that keeps repeating: evil is present and close at hand. The word "law" here does not mean a commandment, but a constant rule or pattern. The word "find" means to discover or to become aware of something.

The apostle Paul speaks here in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He describes the struggle between what his mind approves in God's law and the inclination to sin that remains within him. Scholars debate whether he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ or of his experience as a believer. What is clear is that it shows the law alone cannot give us the power to overcome sin.

Today, do not be surprised or sink into guilt when you notice that inner struggle. Acknowledge it honestly, ask God for help each day, and rely on his grace, not only on your own willpower.
exp.1:5:
He says that God, in his judgment, will give each person what is due according to what they have done. The word "render" means to give a fair response, and "deeds" refers to the way a person lives, not only to isolated acts. No one is left out of this judgment.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he speaks to the one who judges others and thinks he will escape God's judgment. He reminds them that God's kindness and patience are not permission to carry on as before, but an invitation to repent. The verses that follow show that our deeds reveal where the heart is heading. Christians understand this passage together with the rest of the letter, where Paul teaches that salvation is by grace through faith.

Today you can see God's patience as an opportunity, not an excuse. Ask yourself: "Does my way of living show that I have truly turned to Him?" Come to God with humility and sincerity.
exp.7:0:
They who are united to Christ Jesus no longer live under condemnation, that is, under a sentence of guilt. To "walk" means to live, to conduct oneself day by day. "Flesh" refers to human nature, weak and dominated by sin, not to the body itself. "Spirit" points to living guided by the Spirit of God. The words "á" and "mas" are old forms of "a" and "sino". Some ancient manuscripts end the verse at "Christ Jesus"; the second part was probably added later.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier, in chapter 7, he spoke of his struggle with sin. Now he answers with hope: sin and the law do not have the final word, because God acted in Christ. The following verses explain that God sent his Son to overcome sin.

Today, when you feel guilty over past failures, remember that if you trust in Christ, God does not condemn you. Come before him with sincerity and ask him for help to walk again.
exp.4:16:
It says that death came to rule over everyone because of the sin of one man, Adam. But what Christ offers is far greater: those who receive the abundant grace and the gift of being declared righteous by God will reign in life through Jesus Christ.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and compares Adam with Christ. His purpose is to show that God's grace is more powerful than sin and death. Some understand this "reigning in life" as a reality already present, and others as a future hope; it probably includes both.

Today you can stop trying to earn God's love. Receive his forgiveness each day as a gift, and live with the confidence that sin and guilt no longer hold power over you.
exp.4:18:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Jesus Christ. Through Adam's disobedience, the many were made sinners, that is, placed or declared in the condition of sinners. Through Jesus' obedience, the many will be made righteous, that is, placed in right relationship with God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that everyone needs salvation and that it is received by faith. Here he shows that just as sin entered the world through one man, grace also came through one man. Christians debate how the effect of Adam's sin is passed on, but all agree that Christ is the solution.

For today: you do not have to earn God's acceptance by your own efforts. Rest in the obedience of Christ, and let that grace move you to obey him out of gratitude, not fear.
exp.11:9:
It says we should love fellow believers the way one loves a blood brother, with sincere affection. "Brotherly love" means family love. "Giving honor ahead of the other" means going first in showing respect and value to the other person, without waiting for them to do it first.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, who is writing to the Christians in Rome. After explaining God's grace, he now teaches them how to live together in community. Just before this, he speaks of gifts and of a love without pretense; this verse shows how that love looks in everyday life.

For today: this week, look for a chance to be the first to acknowledge or thank someone in your church or family. A message, a sincere compliment, or a gesture of respect can make that genuine love visible.
exp.7:8:
Paul tells the believers in Rome that they no longer live "in the flesh," that is, controlled by their old nature that opposes God, but "in the Spirit." This is so if the Spirit of God truly lives in them. And whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome. Earlier he contrasted two ways of living: one centered on oneself and far from God, and another guided by the Spirit. Here he encourages the believers: their identity no longer depends on their own efforts, but on Christ dwelling in them through his Spirit.

For today: instead of living afraid of not being good enough, ask the Spirit to guide you each day. Your life with God rests on the fact that he lives in you, not on your own perfection.
exp.13:22:
Romans 14:23 says that whoever doubts whether something is right and does it anyway is condemned, because he did not act from faith, that is, from a conviction held before God. Whoever has doubts in his conscience is the one described here. Being condemned means being found guilty. Anything done against one's own conviction, without trust in God, is sin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where some believed certain foods or days were forbidden and others felt free. He asks them not to despise or judge one another. Here he teaches that each person should act according to his conscience before God, without causing others to stumble. The word "faith" here is understood mainly as a conviction of conscience, though some read it more broadly.

Today: before doing something questionable, pray and ask yourself whether you can do it with peace before God. And do not pressure others to act against their conscience.
exp.2:4:
Here Paul raises an objection: if our wrongdoing makes God's righteousness shine more brightly by contrast, would it be unjust of God to punish us?

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the unbelief of some does not cancel God's faithfulness. He imagines an opponent who answers him with this objection, and Paul rejects it at once: "God forbid." God does judge the world, and for that reason he cannot be unjust.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to sin. That God can bring something good out of our failures does not make the failure good. Rather, acknowledge your wrong with humility and trust that God is just and merciful.
exp.0:0:
Paul introduces himself with three descriptions. He is a "servant" of Jesus Christ, that is, someone who belongs to his Lord and lives to obey him. He was "called to be an apostle," meaning sent out with a special mission. And he was "separated unto the gospel of God," set apart to proclaim the good news from God. Old-fashioned spellings and words: "unto" means "to," and "gospel" means "good news."

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the start, he explains who he is and with what authority he speaks to them. He says that his message is not his own invention but the gospel of God, which had already been promised in the Scriptures.

For today: before speaking of what you do, remember to whom you belong. Your worth and your purpose come from God's calling, not only from your achievements. Ask him to show you where he wants you to serve him today, in your home, your work, or your community.
exp.0:21:
They said they were wise, but in reality they became foolish. The word "fatuous" is an old-fashioned term meaning foolish, empty of true understanding. Thinking oneself wise without acknowledging God ends in a deep foolishness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that creation shows the power and greatness of God, so no one has an excuse. Here he describes those who, even knowing something about God, did not honor him or give him thanks. They relied on their own reasoning, and this led them to worship created things instead of the Creator.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in some area of life, we trust our own intelligence more than God. A good practice is to begin the day by thanking him and asking him for wisdom with humility, accepting his guidance even when we do not understand everything.
exp.9:0:
Paul says that what he desires most from the heart, and what he asks of God in prayer for Israel, is that they may be saved. The word "health" here means "salvation," not good physical condition. "Desire" means a deep longing of the will.

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained, in the previous chapter, his sorrow over his fellow Jews, most of whom had not recognized Jesus as the Messiah. Although they make great efforts to please God, the text that follows says they lack correct knowledge. For this reason Paul does not judge them coldly, but prays for them with affection.

For today: let us think of someone who does not yet know Jesus, even someone who makes us uncomfortable or who rejects us. Instead of arguing or criticizing, we can pray every day for that person with a loving heart, and look for a kind opportunity to share our faith.
exp.4:6:
It is very rare for someone to give their life for a righteous man, that is, someone upright and faithful to the law. Perhaps, somewhat more readily, someone might dare to die for a good person, someone generous and beloved.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that God's love is certain. First he speaks of how uncommon human sacrifice is, and then, in verse 8, he emphasizes that Christ died for people who were neither righteous nor good. Some scholars debate the exact difference between "righteous" and "good," but the central idea is clear.

For today: when you doubt that God loves you, remember that Christ died for you before you deserved it. Rest in that love and treat others with the same grace.
exp.9:16:
It says that faith is born from hearing the message, and that this message is the word of God. "So then" means "therefore," and "hearing" here is more than catching sounds: it means receiving with attention what is announced. The verse reads "the word of God," though some early manuscripts read "the word of Christ"; in both cases it speaks of the message of the gospel.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs to hear the gospel in order to believe. For this reason he speaks of messengers who are sent and of Israel's response, which not everyone accepted. Then he insists that they have indeed heard.

For today: make room each day to listen to the Bible, whether by reading it or hearing it with others. And if you want others to believe, share the word of God simply, trusting that He makes faith grow.
exp.4:7:
This verse says that God shows and makes clear his love for us. The proof is that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. "Commendeth" means "makes clear" or "shows plainly." "Love" here means the same as the word translated "love" in the verse, and "but" is what the word "But" means at the start of the verse.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that God declares people righteous through faith. He makes a comparison: hardly anyone would die for a righteous man, though perhaps someone might dare to die for a very good person. God, on the other hand, acted on behalf of people who did not deserve it. Paul then concludes that, since we have already been reconciled, we can trust in our final salvation.

For today: you do not have to make yourself right first in order to draw near to God. His love came before your improvement. Come to Him honestly, and let that love give you peace and teach you to treat with grace those who fail.
exp.15:17:
Paul says that certain people do not truly serve Christ, but serve their own desires. The phrase "their bellies" is a way of speaking about their appetites and their comfort. With smooth words and flattery, they deceive the hearts of the simple, that is, the naive, those who do not suspect evil.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and, as he closes the letter, warns them about those who cause divisions and turn away from the teaching they have already received. He asks them to stay away from such people. Then he praises them for their obedience and asks them to be wise in what is good and innocent when it comes to evil.

Today we might ask ourselves: does this message agree with what the Bible says, or does it only sound pleasant? A good habit is to compare what we hear with the Scriptures, without being carried away by the charm of the one speaking.
exp.11:11:
This verse brings together three attitudes of the believer: rejoicing because of the hope they have in God, being patient and steadfast when trials come, and not giving up on prayer. The word "patient" here means someone who endures without giving in. "Trouble" means affliction or difficulty. "Continuing" means persevering, someone who keeps praying again and again.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. In this part of the chapter he describes how faith is lived out in everyday life, after having explained what God has done for them. His words sit between the call to serve the Lord with enthusiasm and the call to help those in need and bless those who persecute them. It was a church facing pressure, and Paul encourages them to hold on in this way.

For today: when you go through a difficult time, do not stop praying. Set aside a few minutes each day to speak with God, and remember one of his promises that gives you hope.
exp.15:1:
What it says: Paul asks the Christians in Rome to welcome Phoebe "in the Lord," that is, as a sister in the faith, in a way that is worthy of the saints (the believers). He also asks them to help her in whatever she needs.

Context: Paul writes this letter from Corinth, and Cenchreae was a nearby port. Phoebe probably carried the letter to Rome, although the text does not say so outright. Paul recommends her because they did not know her, and he emphasizes that she had helped many people, including him. Some understand "deaconess" as a servant of the church, and others as a formal office; this is debated.

For today: When someone new comes to your church, welcome them warmly and ask how you can help. Serve generously too, as Phoebe did.
exp.9:1:
Paul says that the Israelites are sincere and passionate about God. "Zeal" means enthusiasm, intense fervor. But that fervor is "not according to knowledge": it is not grounded in correct understanding, in grasping well what God really asks for. They have passion, but they lack clarity.

Paul, a Jew himself, writes to the believers in Rome. He feels deep sorrow for his people and prays for their salvation.
