He recognizes that his fellow countrymen seek God with effort, but the following verses explain the problem: they wanted to establish their own righteousness and did not accept the righteousness that God gives through Christ.

Today we can be very devoted in religious matters and still be mistaken. It is wise to combine enthusiasm with the study of the Bible and with the humility to be corrected, remembering that we are accepted by the grace of God in Christ, not by our own effort.
exp.0:29:
This verse continues a list of behaviors that Paul describes in people who have turned away from God. Those who whisper complaints about others in secret are gossips, and those who slander and damage other people's reputations are slanderers. "Haters of God" can be understood as people who hate God or as people whom God views with displeasure; it is interpreted both ways. The insulters attack others with contempt, and the proud and arrogant believe themselves superior to everyone else, while the inventors of evil seek new ways to do harm.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that all of humanity needs the gospel, because when God is rejected, life becomes disordered. This list prepares the ground for saying that all of us need the grace of God.

Today we can examine our words: do we complain about someone or speak badly of them? This week, let us ask God for help to bless rather than criticize, and to honor our parents with respect and gratitude.
exp.9:2:
Paul says that many of his people did not understand how God declares a person righteous. They wanted to stand before God with a righteousness achieved by their own efforts, and so they did not accept the way God himself offers. "Ignorant" means not knowing or not understanding; "submitted" means yielding or accepting with humility.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and speaks with grief for Israel, his own people. He acknowledges that they had genuine zeal for God, but a zeal without right understanding. They believed that keeping the law gave them a righteousness of their own, and they did not see that Christ is the fulfillment and goal of that law, as the next verse says.

For today: it is easy to trust in our good works or in our religiousness to feel accepted by God. We can ask him to teach us to rest in the righteousness he gives through Christ, and to obey him out of gratitude, not out of pride.
exp.15:24:
This verse begins a final song of praise. It says that God has the power to strengthen and establish believers. He does this through the gospel that Paul proclaims, which is the message of Jesus Christ. The word "stablish" in the verse above means to make firm, so this is the sense of the phrase. "Mystery" refers to a plan of God that was hidden for ages and has now been made known.

Paul is ending his letter to the Christians in Rome, probably written from Corinth, as the closing note indicates. After sending greetings, he closes with praise to God. He sums up his letter: the gospel is the good news that God has revealed, and it is God who sustains his people, not human effort.

For today: when you feel weak or unsure in your faith, do not rely only on your own strength. Return to the message of Jesus Christ, read it, meditate on it, and ask God to establish you. He is able to uphold you.
exp.14:27:
Paul says that, once he has finished delivering the collection gathered for the poor Christians in Jerusalem, he will visit the believers in Rome on his way to Spain. "Having sealed this fruit" means "having safely delivered this gift." "Fruit" is the result of the love and generosity of the churches.

Paul writes this letter to the Romans from Corinth, as is commonly understood. He tells them of his plans to travel to Rome and then on to Spain. First he must bring the aid from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem. The Bible does not clearly say whether Paul actually reached Spain, so this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: first fulfill the commitments you have already made, even when you have great plans ahead. And if you have received something good from others, look for ways to bless them too with what you have.
exp.3:19:
This verse says that Abraham did not waver or become filled with distrust at what God promised him. On the contrary, he grew strong in his faith and gave glory to God.

Pablo writes to the Christians in Rome to explain that God declares a person righteous through faith, not through their works. He uses Abraham as an example. God had promised him a son, even though he was nearly a hundred years old and Sarah could not have children. His faith did not ignore the difficulty; he saw it and still trusted God.

For today: when your situation seems impossible, you do not have to pretend there is no problem. You can acknowledge it honestly and still rely on what God has said, thanking him in advance for his faithfulness.
exp.1:17:
He says that this person knows what God wants and is able to tell what is better, because they have been taught the law since childhood. The phrase "approvest the things that are more excellent" can also be understood as "test the things that differ" or "distinguish what matters"; scholars translate it in both ways.

Paul is speaking to Jews who boasted of their knowledge of the law. He recognizes their real privileges, but he is setting up a point: having the law and knowing it is not enough if it is not lived out. Paul wants to show that all of us, Jews and non-Jews alike, need Jesus Christ.

Today: knowing the Bible is a gift, but it is not the same as obeying it. Ask yourself this week: "What is one thing I already know about God that I am still not practicing?" And take that step with humility.
exp.1:26:
It says that a person who is not Jewish by birth, but who obeys what God commands, will end up judging the one who does have the sign of circumcision and the written law, yet disobeys it. Breaking the law means being a transgressor of it. "Through the letter" refers to the written law. "By nature" means by birth.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He shows them that having religious signs or knowing the law is not enough if life does not go with it. Some understand the judging as a comparison that exposes the hypocrite, not as a final judgment.

Today we can ask ourselves: am I content with being in church, with knowing the Bible, or with doing religious things? God looks for a heart that truly obeys. Let us ask him that our faith show in what we do each day.
exp.0:13:
Paul says that he has an obligation to all people: to Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to those without learning. The word "barbarians" here does not mean savages, but people who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture. To be "debtor" means someone who owes something and must pay it back.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He explains that he has wanted to visit them many times, but has been prevented from doing so. His obligation is not because he received money from them, but because God entrusted him with announcing the gospel to everyone. For this reason he feels bound to share it with people of every culture and social level.

Today we can remember that the gospel is not only for those we like or who are similar to us. Let us ask God for an opportunity this week to treat someone very different from us with respect and to share his hope with them.
exp.10:18:
Someone might think: "The branches were cut off so that I could be grafted in in their place." "Grafted in" is an older way of saying joined to a tree that already exists. The wild olive is a tree that grows without cultivation.

The apostle Paul speaks to believers of non-Jewish origin in Rome. He uses the image of an olive tree, which represents God's people. Some branches, Israelites who did not believe, were broken off. Paul anticipates a proud attitude on the part of the non-Jews and corrects it: they do not hold up the root, but the root holds them up.

For today: remember that your place before God is a gift of his grace, not something you earned. When you feel tempted to look down on others, give thanks, be humble, and pray for them with compassion.
exp.8:20:
The potter, the explanation says, has the right, or "power," to take the same clay and make from it one vessel for an honorable use and another for a common use. The word "shame" here does not mean something bad in itself, but a less distinguished use.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He speaks of God's freedom to show mercy, and he answers the person who objects that this would be unfair. He uses the image of the potter, taken from the Old Testament (as in Jeremiah 18). Christians have understood in various ways how this relates to election and human responsibility. But the text emphasizes that God is God, and we are not the ones who judge him.

For today: when you don't understand something of God's ways, pray with humility and trust. He is wise and good, and your place in his hands is not a neglect, but rather is under his care.
exp.13:1:
Here the explanation says that some people have the freedom of conscience to eat anything, without worrying about rules about food. Another person, whom Paul calls "weak" in the faith, eats only vegetables, that is, herbs and greens. The word "weak" here is not an insult; it speaks of someone whose conscience still feels bound by certain restrictions.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where believers of Jewish background and believers of non-Jewish background lived side by side. There were disagreements about food, and not all the reasons are known for certain; they could have been rules from the law, or avoiding meat offered to idols. Paul does not want these differences to divide the church.

For today: when another believer acts differently from you in secondary matters, do not despise or judge them. Receive them with respect, and remember that you both answer to the same Lord.
exp.14:1:
It says that each of us should try to please our neighbor, that is, the people who are near us. But not to flatter them or to look good, but for their good and for their edification, that is, to help them grow and be strengthened in faith.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were differences among believers about foods and special days. He asks that the stronger in faith be patient with the weaker and not think only of themselves. Right away he gives Christ as the example, who did not seek his own.

Today, before you give an opinion or act, you can ask yourself how to help that person grow. For example, being patient with a brother or sister who is just beginning in the faith, encouraging them kindly instead of criticizing them.
exp.11:2:
Paul says that no one should think of himself as more important than he really is. Instead, each person should think of himself with sound judgment (the word "soberly" means self-control and balance), according to the measure of faith that God has given him. This phrase is understood in several ways: as faith itself, or as the gifts and abilities that God distributes.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just urged them to offer themselves to God and to renew their minds. Now he applies this to life in community, and he says that he speaks through the grace given to him, that is, with the authority God gave him as an apostle. Right after this, he compares the church to a body with many members.

Today, before you compare yourself with others or boast about your talents, remember that everything you have is a gift from God. Value yourself with humility and honesty, and serve others with what you have received.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that a person who does not work to earn God's approval, but trusts in God, who forgives the sinner, has their faith credited to them as righteousness. An "ungodly" person is someone who lives without God. To be "counted" or "credited" means to be placed into someone's account. "Righteousness" means being right before God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and uses Abraham as an example. Before the law of Moses, Abraham believed God, and God accepted him. Paul compares this to wages: the one who works receives what he has earned, but God's righteousness is a gift. Then he quotes David, who spoke of the happiness of being forgiven.

Today, you do not have to wait until you are "good enough" to come near to God. Trust in Jesus, thank him for his forgiveness, and let that gift move you to obey him out of love, not out of fear.
exp.6:19:
What the passage says: Paul explains that when he does the wrong he does not want to do, it is no longer only his will that is acting, but the sin that dwells within him. The word "dwelleth" means "lives" or "remains." "Do" means "carry out" or "perform."

Context: Paul speaks in the first person about the struggle between the desire to obey God's law and the weakness of the flesh. Scholars debate whether he is describing his life before knowing Christ, his life as a believer, or a general experience, and Christians have understood it in different ways. What is clear is that he wants to show that the law reveals sin but does not give the strength to overcome it.

For today: When you fail, do not use this as an excuse, but do not sink into despair either. Acknowledge your weakness honestly, confess your failure to God, and ask him for help every day, for Paul soon points to Christ as the way out.
exp.10:28:
It says that God does not take back what he gives or whom he calls. The "gifts" are the blessings or favors God bestows, and the "calling" is his summons. The phrase "without repentance" means that God does not draw back or change his mind about them.

Paul writes to believers in Rome, most of whom were not Jewish. He is speaking about Israel, which for the most part had not accepted Christ. Paul wants the believers not to feel superior, and he reminds them that God remains faithful to his promises to the people he chose. Christians have received mercy, and that same mercy remains open to Israel.

For today: if God is faithful even when people fail, we can trust that his calling on our lives does not depend on our performance. And we should treat others with humility, without boasting, because we have all received everything through mercy.
exp.4:5:
This verse says that Christ died for the ungodly, that is, for those who lived without God. He did this while we were still without strength, unable to save ourselves. "In due time" means at the right moment, the one God had appointed.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the hope that does not disappoint, because the love of God fills the heart through the Holy Spirit. Now he shows the foundation of that hope: Christ died for us before we could do anything to deserve it. The verses that follow reinforce this: God showed his love when we were sinners.

For today: you do not need to fix your life first in order to draw near to God. If you feel weak or unworthy, come to him just as you are, trusting that his love reached you before you could respond.
exp.12:4:
It says we should submit to civil authorities for two reasons: to avoid punishment and, above all, out of conscience, that is, from an inner conviction that it is the right thing before God. Submit means living in obedience and respect. The rulers are the authorities, and the sword symbolizes their power to punish.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city that was the center of the empire. He explains that God uses the order and justice of the authorities to restrain evil and protect people. The verses that follow apply this to paying taxes. Christians have debated how far this obedience extends when a government commands something unjust or contrary to God, and this passage does not address that case directly.

Today, fulfill your obligations, such as paying taxes and respecting the laws, even when no one is watching, because you do it for God and with a clear conscience.
exp.10:14:
This verse says that the rejection of Israel, that is, their turning away from God, brought about the reconciling of the world, because the gospel reached the Gentiles. Then Paul asks what will happen when Israel is accepted again. His answer is that it will be life from the dead, an expression that some understand as a great spiritual renewal and others as the final resurrection.

Paul, the apostle to the Gentiles, speaks to the non-Jewish believers in Rome. He honors his ministry and hopes that his own people will feel holy jealousy and that some will be saved. Right away he uses the picture of the olive tree to show that the Gentiles must not look down on Israel.

Today we can guard against spiritual pride. If God has received us by pure grace, we should pray for those who have turned away and treat them with hope, not contempt.
exp.7:9:
It says that if Christ lives in the believer, the body is still subject to death because of sin, but the spirit has life because of righteousness. Some understand "spirit" as the human spirit made alive; others understand it as the Holy Spirit. Both readings are possible.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining the difference between living according to the flesh and living according to the Spirit. He wants to encourage them: although the body suffers and grows old, whoever belongs to Christ already has true life, and the next verse promises that God will also give life to their mortal bodies.

For today: when you feel tired, sick, or weak, remember that your worth and your hope do not depend on your body. Ask God to sustain you today, and trust his promise of resurrection.
exp.3:24:
This verse says that Jesus was handed over to death because of our sins, and that God raised him up so that we would be declared righteous. "Offences" are the wrongs or faults committed against God. "Justification" means being declared righteous before God, as if there were no guilt. "Was delivered" is understood as handed over to the cross.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken about Abraham, whose faith God counted to him as righteousness. Now he says that this same principle applies to us, who believe in God, who raised Jesus from the dead. With this verse he closes the chapter and sums up the gospel: the cross and the resurrection go together.

For today: when you feel guilty for your failures, remember that Christ has already paid for them and that his resurrection confirms your forgiveness. Rest in that promise and respond with confidence and gratitude.
exp.14:20:
The explanation says that Paul relies on Scripture to explain his goal: to bring the gospel to those who had never heard of Christ. He quotes Isaiah 52:15: those who had not been told about him will see, and those who had not heard will understand. The explanation notes that the word "they shall see" means that they will be given the news, and that is the whole of the sentence's meaning.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He tells them that he has preached from Jerusalem to Illyricum and that he made it his aim not to build on the work of others. He uses Isaiah to show that his mission fits with what God had already announced. He also explains why he had not been able to visit them before. Many understand the Isaiah text to speak of the Servant of the Lord, and Paul applies it to his own labor.

For today: ask yourself who near you has not yet heard the gospel clearly. Pray for that person, and look for a simple and kind way to share what Christ has done for you.
exp.15:3:
They say that Priscilla and Aquila "laid down their necks" for Paul's life, meaning they took great risks, perhaps even facing death, to protect him. Paul gives them thanks, and makes clear that he is not the only one: all the churches of the Gentiles (the non-Jews) are also grateful to them.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome and, at the end, greets several co-workers. It is not known exactly when or how they saved his life; some think of the uproar in Ephesus (Acts 19), but the text does not say so. What is clear is that their courage benefited many churches.

For today: Let us learn to thank out loud those who have cared for us at great cost, and to be willing to serve others even when it costs us.
exp.10:29:
What it says: Paul reminds the believers who were not Jews that they once lived without obeying or believing God. Now, however, they have received his mercy, that is, his compassionate love that forgives. He says this happened "through their unbelief," meaning the people of Israel. Old words: "you" in the older wording is simply "you," and "obtained" means "received."

Context: Paul writes to the church in Rome, made up of Jews and non-Jews. Some of the non-Jewish believers felt superior to Israel. Paul shows them that the rejection of the gospel by many Jews opened the door to the other peoples. But God has not abandoned Israel, and his plan continues. How exactly these events fit together, scholars explain in several different ways.

For today: If you have faith today, remember that it is a gift of God's mercy, not something you earned. That frees us from pride and leads us to pray with love for those who do not yet believe.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that the righteousness that comes through faith speaks as if it were a person. It warns us not to say in our heart, "Who will ascend into heaven?" as if it were necessary to go up there to bring Christ down to earth. The word "But" means "however," and the word "to" is simply the word "to."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that Moses taught that whoever does the law will live by it, and that Christ is the end, or the goal, of the law. Now he quotes and adapts words from Deuteronomy 30, where it was said that the commandment was not far away. Paul shows that salvation is already near, because Christ has already come. Scholars explain in several ways how Paul uses that text.

Today, if you doubt that God accepts you, you do not need to do something extraordinary to reach Him. Trust in what Christ has already done, and speak with Him simply and in faith.
exp.14:15:
Paul says that God gave him the task of being a minister of Jesus Christ to the non-Jews (the Gentiles). His work is to proclaim the gospel of God, like someone serving in a sacred act. His goal is that the Gentiles become an offering acceptable to God, set apart for him (sanctified) by the work of the Holy Spirit. "Ministering" means serving or carrying out a service.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, whom he praised for their goodness and knowledge. He explains that it was a bold thing for him to write to them because God gave him that responsibility. He uses temple language, like a priest presenting an offering, but the offering is the people who believe in Christ.

God does not only save us; he also sets us apart for himself through his Spirit. If you share the gospel, remember that your service is valuable to God, and that the change in people is his work.
exp.11:5:
Paul says that each believer has different gifts, and that these gifts come from God's grace, not from our merit. He begins with the gift of prophecy, which is speaking on God's behalf to encourage, correct, or guide. It must be used "according to the proportion of faith." That phrase can be understood in two ways: according to the faith that God gives to each person, or according to the Christian faith already received. Both ideas call for humility.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just compared them to a body: many members, each with its own function, but all united in Christ. He wants them not to think themselves superior or to despise one another, but to serve together.

For today: think about what God has given you, whether teaching, helping, encouraging, or giving, and use it with humility in your church, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.10:19:
Paul says it is true: the Jewish branches were broken off because of unbelief, and you, as a Gentile, stand firm by faith. Therefore you must not be proud, but have a reverent fear before God. "Being highminded" means being filled with pride; the word "fear" here speaks of humility and seriousness, not of terror.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers of both Gentile and Jewish origin. He uses the image of an olive tree: Israel is the original branches and the Gentiles are grafted-in branches. He wants to keep the Gentiles from looking down with contempt on the Jews who did not believe.

For today: our faith is a gift, not something we earned. When you see someone far from God, do not think you are better; give thanks, stay humble, and keep trusting in Christ each day.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that if you openly acknowledge with your words that Jesus is Lord, and truly believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. The verse uses the word "confess" and the word "believe," and these mean the same as "acknowledge" and "trust." To be raised from the dead means that God brought him back to life. To be saved means to be rescued and forgiven by God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he explained that salvation is not earned through human effort, whether by going up to heaven or down into the depths, because God has already brought it near in Christ. The message of faith that Paul preaches is close at hand, in the mouth and in the heart. The verses that follow say that inner faith and spoken confession go together.

For today: if you trust in Jesus, do not hide your faith. Today you can tell God, or someone close to you, simply: "Jesus is my Lord, and I believe that he rose again."
exp.9:9:
It says that faith begins in the deepest part of a person, in the heart, and that God declares us righteous when we truly believe. But that faith does not stay hidden: it is expressed with the mouth, by confessing Jesus. "Righteousness" means being accepted as righteous before God. "Salvation" here means salvation, not just good health of the body.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that salvation is not earned by keeping the law, but is received through faith in Christ. He quotes Deuteronomy to show that the message is near to everyone and that it is for Jews and Greeks alike. The verses that follow stress that God is generous with everyone who calls on him.

For today: do not keep your faith only in your mind. This week, tell someone simply and without pressure what Jesus has done in your life.
exp.14:22:
Here Paul says that he no longer has any room left in these regions, meaning that he had already proclaimed the gospel throughout that area of the eastern Mediterranean. In addition, for many years he had longed to visit the believers in Rome.

Paul probably wrote this letter from Corinth. Earlier he had explained that his aim was to preach where Christ was not yet known. That kept him from going to Rome many times. Now he feels that his work in those lands has reached its conclusion, and he thinks of Spain, passing through Rome. Scholars are not certain whether he actually went to Spain.

For today: let us learn from Paul to have clear goals and to wait with patience. God may delay our plans while he uses us somewhere else, and that waiting is also part of his purpose.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that God wanted to make known the greatness and richness of his glory. He did this through "vessels of mercy," meaning people who receive his compassion. God prepared them beforehand to share in his glory. The second part of that comment, about the word that means "known" and the word that means "showed," is not something your reader can check in the verse, so it has been left out.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God acts with freedom and patience. He uses the image of the potter. In the following verse he makes clear that these vessels include both Jews and non-Jews. Christians have debated for centuries how God's decision and the human response relate here, and there are several interpretations.

For today: if your faith depends on God's mercy and not on your own merits, you can live with humility and gratitude. Today, give thanks for one concrete sign of his compassion, and show that same compassion to someone who needs it.
exp.7:5:
It says that the mindset of the flesh, that is, the way a person thinks, what they desire, and where they lean, ends in death. By contrast, the mindset of the Spirit leads to life and peace. Here "flesh" does not mean the physical body, but a life lived apart from God, driven by selfishness and sin. "Spirit" refers to the Holy Spirit who guides the believer.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that Christ freed us from condemnation and that the believer now lives led by the Spirit. In this verse he contrasts two paths: what fills each person's mind shows where their life is heading. Some scholars understand "death" as separation from God, and others also see it as the decline of present life. Perhaps it includes both.

Today we can ask ourselves: what do I fill my thoughts with most? Praying, reading the Bible, and asking God for help every day directs the heart toward his peace.
exp.3:12:
Paul says that God promised Abraham and his descendants (the "seed") that they would be heirs of the world, but not because Abraham kept the law. That promise came through the righteousness of faith, meaning that Abraham believed God and God counted him as righteous.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that both Jews and non-Jews are accepted by God through faith. Abraham lived long before the law of Moses existed, so his example proves that the promise did not depend on it. Scholars understand in various ways what "heir of the world" means, but Paul connects it with the blessing for all nations.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's favor through effort or merit. Trust in His promise, and live grateful and obedient out of that trust.
exp.2:20:
It says that now God has openly shown his righteousness, that is, his way of declaring people right before him, and that he did this without depending on the law of Moses. The word "but" at the start of the verse introduces this contrast. The explanation also notes that this righteousness is not something new or contrary to Scripture, since the law and the prophets, that is, the Old Testament, already spoke of it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that no one becomes righteous before God by keeping the law, because the law shows sin but does not remove it. With "but now" he changes the subject: after the bad news, he announces the solution. The following verse clarifies that this righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's favor through efforts and merits. If you feel insufficient, trust in Jesus and rest in what God has already done. From there, obey with gratitude, not with fear.
exp.15:25:
This verse says that the mystery of God, which had been hidden before, has now been revealed. It was made known through the writings of the prophets, following the command of the eternal God, and it is announced to all nations so that they may believe and obey. The word "nations" in the verse refers to peoples or nations. The phrase "obedience of faith" means responding to God by trusting in Christ.

Paul is closing his letter to the Romans. In this final sentence he sums up his message: the plan to save both Jews and non-Jews had already been announced in the Old Testament, but now it is understood clearly through Jesus Christ. Some scholars debate whether these final verses were part of the original letter, but they appear in most Bibles.

For today: if the gospel is for all peoples, we should not exclude anyone. This week, share a word of hope with someone outside your usual circle.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the gospel is about the Son of God, Jesus Christ. In his human nature, he was born as a descendant of King David. The word "seed" means descendants, and "was made of" means that he came into being, or was born, as a human being in that family.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and introduces himself before he enters the subject. He says that the gospel had already been promised in the Scriptures. That is why he highlights that Jesus comes from the line of David, as the prophets announced about the Messiah. In this way he connects the Old Testament with the good news of Christ.

For today: Jesus is truly human, and so he understands our lives, our struggles, and our pain. You can approach him with confidence and speak to him honestly, knowing that he fulfills God's promises.
exp.4:4:
This verse says that Christian hope does not leave us in shame, meaning it does not disappoint us or end in nothing. The reason is that God has poured out his love into our hearts, like water that fills completely. He does this through the Holy Spirit, whom God has given us as a gift.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He had been speaking about how, having been made right with God through faith, we have peace with God. For that reason he can say that even trials bear a fruit: patience, proven character, and hope. Then, in the verses that follow, he shows the greatest proof of that love: Christ died for us while we were weak and did not deserve anything.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, do not look only at the problem. Remember that God loves you and that his Spirit can confirm it to you. Ask him to give you that assurance and rest in it.
exp.10:32:
Paul stands in wonder before God. He says that God's wisdom and knowledge are like a treasure so deep that its bottom cannot be seen. "Incomprehensible" means that they cannot be grasped by the mind, and "unsearchable" means that they cannot be fully traced out. God's judgments are his decisions and his way of governing; his ways are the manner in which he acts.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that many of his people, Israel, have not believed, and that God, even so, has a plan of mercy for both Jews and non-Jews. Having reached that conclusion, Paul does not argue any further: he breaks out in praise. He will then go on with questions that show that no one advises God.

For today: when something in your life or in the world does not make sense, you do not have to understand everything in order to trust. Take a moment to thank God for his mercy and hand over that doubt to him, knowing that his wisdom surpasses yours.
exp.7:7:
The explanation says that those who live "in the flesh" cannot please God. "Flesh" here does not mean the physical body, but a way of living controlled by the sinful nature, without God. "So then" shows that this is a conclusion drawn from what came before.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that setting the mind on the flesh leads to death and is hostility toward God, because it does not submit to his law. Right after this, he assures them that they are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in them. It is a comfort, not a condemnation.

Today we can remember that pleasing God does not depend on our effort to be good, but on living united with Christ through his Spirit. Ask him every day to guide your thoughts and decisions.
exp.10:5:
It says that salvation and God's favor come by grace, that is, as a gift that cannot be earned. If it depended on works, it would no longer be a gift. Grace and effort to earn something cannot be mixed as if they were the same thing.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just recalled that, in the time of the prophet Elijah, God preserved seven thousand faithful people. In the same way, in his own time, a group of believing Israelites remained, chosen by grace. Paul wants to show that God has not abandoned his people, and that this remnant exists by God's kindness, not by merit.

For today: if you feel tired of trying to be good enough for God, rest in his grace. Obey him out of love and gratitude, not to buy his acceptance.
exp.7:11:
This verse says that believers have a debt, but not one owed to the flesh. "Owe" means that we must something. "Flesh" here is not just the body, but the old way of living, ruled by selfishness and sin. That is why we are not obligated to live according to it. The sentence is left open, but the next verse completes it: our debt is to the Spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God's Spirit lives in them and that the same power that raised Jesus gives them life. That is why he concludes with "therefore": if we have already received this life, we have a new responsibility.

Today, when an old habit or temptation calls to you strongly, remember that you owe it nothing. Ask the Spirit to help you choose what pleases God, and take one concrete step today in that direction.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that no one is righteous before God by their own efforts. "Righteous" means someone who stands in perfect uprightness before Him. The phrase "There is none righteous, no, not one" allows no exceptions. "As it is written" shows that Paul is quoting the Scriptures, especially passages from the Psalms (such as Psalm 14 and Psalm 53).

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that both Jews and non-Jews are "under sin," that is, under its power and guilt. He wants no one to boast of being better than others, so that he can show afterward that salvation comes through faith in Christ and not through our own merits.

For today: instead of comparing ourselves with others to feel good about ourselves, we can humbly recognize our need for God. This frees us from pride and condemnation, and leads us to thank Him for His grace and to treat others with compassion.
exp.6:5:
The explanation says that believers are no longer under the rule of the law, as someone who is imprisoned would be. "Held" means caught or kept in custody. The phrase about the oldness of the letter speaks of an old, cold obedience based only on written rules. The phrase about newness of spirit is a new life, guided by the Holy Spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the example of marriage: death ends a bond. Thus, through Christ, the law no longer dominates or condemns us. Paul does not say that the law is evil; he immediately clarifies that it is not, but rather that it revealed sin without being able to free us from it.

For today: do not serve God out of fear or by keeping a checklist. Ask the Spirit to renew your heart, and obey out of love and gratitude to Christ, who gave you new life.
exp.14:19:
Paul says he worked eagerly and with determination to preach the gospel in places where no one had yet spoken about Christ. He did not want to "build on someone else's foundation," that is, to build on the groundwork another had already laid.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just described how God worked through him, from Jerusalem to Illyricum. In this way he explains his calling as an apostle to the Gentiles, and that is why at times he could not visit them. He quotes Isaiah to show that those who never heard will understand.

Today we might ask ourselves who has never heard about Jesus: a neighbor, a coworker, or a distant village. We can pray for that person and share the gospel with them in love and simplicity, without belittling the work of others.
exp.4:1:
Through whom, the explanation says, believers have access, that is, an open door, to enter by faith into the grace of God, which is his undeserved favor. In that grace we stand firm, well established. And the phrase "we rejoice," in the original wording, means that we are glad and take pride with joy, not in ourselves, but in the hope of sharing the glory of God.

The apostle Paul is speaking to the Christians in Rome. He had been explaining that God declares us righteous through faith, not through works. For that reason, in the previous verse he speaks of peace with God. Here he shows what follows from it: access, firmness, and hope. Later he will say that this hope sustains even in trials.

For today: when you feel unworthy or insecure, remember that your place before God does not depend on your performance, but on Christ. Pray with confidence and let that hope give you stability.
exp.10:21:
This verse asks us to look closely at two sides of God: his goodness and his severity. He was severe toward the branches that fell, that is, toward those who did not believe. Toward "you" he is good, but on one condition: that you remain in that goodness, that is, that you keep trusting him. Otherwise, you too will be cut off, like a branch removed from the tree. The word rendered "grafted in" means joined in by grafting.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, most of whom were not Jewish. He uses the image of an olive tree: Israel is the natural branches, and believers from other nations are branches grafted in. Paul wants to prevent them from thinking they are superior to the Jews. Interpreters debate what it means to be "cut off": whether it is losing salvation or a serious warning about genuine faith.

Today, live with gratitude and humility. If you have anything good with God, it is because of his grace, not because of your own merit. Keep trusting him every day.
exp.15:20:
Paul sends greetings from his companions to the Christians in Rome. He mentions Timothy, whom he calls "my fellow worker," a word that means a colleague or helper in the work. He also names Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, whom he calls "my kinsmen," that is, relatives or fellow countrymen who were Jews, since the word can be understood in either sense.

Paul is ending his letter to the Romans, probably from Corinth. After his final instructions, he includes greetings from those who were with him. Although he did not know every member of the church in Rome in person, he wanted them to know that he was not working alone. About the exact identity of Lucius and Jason there is uncertainty.

For today: value those who walk alongside you in serving God. Give thanks for them, encourage them with your greeting, and remember that faith is best lived in community.
exp.5:1:
Paul answers with force: "God forbid," that is, "Never!" He says that believers "are dead to sin," meaning that we are no longer under its rule as we once were. So he asks: how can we keep living in something that no longer has power over us?

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. In the earlier chapters he explained that God's grace is greater than sin. Now he corrects a wrong idea: that if grace forgives everything, then we could sin all the more. He shows that grace is not a license to sin, but a power to change. The verses that follow connect this with baptism and with Christ.

For today: when the thought tempts you that "God will forgive me anyway," remember who you are in Christ. Ask him for help, and take one concrete step today toward living in obedience, grateful for his grace.
exp.14:3:
Paul says that whatever was written in earlier times, meaning the Scriptures of the Old Testament, was written down to teach us. Its purpose is that, through steady endurance and through the encouragement the Scriptures give, we might have hope.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where there were tensions between believers from different backgrounds. He has just quoted a psalm about Christ, who endured insults without seeking his own pleasure. Paul shows that those ancient words had a purpose for the church of his own time. Then he prays that God would give them unity.

For today: read the Bible regularly, not only to be informed, but to ask God for strength in difficulties. And when it is hard for you to get along with someone, remember how Christ bore with others, and ask him for patience.
exp.13:3:
Paul asks: "Who art thou that judgest another man's servant?" The other man's servant is the servant of a different master, that is, another believer who belongs to Christ. The question of whether he "stands or falls" means that his own Lord is the one who approves him or corrects him. And the phrase about being "held up" means that he will be sustained, because the Lord has the power to keep him steady.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements about foods and special days. Some ate everything, while others ate only vegetables. He does not call them to fight over this, but to respect one another, since each one tries to honor the Lord according to his conscience. Scholars debate exactly who the two groups were, but the counsel is clear.

Today, when someone lives out his faith differently in secondary matters, do not despise or judge him. Instead, pray for him, trust that Christ sustains him, and seek peace.
exp.8:4:
The explanation says that the Israelites have great ancestors, such as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and that from that people Christ was born in his human nature. It then affirms that this Christ is God over all things, worthy of praise forever. Here "blessed" means praised, and "Amen" means "so be it."

Paul speaks with deep sorrow for his people, who for the most part did not believe in Jesus. He lists the privileges of Israel and culminates with the greatest of them: that the Messiah came from them. Some scholars debate the original punctuation of the Greek text, but most translations and commentators understand that Paul calls Christ God.

Today we can honor Jesus as truly man and truly God, and at the same time love with compassion those who do not yet know him, praying for them as Paul did.
exp.7:15:
The Holy Spirit, directly, confirms deep within our being that we are children of God. The word "witness" means a confirmation, like an inner voice that assures us of something true.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that we no longer live in fear, like slaves, but as adopted children who cry out "Abba, Father," a tender word for calling on God. This verse adds that God himself gives us assurance of that relationship, and then Paul speaks of the inheritance and of present sufferings.

If you doubt your worth or whether God accepts you, pray calmly and trust his promise. Call him "Father" with simplicity, read his Word, and remember that your security rests on what God says, not on your feelings from day to day.
exp.2:26:
It says there is no room left for boasting or for feeling superior before God. "Boasting" means pride or self-importance. "Excluded" means it was shut out. Paul asks by what principle boasting was shut out, and he answers that it was not by the principle of works but by the principle of faith, that is, trusting in what God did in Christ.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and Gentiles. He has just explained that everyone has sinned and that God makes people right with himself through faith in the blood of Jesus. So no one can claim credit of their own, neither the Jews through the law nor the Gentiles through their culture. Right after this he says that God is God of all.

For today: when you feel better than others because of your effort or your service, remember that your place before God is a gift. Be more thankful, compare yourself less, and treat others with humility.
exp.11:0:
Paul asks the believers to offer their whole selves to God, as a living offering. The word "beseech" is a request made with affection, not a command. "Present" means to offer. "Reasonable service" can be understood as reasonable, logical, or spiritual worship; scholars translate it in several ways.

Paul is writing to the church in Rome. For eleven chapters he explained what God has done through Christ: forgiveness, righteousness, and salvation by grace. Now he says "therefore": since God has been so merciful, the natural response is to live for Him. Obedience springs from gratitude, not from fear.

For today: think about your decisions this week, such as your work, your rest, your words, and your time. Offer them to God in prayer each morning, telling Him that you want to live thankful for His mercy.
exp.1:4:
A stubborn person, one who does not want to change their attitude or turn back to God, is building up punishment for themselves, the way someone stores up a treasure, but of wrath. Storing up means gathering and keeping. That punishment will be seen on the day of judgment, when God will show that his judgment is completely just.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He had been speaking against those who judge others for their sins while doing the same things themselves. They think they will escape from God. Paul reminds them that God's kindness and patience are not permission to carry on as before, but an invitation to repent.

For today: do not confuse God's patience with indifference. If there is something God is showing you, do not put it off or make excuses for yourself. Tell the truth to him today, ask for forgiveness, and take one concrete step of change. His kindness is guiding you toward that path.
exp.12:3:
This verse says that civil authority is "minister of God," that is, a servant placed there for your good. If you do what is good, you have no reason to fear it. But if you do what is evil, you should be afraid, because "he does not bear the sword in vain": the sword symbolizes its power to punish. "Avenger to execute wrath" means that it carries out justice against the one who does harm.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, a city with a great deal of political power. He wants them to live in order and not let their faith be confused with rebellion. Some scholars point out that Paul is describing the ideal role of authority, and that the Bible also shows cases where obeying God comes first (Acts 5:29).

Today we can respect the laws, pay our taxes, and be good citizens as part of our witness, praying for those who govern, without ceasing to obey God in what matters most.
exp.14:8:
This verse says that Christ also came so that the Gentiles, that is, those who are not Jews, would give glory to God for his mercy, or in other words, for his compassion and kindness. "To confess" here means to praise or publicly acknowledge God. "I will sing to your name" means to sing to him with gratitude.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, where Jewish and Gentile believers sometimes clashed. He reminds them that Christ served the Jewish people to fulfill the promises made to their fathers, and that God always wanted the nations to praise him too. That is why he quotes the Old Testament (Psalm 18:49), where David promises to praise God among the nations.

For today: God received us through pure mercy, not because we earned it. That invites us to welcome with respect those who are different from us in the church and to praise God together.
exp.7:32:
It says that no one can bring a valid accusation against the people God has chosen, that is, his children. The reason is simple: God himself is the one who justifies them, meaning he declares them free from guilt and accepts them as righteous before him. The words for "accuse" and "chosen" are used the way they would be in a courtroom.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God gave his own Son for us. Confident of that, he asks questions as in a trial: if the Judge has already declared us righteous, who will be able to condemn us? He then goes on to speak of Christ, who died, rose again, and intercedes for us.

For today: when guilt or memories accuse you, do not give them the final word. Come before God trusting in what Christ has done for you, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.3:14:
It says that the law produces wrath, that is, God's righteous anger against sin. The law shows what God requires, and when someone fails to keep it, they stand under judgment. And where there is no law, there is also no violation, which means crossing over a clear command.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that Abraham received God's promise through faith, not by keeping the law. If the inheritance depended on the law, faith would accomplish nothing, because no one keeps it perfectly. That is why the promise comes by grace.

For today: instead of trusting that your efforts make you acceptable before God, humbly acknowledge where you fall short and rest in his grace. That trust also leads you to obey him out of gratitude, not out of fear.
exp.1:12:
It says that hearing what God commands is not enough to be right with Him. What counts is putting it into practice. Those who only hear it are set against those who do it, and "justified" means being declared righteous, approved by God.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. The Jews had the law and felt secure because they knew it. Paul reminds them that God judges with impartiality: whether a person had the law or did not have it, each one answers before Him. Later in this same letter, he explains that no one manages to keep it perfectly and that salvation comes through faith in Christ. Some scholars see here a hypothetical condition; others see a sign of true faith that shows itself in deeds.

For today: don't be satisfied with only listening to sermons or reading the Bible. Choose one thing God has shown you this week and put it into practice.
exp.5:9:
He says that when Christ died, he died to sin "once," meaning one time and for all time. His death is not repeated. And the life he now has, he lives for God. The expression "died to sin" does not mean that Jesus sinned, but that he faced the power of sin and death and completed that work entirely.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that, through faith, whoever is united with Christ shares in his death and his resurrection. He sets Christ forward as both model and foundation: if he is no longer under the power of death, those who are in him must not live under the rule of sin either.

Today we can remember that sin no longer has the final word over us. When you find yourself trapped in a bad habit, pray and decide to live that day for God, trusting in Christ's strength and not your own.
exp.10:9:
This verse asks that the eyes of certain people be darkened so that they cannot see, and that their back be bent over forever. The phrase about bending the back means that their spine is bowed under a heavy burden, like slavery or constant suffering.

The apostle Paul quotes here Psalm 69:22-23, attributed to David. He speaks of many of his people, Israel, who had not recognized Jesus as the Messiah. But he soon makes clear that their fall is not permanent: in the verses that follow he says that their stumbling opened the door to non-Jews, and that God still has purposes for Israel.

For today: when someone rejects faith, let us not judge them with pride. Better to pray for that person with hope, remembering that God is still at work and that his mercy can reach anyone.
exp.10:30:
This verse says that the people of Israel, for now, have not believed in Christ. But God uses that situation to show mercy to the non-Jews (the Gentiles, that is, "you"). And the final goal is that Israel also receive that same mercy. "Mercy" means compassionate love that forgives us even though we do not deserve it.

Paul, a Jewish apostle, writes to the church in Rome, made up of Jews and Gentiles. He explains that God has not abandoned Israel, because his promises are not canceled (v. 29). Christians have understood in various ways how and when Israel will receive that mercy, but Paul makes clear that God has a plan of compassion.

For today: no one is beyond the reach of God's mercy. If you have received forgiveness, do not boast; give thanks and pray with hope for those who today seem far from God.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that there will be a day when God will judge the hidden things of people, that is, the thoughts, motives and secrets that no one else sees. That judgment will be carried out by Jesus Christ. Paul says "according to my gospel," that is, in line with the message he preaches.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke about the Gentiles, who, without the law of Moses, show in their conscience that they know what is good and evil. This verse closes that thought: God judges with justice, including what is inward. Next, Paul will turn to the Jews who trust that they have the law.

For today: it is not enough to look good before people. God looks at the heart. You can pray sincerely and ask him to examine your intentions, and trust that Christ, who will judge, also offers forgiveness.
exp.4:14:
This verse says that God's gift is not like the fall of Adam, because it is far greater. Through the sin of one man, Adam, many died. But the grace of God, that is, his favor that we do not deserve, and the gift, abounded much more for many through Jesus Christ. The "gift" here is the free gift, and a "trespass" is a fall into sin or disobedience.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that we are made right with God through faith. Here he compares Adam with Christ, who is described as a pattern of the one to come. Adam brought death; Christ brings life. Paul wants to show that grace far exceeds sin. Scholars debate how far the phrase "the many" should be applied, but the central contrast is clear.

Today, when your failure or your past weighs on you, remember that the grace of Christ is greater. Receive it with humility and live thankfully, sharing with others the forgiveness you have received.
exp.9:7:
Paul asks, "But what saith it?" and answers that the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart. That word is the message of faith that the apostles preached. The phrase "the word of faith, which we preach" refers to the gospel message that was proclaimed.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and quotes Deuteronomy 30:11-14. He explains that righteousness by faith does not require impossible feats, such as going up to heaven or down into the deep to find Christ. God has already come near to us in Jesus, and the message is within reach of everyone, both Jews and Gentiles.

Today, you do not need to accomplish anything extraordinary to draw near to God. His message is already close to you. You can open your Bible, believe it sincerely, and speak to him today in prayer, using simple words.
exp.15:15:
Paul asks that Christians greet one another with a holy kiss. It was a greeting of affection and respect between brothers and sisters. He then adds that all the churches of Christ send their greetings.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome and, at the end, greets many people by name. With that greeting he wants to unite the church and show that it is not alone, but part of a larger family. Afterward he warns about those who divide the community.

Today we can care for unity through simple gestures: greeting one another warmly, shaking hands or giving a hug, and reaching out to anyone who feels lonely in the church. Greetings vary from culture to culture, but sincere love remains the same.
exp.14:5:
He says that God wants believers to live in harmony, so that all together, as with one voice, they praise God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. "Agreeing" means being united, in accord. "With one mouth" means "with one voice." "Glorify" means to honor and praise.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were Jews and non-Jews who had differences over customs and food. Before this, he asks that God give them patience and comfort so that they may be of one mind. Unity does not mean thinking identically about everything, but following the example of Christ. The final purpose is that God be praised.

For today: if there is tension with another believer over secondary matters, seek peace first. Pray for that person and, if you can, praise God together. Shared worship helps heal divisions.
exp.2:2:
Paul asks a question: if some Jews did not believe, does their lack of faith cancel out the truthfulness of God? The word "vain" means without value or without effect. The question expects a negative answer, and Paul gives it right away: "By no means."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and answering objections that a Jew might raise. He has just said that the people of Israel were entrusted with the word of God. Now he imagines this doubt: if many did not believe, did God fail in his promise? Paul argues that God is faithful, even when people are not.

For today: the faith of others, or even our own when it wavers, does not change who God is. If you see someone drifting away or failing, do not conclude that the Word has lost its power. Rest in the fact that God is true and keeps what he has said.
exp.7:22:
This verse says that not only creation suffers and groans, but we too, as believers. We have the "firstfruits of the Spirit," that is, the first foretaste, the first sample of what God will give in full. Even so, we sigh inwardly, waiting for the "adoption," which here means the full showing that we are children of God, that is, the "redemption of our body": that our body be transformed and freed from suffering and death.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has been speaking of how the whole creation suffers because of the effect of sin and waits to be set free. He wants to encourage believers: their present pain is not the end, and God has already given them the Spirit as a guarantee of what is coming.

For today: if you feel weariness, sickness, or sadness, do not pretend that everything is fine. Groan honestly before God, but with hope, remembering that the Spirit in you is the promise that the best is still to come.
exp.14:0:
The explanation says that Christians whose faith is more mature and secure should patiently carry the weaknesses of those who are less firm. The word "bear" means to endure or help carry a burden. The "weak" are those who are weak in faith or in conscience. And "not to please ourselves" means not living only to seek what we enjoy or what suits us.

Paul writes to the believers in Rome. In the previous chapter he speaks of disagreements over foods and special days. Some had a more sensitive conscience and others a freer one. Paul includes himself among the strong and asks them not to despise others, but to support them, following the example of Christ.

For today: if you have more clarity or experience in the faith, do not mock someone who still doubts or struggles. Be patient, listen, help, and avoid doing anything that would make them stumble, even when you have the freedom to act.
exp.10:7:
It says that God gave many of Israel a "spirit of remorse," a word that here does not mean guilt but a spiritual dullness or stupor. They had eyes and ears, but they did not understand what God was doing. And this continued "unto this day," that is, until the time of Paul.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains why many of his people did not receive Christ, while a group chosen by grace did. To support this, he cites the Scriptures, with echoes of Deuteronomy 29:4 and Isaiah 29:10. He does not say that the door was shut forever; later he shows hope for Israel.

Today, ask God for a sensitive heart. Before reading the Bible, pray: "Lord, open my eyes and my ears." And listen with humility, without trusting in your own merits.
exp.13:14:
It says that if your brother is hurt or saddened by what you eat, you are no longer acting in love. And it asks you not to ruin, because of your food, someone for whom Christ died. Paul writes to the believers in Rome, where there were disagreements about food. Some believed certain foods were unclean; others, with a freer conscience, ate everything. Paul says that nothing is unclean in itself, but he asks the strong not to despise or cause to stumble those whose conscience is more sensitive.

Today, before you use your freedom in matters the Bible neither commands nor forbids, think about how it will affect the person near you. Love sometimes means giving way, without imposing your opinion or mocking another's conscience.
exp.2:13:
It says that people's mouths are full of "cursing," an old-fashioned word that means speaking badly about others, cursing, or insulting them. It also speaks of "bitterness," which is a way of speaking full of resentment, anger, and harshness. The words reflect what is in the heart.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. Here he gathers several passages from the Old Testament, especially Psalm 10:7, to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, is under sin and needs God. He is not speaking of one particular person, but of the human condition apart from God's grace. Scholars debate how much of this picture describes each individual, but the central point is our need for forgiveness.

Today we can examine how we speak, at home, at work, and online. Before we respond in anger, let us ask God to heal our hearts and help us speak with kindness and truth.
exp.14:6:
The verse says that we should receive and accept one another, just as Christ received us. The word "receive" here is an older form; in the original Greek the word used means "to receive" or "to welcome." Some modern versions translate it as "welcome one another." The goal is the glory of God.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where Jewish believers and non-Jewish believers lived side by side and had differences over customs and foods. Paul asks them for unity. The verses that follow show that Christ served both Jews and non-Jews, so that all might glorify God.

Today, think of someone in your church or family who thinks differently than you or who is hard for you to get along with. Instead of pulling away, welcome them with patience and respect, remembering that Christ welcomed you with all your failings.
exp.12:9:
It says that love never does harm to another person. For that reason, loving is what fulfills what God's law asks for. The word "love" in the verse is the one we use here; "neighbour" is any person we have near us, and "fulfilling" means the completion of the law, that is, what brings the law to its goal.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, who is writing to Christians in Rome. Earlier he asked them to live in peace and to respect the authorities. Here he sums up the commandments about how to treat others with one idea: love your neighbour as yourself. Afterward he encourages them to wake up and live as people of the light, because the final salvation is nearer.

Before you answer in anger, speak badly of someone, or take advantage of another person, ask yourself: "Does this do good or harm to that person?" Let love guide your decision.
exp.9:19:
Paul says that Isaiah spoke with great boldness (the word meaning here is with daring and without holding back). God declares that he was found by people who were not looking for him, and that he revealed himself to those who did not even ask about him.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains why many from Israel did not believe in Christ, while people from other nations did believe. He quotes Isaiah 65:1 to show that this had already been announced in the Scriptures. God was not failing: his plan had always included all peoples. The verses that follow show his patience with Israel.

For today: do not give up on any person who seems far from God. He can find them without their seeking him. Pray for them, treat them with love, and share your faith simply, trusting that God is the one who takes the initiative.
exp.8:17:
He says God is free to act with mercy toward whomever He decides, and that He also leaves hardened whomever He decides. "Hardeneth" means to make the heart stubborn. "Whom he will" is understood as "the one whom He wills." Salvation does not depend on what we deserve, but on the goodness of God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just recalled Pharaoh, who resisted God, and God used that hardness to show His power. Paul wants to stress that God is sovereign. Christians have debated for centuries how God's will and human responsibility relate here, and not everyone understands it the same way.

For today: instead of boasting of our merits, we can receive God's mercy with humility and give Him thanks. If today you sense His call, do not harden your heart; respond to Him with trust.
exp.0:27:
These people did not want to acknowledge God or keep him in mind. Since they rejected him, God gave them over to a corrupted mind, a twisted mind unable to judge well, and so they did things that are not right, that are harmful and wrong.

The apostle Paul is speaking in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He is showing that all of humanity needs the gospel. Before and after this verse he lists harmful behaviors as the result of turning away from God. That God "gave them over" is usually understood to mean that God allowed them to follow their own path.

For today: do not make little of God in your daily life. Set aside time to pray and read the Bible, and ask him to help you think clearly. If you have drifted away, remember that the same gospel Paul proclaims offers forgiveness and a fresh start.
exp.7:20:
This verse says that creation, here called "the creature itself," will one day be set free from the "bondage of corruption." That means it will be freed from decay, deterioration and death. This freedom will come together with the "glorious liberty" that the children of God will receive. "Creature" refers to creation in general.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He explains that present suffering cannot be compared with the future glory. According to him, creation was made subject to "vanity" (frailty, emptiness) and now waits in hope. Some think he refers to all of nature; others, to all of humanity that does not believe. The first reading is the most common.

For today: when you see pain, sickness or loss, remember that it is not the last word. God promises to restore all things. Care for creation with gratitude and wait with patience.
exp.2:0:
Paul asks a question: if God treats Jews and non-Jews alike, what advantage does the Jew have then? What is the point of circumcision, the sign of the covenant that God gave to Israel? The words "what advantage...?" mean "or what profit is there...?"

Paul is the one speaking. He has just said in chapter 2 that having circumcision saves no one if the heart does not obey. He imagines a Jewish reader might object: "So is there no value in being part of Israel?" That is why he raises the question, and he immediately answers that there is great advantage: to them God entrusted his word.

For today: if we have received much, such as the Bible, a believing family, or a church, that is a gift to live out with humility, not a reason to feel superior. Let us be thankful for what God has entrusted to us and obey him from the heart.
exp.3:15:
The promise of God is received by faith, so that it is a gift of his grace and not a payment for obeying the law. In this way the promise stands firm and secure for all the offspring, that is, the descendants of Abraham. This includes those who have the law (the Jews) and also those who share the faith of Abraham, even though they have not received the law. Abraham is called the father of all who believe.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just said that if the inheritance depended on keeping the law, faith would be of no use. He wants to show that Abraham was counted as righteous because he believed, before receiving the law, and that for this reason the promise reaches everyone who trusts in God.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love by your performance. Trust in Christ and rest in his grace; from there, obey with gratitude and not out of fear.
exp.0:4:
Paul says that, through Jesus Christ, God gave him grace (a favor he did not deserve) and apostleship, that is, the assignment of being sent out as a messenger. His purpose is that people from all nations believe and obey. The obedience that comes from faith can be understood as obedience that springs from faith, or as obedience that consists in believing. Both ideas go together. All of this is done for his name, that is, by the authority of Christ.

Paul presents himself to the believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He has just spoken of Jesus as the Son of God and a descendant of David. Now he explains his mission: to bring this message to all peoples, not only to the Jews. In this way he prepares the Romans for the rest of his letter.

For today: true faith does not stay in words. Today you can ask God to show you one concrete step of obedience to Jesus.
exp.15:6:
Paul sends greetings to Andronicus and Junia. He calls them "kinsmen," which probably means they were Jews like him, and "fellow prisoners," meaning that at some point they were imprisoned with him. He says they are "of note among the apostles," and that they came to Christ before he did. Some understand that the apostles held them in high regard; others take it that they themselves were apostles in the sense of messengers sent out. This is a debated point.

Paul closes his letter to the Romans with a long list of personal greetings. He does not know everyone, but he wants to honor those who have served the gospel faithfully and at great cost.

Today, we can imitate Paul by openly recognizing those who have served faithfully, especially those who suffered or worked without anyone noticing. Thanking someone today for their service to Christ can encourage them greatly.
exp.6:13:
This verse says that God's law is spiritual, meaning it comes from God and reflects his character. By contrast, Paul says that he himself is "carnal," that is, weak and limited by his human nature, and "sold under sin," like someone bound and dominated by sin, like a slave who has been sold.

Paul is speaking here and explaining that the law is not to blame. The law is good; the problem is the sin that is in the human being. Scholars debate whether Paul is speaking here of his life before he knew Christ or of his struggle as a believer. Both views have defenders.

For today: be honest with God about your struggles. Do not blame what is good for your failures; acknowledge your weakness and seek the help of Christ, who gives freedom.
exp.9:13:
Paul asks a chain of connected questions. No one can call on someone they have not believed in. No one can believe in someone they have not heard of. And no one can hear without someone to proclaim the message. The word "call on" means calling on God to ask for his help, and "proclaim" means announcing the message of the gospel.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that God saves everyone who calls on him, whether Jew or Greek. Now he explains that this salvation comes through people who announce the message. In this way he argues that the gospel must be carried to everyone.

For today: faith often comes when someone shares what God has done in their life. Think of a person close to you, and this week look for a simple and kind way to speak to them about Jesus, or to pray for the one who does.
exp.14:7:
Paul says that Christ Jesus became a servant of the circumcision, that is, a servant to the Jewish people (the circumcised). He did this for the truth of God, meaning God's faithfulness to his word, in order to confirm the promises God made to the fathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where Jews and non-Jews had tensions. He asks them to accept one another as Christ accepted them. He reminds them that Jesus first served Israel, fulfilling what had been promised, and that this also opens the way for the Gentiles to glorify God for his mercy, as the following verse says.

For today: if Christ became a servant for others, we can patiently accept those who are different from us in culture or customs, and seek unity so that God may be glorified.
exp.11:1:
It says that we should not live according to the values and customs of this world, but be transformed from within, changing the way we think. The word "world" in this verse refers to the spirit and mindset of the present age. The phrase "be transformed" in the King James reading is the same idea: a real change in the way we think and live. The verse goes on to say that this change lets us prove and discover by experience that the will of God is good, acceptable, and perfect.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained God's mercy, and now he asks them to respond by giving their whole lives to him. This inner change prepares what follows: living with humility and serving in the church, as members of one body.

For today: before deciding something, ask yourself what the world thinks and what God's Word teaches. Spend a few minutes each day reading the Bible and praying, so that God renews your mind little by little.
exp.8:6:
Paul says that being a biological descendant of Abraham does not automatically make someone a true child of God. He cites Genesis 21:12: God said that the promised descendants would be called through Isaac, not through all of Abraham's children, such as Ishmael.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and feels great sorrow because many of his own people have not believed in Christ. Someone might think that God's word has failed. He answers that God has never promised salvation through blood alone, but has always worked through his promise and his calling.

For today: let us not trust our family, church, or tradition as if that could save us. What matters is to respond in faith to God's promise, and to give thanks that his love does not depend on our lineage, but on his grace.
exp.12:7:
It says we should not owe anyone anything, that is, we must pay what is due. But there is one debt that is never fully paid: loving others. The person near us is "neighbor", and whoever loves is already doing what God asks in his commandments.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He had been talking about paying taxes and giving respect to whom it is due. Now he widens the idea: beyond legal obligations, we all have a debt of love. He then explains that commandments such as not killing or not stealing are summed up in loving your neighbor as yourself.

For today: before thinking only about keeping rules, ask yourself how you can treat with love the person in front of you. Pay your bills on time and, in addition, do one concrete act of kindness for someone today.
exp.3:23:
This verse says that what God did for Abraham was not written for his sake alone, but for us as well. To those of us who believe in God, who raised up Jesus our Lord, the same thing will be credited to us. Being credited means having something placed to someone's account; here, God counts us as righteous.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that Abraham believed God's promise and for that reason was counted as righteous, not because of his works. Now he applies that example to all believers: the same faith unites us with Abraham.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor through perfect efforts. Trust in Jesus, who died and rose again, and rest in the fact that God receives you through that faith. From there, live with gratitude and obey with joy.
exp.10:33:
This verse asks two questions whose answer is obvious: no one. No one has fully understood the thoughts of God, and no one has been his counsellor, that is, someone who teaches him what to do.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has explained how God acts with Israel and with the nations, and he concludes that his mercy reaches everyone.
