Faced with something so great, Paul offers no more arguments but worships. He draws on ideas from the Old Testament, such as Isaiah 40:13, to remind us that God is wise beyond what we can measure.

Today, when you do not understand what God allows in your life, you can rest in the fact that he is wise and good. You do not need to have all the answers to trust him and worship him.
exp.1:16:
Here Paul addresses someone who bears the name "Jew," that is, who belongs to the people of Israel. That person rests confidently on the law of Moses and takes pride in their relationship with God. Resting on the law means leaning on it with assurance, and a title or name carried with honor is what is meant here.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, will give account to God. Now he speaks to the one who feels secure simply because they have the law. Many understand that this begins a warning: knowing the law is not enough if it is not lived out.

For today: having a Bible, going to church, or bearing the name of Christian is a privilege, but it does not replace an obedient life. Ask yourself humbly whether your faith shows in your actions.
exp.0:11:
Paul explains what he said before. He wants to visit the Christians in Rome, not only to give them a spiritual gift, but also to be comforted together with them. "Together" means "at the same time" or "with one another." The "mutual faith" is the faith they share: theirs and his.

Paul writes this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. He has just said he wants to strengthen them, and now he corrects himself with humility: he too needs encouragement. In this way he shows that the apostle and the believers help one another.

For today: no one is so mature that they do not need the encouragement of others. When you gather with brothers and sisters in the faith, go ready to give encouragement, but also to receive it. Today, encourage someone with a sincere word, and let others encourage you too.
exp.8:8:
This verse recalls the promise God made to Abraham: "At this time next year I will return, and Sarah will have a son." Paul is citing the story from Genesis 18:10, 14. "I will come" refers to God's visit, and "at this time" means on the appointed date. The important point is that Isaac was born through a word of promise, not through human strength.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He explains that being a descendant of Abraham by blood is not the same as being an heir of the promise. With the example of Isaac, he shows that God carries out his plans in the way he himself determines. Some interpreters discuss how this relates to election, but the central point here is the promise.

For today: trust that God does what he says, even when you cannot see how. Your faith rests not on your own abilities, but on his faithful word.
exp.13:11:
This verse says that each person will have to answer personally before God for their own life. Where it says "give account," the idea is to be accountable, to explain what one has done. "Á" is an old way of spelling "a."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were differences among believers about food and special days. Some were judging others for thinking differently. Paul reminds them that all of us will stand before the judgment seat of Christ, and that the judge is God, not us. For that reason he asks them to stop judging one another and to avoid putting a stumbling block in the way of a brother or sister.

Today, before criticizing someone for the way they live their faith in matters that are not essential, remember that you too will give an account to God. Attend to your own obedience, and treat others with patience and respect.
exp.8:13:
Paul asks a question that some would have been asking: if God chooses Jacob and not Esau, is God unjust? And he answers firmly: "God forbid," that is, "by no means." The words "hated" and "loved" are understood in several ways; many believe they express choice and preference, not human hatred.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just explained that God's promises depend on his calling and not on physical descent. He anticipates an objection and answers it with the example of Moses: God acts by mercy, and no one can claim from him as if he owed them something.

Today, this invites us to trust God even when we do not understand all his ways. We can rest in the knowledge that his mercy does not depend on our merits, and respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.7:21:
Verse 22 says that the whole creation groans and suffers together, like a woman in labor pains, and that it has continued this way until now. The word "creation" here refers to all that God has made, not only to people. The verse says that creation groans together, and "together" means at the same time as one. The labor-pain image is one of suffering that announces something new.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that creation was subjected to corruption and that it will be set free. Some think he speaks of nature as a whole; others, of everything created in general. His point is that the present suffering is not the end, but the prelude to something glorious.

For today: when suffering or a broken world wears you down, do not think that God has forgotten you. You can groan honestly before Him, and at the same time wait with patience, because that pain points toward a promised renewal.
exp.11:14:
This verse asks us to share in the feelings of others. "Rejoice" means to be glad, and "them that do rejoice" are those who are content. So we are glad with the one who celebrates, and we weep with the one who suffers. It is sharing the heart of the other person, without indifference.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. In this chapter he explains how to live their faith day by day. Earlier he speaks of helping those in need, of being hospitable, and of blessing those who persecute. Afterward he stresses unity, humility, and not repaying evil with evil. This verse brings all of that together: to love is to draw near.

Today you can apply it this way: when someone tells you good news, be truly glad for them, without envy. And when someone is suffering, do not rush to give advice; stay with them, listen to them, and weep with them.
exp.1:25:
This verse says that if a person who is not circumcised obeys what God's law requires as right, God will count them as though they were circumcised. The phrase "righteous requirements of the law" means the commandments and what the law asks as upright. An "uncircumcised" person is one who lacks the physical sign of the Jewish covenant.

The apostle Paul is speaking to Jews who trusted in having circumcision and the law, but did not live according to them. He wants to show that the outward sign is not enough if the heart and conduct do not obey God. Gentiles who obey put to shame those who merely boast of their religion.

For today: do not trust in labels, baptisms, customs, or church attendance as if they were sufficient. Ask yourself honestly whether your life reflects obedience and love for God, and ask him to change your heart.
exp.12:12:
Paul invites us to live honorably, as people who live in the full light of day. He names behaviors we must leave behind: eating and drinking to excess, sexual immorality, and quarrels and jealousy. Quarrels are fights or disputes, and jealousy is envy.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the night is nearly over and that the day of salvation is drawing near. For this reason he calls them to put aside the works of darkness and to clothe themselves with Jesus Christ, as the following verse says.

Today we can ask ourselves what hidden or disordered habit keeps us from living in the light. Perhaps it is excess, a harmful relationship, or resentment. Today you can bring it to God in prayer and ask him for strength to begin again.
exp.2:29:
Paul says that God is one, and for that reason there is only one way to be declared righteous before Him: faith. The words "circumcision" and "uncircumcision" refer to Jews and to those who are not Jews. The verb "justify" means that God declares them righteous, free of guilt before Him.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and non-Jews. Some believed that Jews had a special advantage for being saved through the law. Paul answers with a basic truth: if God is one, He is the God of all, and He treats everyone equally. He then makes clear that this does not overturn the law but upholds it.

Today, no matter your background, your church, your culture or your past, no one has an advantage before God. Trust in Christ, and treat other believers as equals, neither feeling superior nor inferior.
exp.13:4:
Paul says that some believers give more value to certain days than to others, while others think all days are the same. He then adds that each person should be "fully persuaded in his own mind," that is, firmly convinced in his mind and heart about what he does before God. Here the word "esteem" means to regard or value.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers from different backgrounds who argued about foods and special days. It is not known with certainty which days were meant, although many think they were Jewish festivals or fasts. He asks for respect in matters that are not essential, because each one acts for the Lord.

Today we can be patient with brothers and sisters who practice their faith in a different way on secondary matters. Before criticizing, ask yourself: is this person doing it to honor the Lord? Seek your own conviction in prayer, and treat with love the one who thinks differently.
exp.0:26:
The verse says that the men left the natural relationship with women and burned with desire for one another, doing shameful things between men. With that, they received in themselves the consequences that belonged to their going astray. "Desires" here means strong and disordered longings; "shameful" means so indecent that it is embarrassing to name them; "payment" here means the outcome or consequence of their error.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs the gospel. In this passage he describes how humanity turned away from God, worshiping created things instead of the Creator, and how God gave them over to the consequences of their rebellion. Scholars debate some details of this text, but the central point is that Paul speaks of a humanity that exchanged the truth for a lie.

This passage reminds us that all of us need the grace of God, for the next chapter warns against judging others. Let us examine our own hearts with humility and draw near to God with confidence.
exp.4:3:
It says that patience (the ability to endure with steadiness) produces proof, that is, a tested character, like metal that comes out of the fire clean and strong. And that tested character produces hope. Other versions translate this as "approved character." The word "weak" in the next verse means feeble.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that we are made right with God by faith, not by works. Now he shows that difficulties are not a sign that God has abandoned us. On the contrary, God uses them to form our character, and hope does not end in shame because God has already shown his love to us in Christ.

For today: when you go through a difficult situation, don't only ask "why me?" Also ask "what is God forming in me?" Endure with confidence in him, and your hope will grow.
exp.2:28:
Paul asks a question and answers it himself: is God only the God of the Jews? No, he is also the God of the Gentiles, that is, of all the peoples who are not Jews. The word "yes" here means "without any doubt."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, among whom there were believers who were Jews and believers who were not. He has just said that no one is saved by keeping the law, but by faith. If salvation came through works of the law, God would belong only to those who received it. But since it is by faith, the door is open to everyone. That is why he insists that God is one.

Today we can remember that God has no favorites by origin, country, culture or history. If God receives everyone through faith, then we too should welcome with respect and kindness anyone within the church who thinks or lives differently from us.
exp.12:5:
The explanation says that Christians pay taxes because the authorities are God's servants, that is, servants whom God allows to maintain order. Taxes are the money people pay to the government. The phrase "attending continually upon this very thing" means they devote themselves to that task: governing, protecting justice, and restraining evil.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, who lived under the empire. He had been speaking about submitting to the authorities, not only out of fear of punishment but out of conscience. Paying taxes was a concrete way of living out that attitude. Some scholars think there were tensions over taxes in Rome, but this is debated.

For today: fulfill your obligations, such as declaring and paying what is owed, with honesty and without resentment. Do it as an act of integrity before God, even when you do not agree with everything the government does.
exp.5:15:
We all become servants of whatever we yield ourselves to in order to obey. There are two paths: obeying sin, which ends in death, or obeying God, which leads to righteousness, that is, to a upright life before Him.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that they are under grace, not under the law, and he anticipates an objection: "Shall we sin, then?" He answers with an emphatic "God forbid." Grace is not permission to sin, because whoever gives himself over to sin becomes a slave to it again. He then thanks God that they have already been set free.

For today: no one is completely neutral; what we repeat and obey shapes us. Today you can ask yourself which habit is mastering you, and hand it over to God, asking for His help to obey Him in one specific thing.
exp.11:16:
It says that we should not return harm for harm. If someone does us wrong, we do not answer with another wrong.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he explains how to live out love in practice: with humility, unity, and compassion. Shortly after, he asks them to seek peace as far as possible and to leave vengeance to God, quoting the Scriptures (Deuteronomy 32:35). This shows that wrong received is not answered with self-righteous justice, but by trusting in God.

Today, when someone offends you, whether in person or on social media, do not repay them in kind. Wait, breathe, pray, and choose a calm and respectful response. In this way your witness speaks well of Christ.
exp.9:18:
Paul asks, "Did not Israel know?" and answers with Moses. God said he would make Israel jealous with "a people that are no people," that is, with nations that were not the chosen people. The word "foolish" in the verse refers to a people without understanding, and "anger" means strong displeasure. To provoke someone to jealousy means to stir up envy.

Paul, the apostle, explains why many of his own people did not believe in Christ. It was not for lack of warning: Israel had heard and had the Scriptures. He quotes Deuteronomy 32:21 to show that God had already announced that his message would also reach other nations.

Today, we must not think of ourselves as owners of God's grace or look down on anyone. God calls those whom no one expects. Furthermore, we can live our faith with such humility and joy that others feel a desire to know him.
exp.0:1:
It says that the gospel of God is not a new idea. God "had promised beforehand" this good news through his prophets, and that promise was written in the holy scriptures, that is, what we today call the Old Testament. The word "beforehand" indicates that God announced it long ago.

Paul introduces himself to the Christians of Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. He makes clear that the message he preaches does not contradict the faith of Israel, but fulfills it. This was important because that church included believers of Jewish background and believers of non-Jewish background. The following verse explains that this promise concerns Jesus, the Son of God.

For today: read the Old Testament too. You will see how God was preparing the way for Jesus, and that will strengthen your confidence that God keeps what he promises.
exp.13:10:
This verse says that God himself promises, with an oath ("as I live"), that every knee will bow before him and every tongue will openly acknowledge him. The phrase "as I live" is a solemn oath by God's own life, and "every tongue shall confess to God" means acknowledging and praising God.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome who were arguing with one another about foods and special days. He quotes the Old Testament (it appears to be taken from Isaiah 45:23) to remind them that the only Judge is God. In context, the judgment seat is Christ's, and all of us will give an account, not to other believers, but to him.

For today: when you feel the urge to criticize or look down on another believer over secondary differences, remember that you and he will both give account to the same Lord. Better to pray for that person, treat them with respect, and take care that your way of living does not make them stumble.
exp.5:2:
Paul asks whether believers do not know that, having been baptized into Christ Jesus, they were baptized into his death. The word "know" in the verse is the same as "know" here: he means that the baptism joins the person with Christ, even in his death. Some understand this as a real spiritual union, and others as a picture of that union; Christians explain it in different ways.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God's grace is abundant, and now he answers an objection: if grace grows where sin is, may we go on sinning? He answers no, because whoever belongs to Christ has already died to sin.

For today: when you feel the temptation to excuse a bad habit by saying that God will forgive you, remember that in Christ you have a new life. Ask God for help to live according to what you already are in him.
exp.15:14:
Paul asks that a group of people be greeted: Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas. He also sends greetings to all the believers who are with them. The word "greet" in this verse is the instruction to pass on greetings from him. "Saints" refers to the Christians, the people set apart for God.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, and at the end he names many people. These were probably groups that met in homes. The Bible says nothing more about exactly who they were; some think Philologus and Julia were a married couple or relatives, but that is not certain.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom almost no one remembers. We can follow Paul's example by encouraging others by name: today, write to or greet someone in your church and thank God for their faith.
exp.7:19:
This verse says that all creation was subjected to "vanity," that is, to emptiness, frailty and frustration. It did not do so willingly, but because of the one who subjected it, and it was subjected in hope. Here "creatures" refers to creation in general.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the sufferings of the present and of the glory that is to come. Many understand that "the one who subjected it" is God, who allowed this condition after the fall of Adam (Genesis 3). Others think of Adam himself. Paul makes clear that this subjection has a purpose full of hope.

For today: if you suffer or see a broken world, remember that you are not the only one who groans. God has a plan of restoration. Wait with patience and care for his creation in the meantime.
exp.10:27:
Regarding the good news of the gospel, the people of Israel appear as "enemies" of God, since most of them did not accept it, and this turned out for your good, you non-Jewish believers. But regarding the choosing, that is, God's selection of them, they remain deeply loved because of their ancestors: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The word "you" in the first part refers to the same people addressed here.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were a mix of Jews and non-Jews. He explains to them that the rejection by many Israelites is not the end of the story. God opened the door to the nations, but he has not forgotten his promises to Israel. Some understand "enemies" as enemies of God, and others as opponents of the gospel; the text allows both readings.

Today we can treat with humility and love those who do not yet believe, without looking down on them with pride. If God remains faithful to his promises, we too can trust that he will not abandon us.
exp.8:16:
Paul quotes what God said to Pharaoh in Exodus 9:16. The phrase "raised thee up" means that God placed him in his position of power, or kept him standing. The purpose was to show God's power in him, so that his name would be known throughout all the earth.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that salvation depends on God's mercy, not on human effort. He uses Pharaoh as an example, since God acted in Pharaoh's story to make his name known.

Interpreters debate how God's decision and Pharaoh's own hardness relate to each other; the Bible says that Pharaoh hardened his heart and also that God hardened him.

Today we can rest in the knowledge that God governs history, even when evil seems to win. It is also a call to humility: we cannot boast about what we have received, because everything comes from his mercy. Let us respond with gratitude and with hearts ready to listen to him.
exp.0:15:
Here, Paul says he is not ashamed of the gospel, that is, the good news about Jesus. He calls it "the power of God," meaning God's power at work, for salvation, which here means being saved. That salvation is for everyone who believes, without exception. The phrase "to the Jew first" indicates that the message came first to the Jewish people, and then also to the Greeks, who represent the other peoples.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, a powerful and cultured city, which he still wished to visit. He felt a debt to everyone, cultured or not, and that is why he wanted to proclaim the gospel to them. What follows explains why the gospel is the power of God: in it the righteousness of God is revealed, and it is received through faith.

For today: you do not need your faith to look impressive in order to share it. Trust that the power is in the message, not in your own skill. Share with simplicity and kindness what Christ has done for you.
exp.3:20:
Paul says that Abraham was completely certain that God would do what he had promised, because God has the power to carry it out. "Fully persuaded" means he had no doubts. "Able" means God has the capacity and the strength to do it. Old spellings and forms of the verbs are not part of the wording your reader sees.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans. He presents Abraham as an example of faith. Although Abraham and Sarah were already very old to have children, he trusted God's promise. Paul wants to show that God counted him as righteous because he believed, not because of his works.

For today: when a promise of God seems impossible, remember who God is and not only how your situation looks. You can pray and trust that he is faithful and capable, and keep going with patience.
exp.8:21:
He says that God wanted to show his anger against sin and make his power known, yet still bore with great patience those who are headed toward destruction, described as the vessels of wrath. Patience is the word for the gentleness and forbearance God showed. The word that is rendered as well known simply means known to all.

The phrase about those prepared for destruction is understood in different ways: some see that God prepared them, while others see that they prepared themselves by rejecting him.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He uses the image of the potter to show that God is free and just in his decisions. He asks, "What if...?", to show that God does not act in haste but with patience, and that his mercy also reaches the Gentiles.

For today: when you see that God is slow to judge evil, remember that his patience is an opportunity for us to repent. Make use of it with humility and trust in him.
exp.2:18:
It says that everything Scripture teaches as law is addressed to those who received it, that is, to the Jews. Its purpose is that no one has an excuse, and that everyone is silenced, with nothing to say in their own defense. Thus the whole world comes under accountability before God.

Here the apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Romans. He has just cited several texts from the Old Testament that show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, is under sin. With this he prepares the way to explain that salvation does not come from keeping the law, but from the grace of God.

For today: instead of justifying ourselves or comparing ourselves with others, we can humbly recognize that we need God. That honesty draws us closer to his mercy.
exp.13:6:
It says that none of us lives only for himself, and no one dies only for himself. Our life and our death have to do with others and, above all, with God.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking to the Christians in Rome. There were disagreements among them about which days to keep and which foods to eat. Paul reminds them that, although they think differently on those matters, each one seeks to honor the Lord. Therefore they must not judge or look down on one another. The verses that follow explain that we belong to Christ, both in life and in death.

For today: before criticizing a brother who thinks differently on secondary matters, ask yourself whether he is trying to honor God. Respond with respect, patience, and love, remembering that both of you belong to the same Lord.
exp.14:26:
They say the Christians of Macedonia and Achaia gave an offering willingly, but also that they owed it to the believers in Jerusalem. The Gentiles received spiritual blessings through them, so it is fair that they help them with material things. "Carnal" here does not mean sinful, but things of everyday life, such as money and food. "Partakers" means that they shared.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome before traveling to Jerusalem. He is carrying a collection for the poor believers there. He explains that this help is voluntary, but also an act of gratitude, because the gospel reached the Gentiles from the Jewish people. In addition, he wants Rome to understand his mission before visiting them on his way to Spain.

For today: think about who has taught or strengthened you in the faith. Look for a concrete way to thank them, whether with practical help, an offering, or your time, giving with joy and not out of obligation.
exp.11:17:
The explanation says we should do everything possible to live at peace with everyone. "If it is possible" recognizes that this does not depend on one person alone, and "as much as is in you" means "as far as it depends on you." The phrase about the old forms of address, comparing "you all" with other forms, has been removed since it refers to wording not found in the verse.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there was tension and opposition. Earlier he asked for humility and not to repay evil with evil. Then he teaches not to take revenge, but to leave justice to God, and to do good even to the enemy. About the "burning coals," some see an invitation for kindness to awaken shame and repentance; others see it as judgment. It is interpreted in several ways.

Today: if you have a conflict with someone, take the first step. Greet them, ask forgiveness if you were wrong, or respond calmly, without demanding that the other person change.
exp.6:10:
It says that sin seized an opportunity. It used God's commandment, which is good, to deceive Paul and lead him to spiritual death. The phrase "taking occasion" here means seizing the moment or the open door. The problem was not with the commandment but with the sin that used it.

The apostle Paul is speaking, explaining the relationship between God's law and sin. Some believe he draws on his own experience; others think he speaks in a more general way, and there are different opinions on this. What is clear is that he wants to defend the law: in the verses that follow, he says it is holy, just, and good. The fault lies with sin, not with the law.

For today: when a commandment of God shows us our weakness, let us not blame God or ignore it. Let us allow it to lead us to recognize our need of Christ, who does give us forgiveness and life.
exp.3:6:
It says that the people whose wrongdoings God forgives and whose sins he covers are happy, or blessed. "Blessed" here means deeply happy and favored. "Wrongdoings" are acts of evil, and "covered" means that God no longer holds them against those people.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. To show that God declares us righteous through faith and not through our works, he quotes King David in Psalm 32:1-2. David speaks of the joy of someone who has been forgiven without deserving it. Paul uses this as an example that forgiveness is a gift.

For today: if you trust in Christ, you do not have to live carrying old guilt. Bring your failure honestly to God, receive his forgiveness, and walk in joy and gratitude.
exp.2:8:
It says that neither the Jews nor the other peoples have an advantage before God. Paul asks, "Are we better than they?" and answers firmly, "In no wise." The phrases "accused" and "under sin" mean that he had already shown that all people are under the power and guilt of sin. "Gentiles" are people who are not Jewish.

The apostle Paul is speaking, writing to the Christians in Rome. He had just defended that God is just, even when some criticized him or twisted his words. Now he sums up what he explained in the earlier chapters: Jews and non-Jews alike need the mercy of God. Next he will cite the Scriptures to support this.

For today: do not compare yourself with others to feel more acceptable before God. Recognize with humility your need for Him, and treat with compassion those who also struggle with their failings.
exp.15:23:
The verse is a blessing: Paul wishes that the grace of Jesus Christ, that is, his undeserved favor and kindness, be with all the believers in Rome.

Paul dictates this letter, and Tertius, his secretary, writes it down and adds his own greetings. Paul is probably in Corinth, surrounded by companions and friends such as Gaius and Erastus, who send greetings to the brothers and sisters in Rome. Many scholars note that this verse is missing from some ancient manuscripts, where a similar blessing appears in verse 20, and the letter ends with the praise in the verses that follow. For that reason the textual tradition shows some variation.

For today: before you say goodbye to someone, truly bless them. A short prayer or a word of encouragement reminds them that they live by God's grace and not by their own merits.
exp.2:3:
It says that the unbelief of some does not nullify the faithfulness of God. "By no means" is a firm refusal: never! Even if every human being turned out to be a liar, God would still be true. "That thou mightest be justified in thy sayings" means that God is recognized as just and faithful in what he says. "And mightest overcome when thou art judged" means that God wins when someone tries to accuse him.

In this letter Paul writes to believers in Rome, and he answers possible objections from a Jew. If some of Israel did not believe, did God fail in his promises? Paul says no. He quotes Psalm 51:4, where David acknowledges his sin and declares that God is just. Many scholars see the same turn there: human sin brings out the righteousness of God.

For today: when you doubt God or his Word because others fail, or even because you yourself fail, rest in the fact that he remains faithful. Trust what God says more than the changing opinions of people.
exp.8:24:
Paul quotes the prophet Hosea to say that God calls "my people" those who were not his people before, and "beloved" her who had not been beloved.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that God's plan includes both Jews and Gentiles. Hosea originally spoke of Israel, which had turned away from God and yet would be restored. Paul applies those words to the Gentiles who are now being called. Some scholars see here an application of the principle, and others see a broader fulfillment; in either case, the theme is the mercy of God.

No one is so far away that God cannot draw them near. If you feel like an outsider or unworthy, remember that God's mercy calls you by your name. And toward others, show that same welcome.
exp.10:24:
Paul says he does not want the brothers and sisters to be unaware of a "mystery," that is, something God has now revealed that was not understood before. A part of Israel has become hardened, meaning they have closed themselves to believing in Jesus, but this is temporary: it will last until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, which means the complete number of people from the nations.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, many of whom were not Jewish. He has just used the image of the olive tree, in which they are grafted-in branches. He warns them not to look down on Israel. How "and so all Israel will be saved" should be understood is debated among Christians, but Paul insists that God has not abandoned his promise.

Today: if you have received God's grace, do not think yourself better than others. Pray with hope for those who today seem far from God.
exp.14:16:
Paul says he has reason to boast, but only "through Jesus Christ," that is, because of what Christ has done, and in the things that pertain to God, that is, in his spiritual service. To glory means to rejoice in something and speak about it with confidence. The phrase "in those things which pertain to God" means "in what concerns God."

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that God made him a minister of Christ to the Gentiles, that is, to non-Jews. His boasting is not about himself: he quickly clarifies that he speaks only of what Christ accomplished through him, by word, deeds, and the power of the Spirit.

We can rejoice in what God does through our service, but without showing off. When something goes well in your work, your family, or your church, thank Christ first and recognize that everything comes from his grace.
exp.14:31:
Paul says that he hopes to come to the brothers and sisters in Rome with joy, if God permits it, and to be refreshed together with them.

Paul writes at the end of his letter to the Romans. Before going to Rome, he will bring a gift to the poor believers in Jerusalem, and he knows there is danger there. That is why he asks them for prayer. Note that he speaks of God's will: he does not take his arrival for granted, but his plans depend on God. How his journey went, the Bible tells later in Acts.

For today: make your plans with hope, but commit them to God in prayer. And seek the company of other believers, for God uses his people to give us encouragement and rest.
exp.9:10:
This verse says that anyone who puts their trust in Jesus will not be put to shame. "Put to shame" means to be let down or disappointed, like someone who trusted in something and it failed them. The promise is that faith placed in Christ will never end in shame.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and quotes the Scripture, probably Isaiah 28:16. He is coming from speaking about believing with the heart and confessing with the mouth. He then says that this promise is for everyone, Jews and Gentiles, with no difference. Paul wants to show that salvation is offered to everyone who believes.

Today, if you sometimes feel fear or hesitation about speaking of your faith, remember this promise. Trusting in Jesus will not leave you disappointed. You can speak of Him simply, knowing that God keeps what He promises.
exp.1:2:
Paul asks a direct question: if you criticize others for their wrongdoing while doing the same things yourself, do you really think God will not judge you? The phrase "condemn" means "judge," and "such things" refers to the sins Paul described in the previous chapter.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just shown that sin is serious throughout the whole world, and now he addresses the person who feels morally superior. Many believe he is thinking mainly of some Jews, but his warning applies to anyone. The verses that follow explain that God's patience aims to lead us to repentance.

Today, before pointing out someone else's fault, it is good to examine our own heart. If we acknowledge our mistakes with humility, we will be able to treat others with more compassion and turn to God to ask for forgiveness.
exp.8:31:
It says that Israel pursued the righteousness of God, but not through faith. Instead, they tried to earn it as if it could be gained by works of the law.

The phrase "they sought it" means that they chased after it or pursued it with effort. "They stumbled" means that they fell after colliding with something in their path. That "stumblingstone" is the obstacle that made them fall.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and feels deep sorrow for his people, Israel. He explains that many Jews worked very hard, but refused to trust God through Christ. That is why the stone spoken of by the prophets, which most interpreters understand to be Christ, became their stumbling block.

For today: it is not enough to strive to be good. Rest in the grace of Jesus, trust in Him, and stop trying to earn God's favor by your own merits.
exp.9:14:
It says that no one can announce God's message unless they have been sent. Paul quotes Isaiah 52:7: the feet of those who bring good news are "beautiful" because they bring peace with God. "Good things" means good things. "Sent" is the same as "sent."

Paul writes to the church in Rome. He explains that salvation is within reach of both Jews and non-Jews, but to believe, people must hear, and to hear, someone must bring the message. It is a chain: sending, preaching, hearing, believing, calling on the Lord. He then notes that not everyone obeys, as happened in Isaiah's time.

For today: we can be part of that chain. Pray for those who bring the gospel, support them in concrete ways, and, wherever God places you, share simply what Christ has done for you.
exp.13:15:
It says we should not let something good that we have or practice be spoken against by others. "Blasphemed" here means insulted or discredited. "Your good" may refer to Christian liberty, to faith, or to salvation, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where some believed certain foods were unclean and others did not. Paul tells them that the strong in faith have freedom to eat, but that they should not use it in a way that wounds their brother. If the disagreement causes quarrels or stumbling, even good liberty can come to look bad before others.

For today: before using your freedom in matters that are optional, ask yourself whether it helps or hurts the people near you. Sometimes love means giving up something that is permitted, so that the witness of Christ may be seen as clean and full of peace.
exp.1:9:
He says that God will give glory, honor, and peace to every person who practices good. This applies to the Jew first and also to the Greek, that is, to all the other peoples. The word "whoever" means "anyone who." The phrase "does good" refers to living by doing what is good and right.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke of God's judgment on the one who does evil, and here he shows the other side: God also rewards good. He insists that Jews and non-Jews are treated with the same justice, as the following verse confirms: "there is no partiality with God." Some understand that this passage speaks of the fruit of a true faith, not of earning salvation by works.

For today: do not compare yourself to others or judge them by their origin or their position. Do good with simplicity, knowing that God looks at the heart and treats everyone with justice.
exp.5:7:
It says that if we are united with Christ in his death, we trust that we will also share in his life. "We believe" means we affirm it with faith, not as a mere opinion. "Dead with Christ" does not refer to physical death, but to the fact that, through faith, our old way of living under sin was joined to the cross of Jesus.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God's grace is no excuse for continuing to sin. Earlier he spoke of baptism as a sign of this union with Christ. Now he affirms that dying with Christ leads to a new life, like that of Jesus risen, who no longer dies. Many understand that this life begins today and is completed in the final resurrection.

When sin tempts you, remember who you are in Christ. You no longer have to obey it. Ask God for strength and choose today one concrete action that reflects your new life.
exp.7:23:
This verse says that we were saved with our eyes fixed on the future. "We are saved in hope" means that we have already received salvation, but we do not yet see its fullness. Hope, by definition, concerns something that is not in plain sight. If we already see it, there is nothing left to hope for. "Why hope for what we already see?" is the sense of the verse's question.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of creation groaning and of us, who also groan, waiting for the redemption of our bodies. He recognizes that present life carries pain, but he places it within a promise that has not yet been fulfilled.

For today: when you go through a difficult wait, do not lose heart because you cannot yet see the result. Entrust your patience to God and remember that waiting for what is not yet seen is a normal part of Christian faith.
exp.6:17:
Paul says that in him, that is, in his weak human nature (the flesh), nothing good dwells. He wants to do what is right, but he does not manage to carry it out. The phrase "dwelleth" is the verse's word for "lives" or "dwells," and "perform" means "carry out," while "I find not" means "I cannot do it."

Paul speaks in the first person as he explains the relationship between God's law and sin. He maintains that the law is good, but it has no power to change the heart. Scholars debate whether he describes his life before knowing Christ, his struggle as a believer, or an experience that represents everyone. What is clear is that he shows our need for divine help.

For today: when you fail even while wanting to do good, do not remain in discouragement or make excuses. Acknowledge your weakness with sincerity and ask God for his strength, for true change comes from his grace.
exp.3:5:
Paul says that David also spoke of the happiness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without that person having done works to earn it. The word "blessed" means happy, joyful, favored. "Credits" means that God places to someone's account a righteousness that the person did not earn by their own merits.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and explains that no one is saved by their works. Earlier he spoke of Abraham, and now he cites David, who in Psalm 32 celebrated God's forgiveness. With this he shows that Scripture teaches the same thing throughout its history: God justifies by grace, not by payment.

For today: you do not have to strive to earn God's love. You can come to Him with confidence, thankful for His forgiveness, and obey Him out of gratitude, not out of fear or to win His approval.
exp.10:17:
It says we should not boast or look down on the branches, that is, the Jews who were broken off from the olive tree. If someone feels superior, he should remember that it is not he who supports the root, but the root that supports him.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, and he speaks above all to believers who are not Jews. He uses the image of an olive tree: the root represents God's promises to Israel, and the Gentiles were grafted into that tree. Paul wants to prevent pride and contempt toward the Jewish people.

Today we can remember that our faith rests on what God has done, not on our own merit. This leads us to live with humility and to treat with respect those who think differently or do not yet believe.
exp.3:17:
Abraham believed when, humanly speaking, there was no longer any reason to hope. The phrase "hope against hope" means that, although everything seemed impossible, he kept trusting God. In this way he would become "the father of many nations," that is, of many peoples. "Seed" means descendants, and "so shall it be" points to the promise that his descendants would be countless, like the stars (Genesis 15:5).

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that God accepts people by faith and not by keeping the law. Abraham is his example, because he believed God's promise before the law was given. For this reason he is the spiritual father of all who believe, whether they are Jews or not Jews.

For today: when your situation seems closed, do not trust in what you see, but in what God has promised. Pray, keep going with patience, and remember that God is faithful, even when you cannot see how.
exp.2:24:
He says that God publicly presented Jesus as a "propitiation," that is, the means by which the wrath against sin is satisfied and we are reconciled with God. This is received through faith in his blood, which speaks of his death as a sacrifice. In this way God shows that he is just, since in his patience he had let the earlier sins pass without punishing them fully. The word "forbearance" in the verse means holding back punishment out of patience.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, has sinned and needs to be justified freely. Here he explains how God can forgive without ceasing to be just: Christ bore the punishment. He then concludes that no one can boast about their works.

For today: when guilt weighs on you or you feel unworthy, remember that your forgiveness does not depend on your effort, but on what Christ has already done. Trust in him and live with gratitude, not with pride.
exp.2:12:
The explanation says that the words of sinners can be deadly and deceitful. "An open tomb" is an uncovered grave, from which comes a foul smell and death. "They deceive" means they use the tongue to mislead. "Vipers" are poisonous snakes; the poison hidden under the lips speaks of evil disguised as kind words.

Paul, the author of the letter, is speaking to believers in Rome. Here he gathers several quotations from the Old Testament, especially from the Psalms (Psalm 5:9 and 140:3), to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, needs God. His point is not that every person is equally bad, but that sin reaches all of humanity, including the way we speak.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself whether your words give life or wound. Ask God to cleanse your mouth and your heart, and seek to speak the truth with love.
exp.5:4:
Paul says that if we are united with Christ in a death like his, we will also be united with him in a resurrection like his. "Planted together" speaks of a plant that takes root and grows joined to another. The phrase "in the likeness of" means the same as "in a way like" the verse's wording. "We shall be" points to the new life God gives, which begins now and is completed in the final resurrection.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that grace abounds where sin is, and now he answers those who might think that one may therefore keep on sinning. He reminds them that baptism shows that whoever belongs to Christ has already died to the power of sin and received a new life.

For today: when you feel tied down by a bad habit, remember that you belong to Christ. Ask God for his strength, and take one concrete step today to live out that new life.
exp.7:30:
Paul asks, "What shall we then say to these things?" and answers with another question: if God is for us, who can be against us? He does not say there will be no opposition, but that no one can defeat the one whom God supports.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained God's plan: to know, call, justify, and glorify his people. After saying all of that, he concludes there is no reason for fear. Right away he reminds them that God gave his own Son for us, proof that he is on our side.

When you feel threatened, judged, or alone, remember that God has already shown his love in Christ. Pray with that confidence and take the next step without fear.
exp.3:7:
It says that the person is truly happy, blessed in the full sense, to whom God does not count their sin against them. The word "blessed" here means very happy and favored. The word "man" refers to a person, and "impute" means to record something to someone's account.

Paul is explaining that God declares people righteous through faith and not because of their works. To support this, he quotes King David, who in Psalm 32 speaks of the joy of being forgiven. Paul uses David and Abraham to show that this applies to Jews and non-Jews alike.

For today: when you feel the weight of your failures, do not try to earn forgiveness through effort. Come before God with sincerity, trust in what Christ has done, and rest in his forgiveness.
exp.14:32:
This verse is a short blessing. Paul wishes that the God who gives peace will be with all the believers in Rome. The explanation of the word "you all" and the word "Amen" are not needed for the reader, so they are dropped.

Paul writes at the end of his letter to the Romans. He has just asked them to pray for him: that he would be rescued from those who oppose him in Judea, that the help for the poor in Jerusalem would be well received, and that he could visit them with joy. After speaking of dangers and tensions, he closes with this wish of peace for the whole church.

For today: when you feel pressure or worry, pray for others and ask that God's peace be with them, and with you too. You can bless someone today with a simple prayer: "May the God of peace be with you."
exp.8:19:
Here the explanation says that a human being has no right to argue with God or to bring charges against him. It uses the image of a clay pot that asks the one who shaped it, "Why did you make me like this?" Where the explanation mentions a word meaning "argue," it means arguing back or disputing with words, as in the verse's question of who you are to talk back to God.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of God's mercy and of his freedom to act. Imagine someone objects, "If God decides, how can he still blame us?" Paul answers by reminding them that God is the Creator and we are his creatures. Some read this passage mainly as personal election, others as God's plan for nations; Christians have understood it in several different ways.

When you do not understand what God allows, do not accuse him. Bring your questions to him with humility and trust, remembering that he is wise and good.
exp.0:25:
The explanation says that, because they had rejected God, he left them given over to shameful passions. "Shameful passions" are desires that dishonor the person. The word "changed" here means they exchanged one thing for another. Paul mentions that some women exchanged natural sexual relations for one that is against nature, according to the order of creation as he understands it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He is showing that all humanity needs the gospel. His argument is that those who exchanged the truth of God for idolatry ended up distorting their own lives as well. The phrase "gave them up" indicates that God allows them to suffer the consequences of their own decisions. Scholars discuss how this passage should be applied, but almost all agree that its purpose is to show that all of us sin.

For today: before pointing out the sins of others, let us examine what we put in God's place, and remember that all of us need his grace.
exp.9:6:
The explanation says that no one needs to go down into the deep, that is, into the place of the dead, to bring Christ back up. The word "deep" here means the depth where the dead go. "Will descend" means "will go down," and "bring up again" means "bring back up from." Paul shows how absurd it would be to think that we would have to do something like that.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and speaks about the people of Israel. He uses words from Deuteronomy 30:12-14, where Moses says that the word of God is near. Paul applies this to Christ: he has already come and has already risen. Salvation is not earned through impossible efforts, because God has already accomplished it.

Today you can rest from the idea that you must earn God's favor. Christ has already done the work. Trust in him and tell him sincerely that Jesus is your Lord.
exp.9:17:
Paul asks a question: "Have they not heard?" And he answers that they have. "Their sound" and "their words" refer to those who proclaim the message. He says their voice has gone out into all the earth, "unto the ends of the world," that is, to the farthest limits of the known world.

Paul quotes Psalm 19:4 to show that God's message has reached very far. He has just said that faith comes by hearing. Someone might object that Israel did not believe because they did not hear. Paul answers that they did hear. Some think the psalm is applied here to creation and others to the spread of the gospel; the text allows for both.

Today we can remember that God wants everyone to hear his word. We can speak of Christ simply to those around us, trusting that God makes faith grow.
exp.9:11:
This verse says there is no difference between the Jew and the Greek, that is, between the people of Israel and the other nations. Jesus is the same Lord over all, and he is generous with everyone who calls upon him, that is, who asks him for help and salvation in faith.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, made up of both Jews and non-Jews. He has just explained that salvation is received by believing in the heart and confessing with the mouth. Here he makes clear that this promise is for everyone alike, with no privilege based on origin. He will go on to say that everyone who calls upon the Lord will be saved.

Today, this text invites us not to look down on anyone or to think that someone is too far from God. We can pray and speak about Christ with anyone, knowing that he receives with generosity everyone who seeks him.
exp.10:13:
Paul says that he honors his ministry in the hope that, when his own people see the blessings the non-Jews are receiving, they will feel jealousy, that is, a desire for what those others have. In this way some of them might be saved. "Mine own flesh" means his fellow countrymen, the Jews. To "provoke to emulation" is to stir up a holy desire to return to God.

Paul, an apostle sent to the Gentiles, writes to believers in Rome. Although most of Israel had rejected Jesus, he does not give them up for lost. He speaks to the Gentiles so that they will not feel superior, and he reminds them that God still loves Israel. Paul does his work in the hope that some will be saved.

For today: live your faith in a way that is so attractive and humble that others feel a desire to know God. And never give up on any person; pray for those who are still far away.
exp.2:14:
They are quick to act, without God, in order to do harm. The verse says their feet are swift to shed blood, which means they rush to hurt or kill. The phrase shows that violence is not something that costs them effort, but something they run toward.

Paul is writing in his letter to the Romans. Here he gathers several passages from the Psalms and Isaiah (such as Isaiah 59:7) to show that everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, is under sin (Romans 3:9-12). He does not say that every person is equally violent, but that sin affects everyone and can lead to these extremes.

For today: violence begins in the heart, with anger, contempt, or harsh words. Today you can ask God to heal your anger and seek peace with someone before the resentment grows. Christ is the one who gives us forgiveness and a new heart.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that, because of the faith Abraham had, God considered him righteous. The words "credited" and "counted" mean that God put it to his account, that is, He recognized him as righteous. "Was" was written with an accent mark back then; today it is simply "was."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that no one becomes righteous before God by keeping the law, but by trusting in Him. He holds up Abraham as an example: Abraham believed that God would keep His promise to give him a son, even though it seemed humanly impossible. Paul adds that this was not written only for Abraham, but also for those who believe in God, who raised Jesus from the dead.

For today: you do not have to earn God's favor through perfect effort. Trust in His promises, even when you cannot see how they will be fulfilled, and rest in what Christ has already done for you.
exp.0:5:
Paul tells the believers in Rome that they too belong to the nations among whom God calls people to obey through faith.

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. In the verses before this one, he explains that God gave him the task of calling all the nations to faith. Here he reminds them that they are not outside that plan, but inside it.

For today: your faith is not an accident or an achievement of your own, but a response to a call from Jesus. That gives you identity and purpose. Live today with the assurance that you belong to him and that he invited you first.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that the people it describes have no respect or reverence for God. "Fear of God" does not mean living in dread, but taking him seriously and honoring him. "Before their eyes" means that God is not in their minds or guiding what they do.

Here the apostle Paul is speaking. In Romans 3:10-18 he joins several quotations from the Psalms and from Isaiah to show that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, is under sin. This verse closes that list and returns to Psalm 36:1. Paul wants to reach his conclusion: no one is saved by keeping the law, but everyone needs the grace of God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, in our everyday decisions, we take God into account. Let us ask him for a heart that respects him and seeks to please him, with humility, knowing that we depend on his mercy.
exp.5:16:
Paul thanks God that the believers in Rome, who had once been slaves to sin, now obeyed from the heart the teaching of the gospel they received. The word "but" in the verse has a sense of contrast, and "form of doctrine" refers to the pattern or model of Christian teaching. "Delivered" suggests that they were placed under that teaching, like someone passing into the care of a new master.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just asked whether we may keep sinning because we are under grace, and he answers with a firm "God forbid." He explains that we all serve something: either sin or obedience. Here he celebrates that they have already changed masters.

For today: grace is not permission to sin, but power to live differently. Today you can thank God for your freedom and obey him from the heart, not out of mere obligation. Ask yourself in which area you need to stop serving old habits.
exp.6:21:
It says that, in the deepest part of his being, Paul takes delight in and loves what God commands. The "inward man" is the most intimate part of a person, where desires and conscience dwell. To "delight" means he feels joy and pleasure, not just obligation.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and describes an inner struggle between what he desires to do and what he actually does. Scholars disagree about whether he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ or of his experience as a believer. In either case, he shows here that his heart loves God's law, even though sin still drags him down.

If you sometimes long to obey God and still fall short, do not lose heart. That desire to do good is a sign of a heart that is sensitive to God. Bring your struggle to him honestly, and ask for his help each day.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that if God has already declared us righteous through the blood of Christ, then much more will he save us from his wrath. "Justified" means declared righteous, forgiven, and accepted before God. "His blood" points to the death of Jesus on the cross. "Saved from wrath" refers to being delivered from God's judgment against sin.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he said that Christ died for us while we were still sinners. Now he reasons this way: if God did the hardest thing when we were enemies, he will surely do the rest now that we are his friends. He wants to give them security and hope.

For today: when you doubt whether God still accepts you, remember that your salvation rests on what Christ has done, not on your performance. Rest in that security and live thankfully, with confidence.
exp.2:6:
Here Paul repeats an objection that some people raised against him. He says: "If my lie made God's truth shine more and gave him glory, why am I still judged as a sinner?" The old words are "however" (but) and "increased to his glory" (grew his glory).

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and uses the style of a debate. Picture an opponent looking for excuses: if sin makes God's faithfulness look better, then God would not be just to punish. Paul answers firmly that this is absurd, because God does judge the world. Then he says that those who hold that idea deserve condemnation, since in the end everyone, Jews and Gentiles, is under sin.

For today: do not use God's grace as an excuse to justify your failings. That God can bring something good out of our mistakes does not make them good. Acknowledge your sin with humility and seek his forgiveness.
exp.11:18:
Paul tells believers not to take justice into their own hands. The phrase "Dearly beloved" shows his affection for them. The words "give place unto wrath" mean leaving room for God's anger to act, without wanting to get even ourselves. The statement "Vengeance is mine" quotes the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 32:35): God keeps the judgment for himself.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where some were suffering rejection and mistreatment. Before and after this verse he teaches them to pursue peace and to respond with kindness. About the "burning coals of fire" there are several interpretations: that shame may stir repentance, or that it refers to God's judgment. What is clear is that we should overcome evil with good.

Today, when someone offends you, do not pay them back with words or gossip. Pray for that person, do the good you can, and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.14:10:
Paul quotes an invitation for all the nations that are not Jewish to praise the Lord. "Gentiles" means the peoples who do not belong to Israel. The word "all" shows that no one is left out of this invitation.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, where Jewish and non-Jewish believers were experiencing tension. Here he quotes the Old Testament, which appears to be Psalm 117:1, to show that God always wanted the nations to praise him. It is the third quotation in a row with that same purpose: to encourage them to accept one another and to worship together.

For today: praise belongs to no one and has no boundaries. This week, look for a way to praise God alongside someone very different from you, from another culture, age, or church, and welcome that person as God welcomes them.
exp.1:1:
He says that God judges with truth, that is, with justice and without deception. "Such things" are the evil practices Paul described in chapter 1. "But we know" means that this is something everyone recognizes: God's judgment is not based on appearances or opinions.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken about the sin of the pagans, and now he addresses the one who feels better than they are and points a finger at them. Paul reminds him that God also sees his own life, and that he does similar things.

Today, before criticizing others, it is wise to look honestly at my own heart. God is not fooled by appearances, but he is also patient and invites us to repentance. We can pray: "Lord, examine me, forgive me, and teach me to treat others with mercy."
exp.12:6:
This verse asks us to give each person what is owed to them. "Tribute" is the taxes paid on people or goods; "tax" is another payment or contribution to the government, according to the older wording. "Fear" is serious respect toward those who hold authority, and "honor" is respectful treatment toward those who deserve it.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who lived under a powerful government. Earlier he explained that the authorities play a role in keeping order, and that obeying them is also a matter of conscience. Here he sums this up with concrete examples. Then he adds that the debt that never ends is love for one's neighbor.

For today: be honest in your duties, such as paying your taxes on time and treating with respect those who hold authority, even when you do not agree with them. Do it as part of your witness and your love for others.
exp.11:10:
It says not to be lazy in what we have to do, to keep our hearts burning, and to do everything serving the Lord. Here "diligence" means earnestness or eagerness about things. "Fervent in spirit" speaks of an inner zeal, and some believe it refers to the Holy Spirit, others to our own spirit.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. After explaining what God has done for them in Christ, he shows them how to live together in community. Before this he speaks of sincere love and mutual honor; afterward, of hope, prayer and hospitality. This sentence joins love with daily service.

For today: do your work, your household chores or your help in the church with diligence, and offer it to God as service. Begin each morning in prayer: "Lord, I do this for you."
exp.10:20:
This verse says that if God did not spare the natural branches, that is, the people of Israel who did not believe, then he will not spare the non-Jewish believers either if they become proud. "Spared" here means he did not let them pass or free them from punishment. "Grafted in" means joined on by grafting.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the image of an olive tree: Israel is the original branches, and the non-Jews are branches grafted in. He warns them not to think themselves superior to Israel, since all of them stand only by faith. How this warning applies to the security of salvation, Christians have understood in different ways.

For today: when you feel firm in your faith, do not become proud or judge others. Live with humility and gratitude, trusting each day in the goodness of God.
exp.10:12:
Paul now addresses the believers who were not Jews, whom he calls "Gentiles." He reminds them that he is an apostle sent to them, and he says that he magnifies his ministry, meaning that he values it and carries it out with seriousness and joy.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were both Jewish and non-Jewish believers. He has just explained that the fall of many of his people opened the way for others to receive salvation. Here he clarifies that his work among the Gentiles has a broader purpose: according to the next verse, he hopes it will stir in some Jews the desire to turn back to God.

For today: value the calling God gave you and do it well, but without looking down on anyone. Let your faith and your service be so attractive that others want to know God.
exp.2:16:
It says that the people described have not known the path of peace. "Have not known" means they have not walked on it or made it their way of life. Peace here is not merely the absence of quarrels, but living in harmony with God and with others.

In his letter to the Romans, Paul brings together several quotations from the Old Testament, mainly from the Psalms and Isaiah (Isaiah 59:7-8), to show that everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, is under sin. The verse before speaks of violence and harm; this one says that no peace comes out of that. His aim is that no one should justify themselves and that everyone needs God.

For today: before judging others, let us recognize that we too need the peace that comes from God. Let us ask him to heal our words, reactions and relationships, so that we may be people who seek peace.
exp.7:37:
Paul says he is completely certain of something: nothing on the list he names will be able to separate us from God's love. He mentions death and life, angels, rulers, and powers (spiritual forces or authorities, and some think human authorities as well), the present, and what is to come. The sentence finishes in the following verse.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of suffering and persecution, and he quotes Psalm 44 to show that believers go through hard trials. Even so, he affirms that they triumph through Christ, who loved them. His certainty does not come from circumstances but from the love of God.

When fear, illness, loss, or an uncertain future make you doubt, remember that your security does not depend on how strong your faith feels at that moment, but on the steadfast love of God in Christ. Tell him so in prayer, and rest in that today.
exp.10:25:
Paul says that Israel will be saved.

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and Gentiles, so that they will not think of themselves as better than the Jews who did not believe in Jesus. He uses the image of the olive tree: the Gentiles are branches grafted in, and the natural branches can be grafted back in. Christians do not agree on what "all Israel" means. Some think of the Jewish people in the future, others of all believers, Jews and Gentiles alike.

Today, do not look down on anyone with pride. If salvation is a gift from God, pray with hope for those who do not yet believe.
exp.11:7:
This verse continues the list of gifts that God gives to his church. It says that whoever has the gift of exhorting, that is, encouraging and advising, should devote himself to it. Whoever gives, that is, shares what he has to help others, should do so with generosity and sincerity, without hidden motives. Whoever leads, that is, directs, should do so with care and diligence. And whoever shows mercy, helping those who suffer, should do so with cheerfulness.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he asked them for humility, and he reminded them that they form one body with many members. Each one has a gift given by the grace of God, and all should use it to serve others. Then the passage goes on to speak of sincere love.

For today: think of one concrete way to serve this week, and do it with a good spirit. Helping with joy, without complaining or seeking applause, relieves the other person and honors God.
exp.15:11:
Paul sends greetings to three Christian women in Rome. He describes Tryphena and Tryphosa as women who "labour in the Lord," that is, who actively serve the work of God. He calls Persis "beloved" and recalls that she "laboured much in the Lord." The word "salute" here means "give my warm greetings."

Paul writes this letter to the church in Rome, and in the last chapter he names many people he knows or has heard about. We do not know with certainty what task each one carried out; the text only says that they laboured in the Lord. Some think Tryphena and Tryphosa were sisters, but this is not certain.

God sees and values faithful service, even when it is quiet. Today we can imitate Paul by thanking out loud those who serve in our church: a message, a phone call, or a sincere word encourages people greatly.
exp.9:4:
Paul says that Moses described the righteousness that comes from the law this way: whoever does all its commandments will live by them. The point is that the law requires complete obedience in order to reach life.

Paul, in his letter to the Romans, speaks about his own people, Israel. They had zeal for God, but they wanted to gain his approval by their own effort, and they did not accept Christ. Paul contrasts this path with the righteousness that comes through faith, which he presents right after. Some scholars debate exactly how this contrast fits together, but the central point is clear: the law demands, faith receives.

Today it is easy to think that God accepts us because of how well we behave. This verse invites us to stop measuring ourselves by our achievements and to rest in Christ, obeying him out of gratitude, not out of fear or to earn his love.
exp.15:12:
Paul sends greetings to Rufus and to his mother. He calls Rufus "chosen in the Lord," meaning a believer who is valued and outstanding in the faith. He also calls the woman "mother of mine."

Paul ends his letter to the Romans with a long list of greetings to people he knew. Some think this Rufus is the same man mentioned in Mark 15:21, the son of Simon of Cyrene, but that is not certain. We also do not know when that woman cared for Paul as a mother; it may have been a gesture of affection and gratitude.

Today we can value those who have cared for us in the faith, even if they are not blood relatives. A phone call, a message, or a word of thanks to someone who has served us with love can encourage them greatly.
exp.13:20:
It is good to refrain from eating meat, drinking wine, or doing anything that may cause your brother to stumble. "Stumble" means that something leads him to sin or to doubt. "Is offended" speaks of being hurt in his conscience, and "is made weak" means that his faith becomes more fragile.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different convictions about certain foods. Some felt free to eat anything; others, with a more sensitive conscience, did not. Paul does not say that meat or wine is bad, since he has already affirmed that all things are clean. He asks that love and peace weigh more than their freedom.

Today, before you use your freedom in something debatable, think about who is watching you. If something of yours may confuse or wound another believer's faith, love may lead you to set it aside for a time.
exp.15:16:
Paul asks the brothers to watch carefully, that is, to be alert to those who cause divisions and stumbling blocks (a "stumbling block" is something that makes others fall away from the faith). These people go against the teaching the believers had already received. That is why Paul tells them to keep away from such people.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome near the end of his letter, after sending greetings. Before saying goodbye, he warns them about those who damage the unity of the church with teachings that go against the gospel. The verses that follow say that such people look out for their own gain and deceive with smooth words. Scholars do not agree on exactly who they were.

Today, knowing the Bible well helps us recognize teachings that divide or lead people away from Christ. With humility and prayer, we can avoid those who insist on them, while still loving everyone.
exp.9:15:
Romans 10:16 says that not everyone who hears the good news about Jesus accepts it or obeys it. Paul quotes Isaiah, who lamented that few had believed his message. The word "report" in the verse above means what was heard or preached, and "obeyed" here includes believing and responding in trust.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome and has his own people, Israel, in mind. He has just explained that faith comes by hearing the message, and that God sends messengers. Even so, many did not respond. By quoting Isaiah (53:1), he shows that this rejection did not take God by surprise.

For today: share the gospel with love and do not be discouraged if some do not respond. Your part is to proclaim it sincerely; believing is a response that only God can awaken in each person's heart.
exp.8:14:
It says that God spoke to Moses and told him that He will have mercy on whoever He chooses to have mercy on. The word "but" is not used here, and the old word for "to" is not used either. The repeated phrases, "on whom I will have mercy" and "on whom I will have compassion," stress that the decision is free and belongs to God.

Paul is the one writing, and he quotes what God said to Moses in Exodus 33:19. Earlier, Paul spoke about Jacob and Esau and asked whether God is unjust. He answers that He is not, because salvation was never something anyone deserved. Christians have understood in various ways how this relates to human freedom, but they all agree that God is merciful.

Today, this verse invites us to humility and gratitude. If you have received God's forgiveness, it was not because of your merits. That helps us treat others with the same mercy we have received.
exp.3:0:
Here Paul asks a question: what did Abraham, whom he calls "our father as pertaining to the flesh," gain or discover? That phrase refers to Abraham being the physical ancestor of the Jewish people. The word "found" in the verse above means something like "attained" or "obtained."

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, both Jews and non-Jews. He has just explained that God justifies by faith, not by the law. Now he uses Abraham, who is highly respected by the Jews, as an example. The verses that follow show his answer: Abraham was not declared righteous because of his works, but because he believed God.

For today: you do not need to earn God's favor through good behavior or a good record. Trust what God promised in Christ, and from there live thankfully and obey with joy.
exp.7:34:
Paul asks who could separate believers from the love of Christ, and he lists hard trials: tribulation (pressure and suffering), distress (a tightness of the soul), persecution, hunger, nakedness (lack of clothing and resources), danger, and the sword. In this older rendering, the sword refers to violence or death.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that God justifies them and that Christ died, rose again, and intercedes for them. That is why no one can accuse or condemn them. Now he applies that security to suffering. He quotes Psalm 44 to show that the pain of God's people is not a sign that God has abandoned them, and he affirms that in all these things they are more than conquerors through Christ.

Today, when you go through a trial, do not take it as proof that God has stopped loving you. Tell him honestly what you feel, and remember that Christ continues to intercede for you.
exp.4:19:
The explanation says that the law of Moses "came in," meaning it arrived later, so that sin "might abound," that is, so that it would become more visible and evident. "Moreover" means "furthermore," and "did much more abound" means that grace went far beyond sin, was much greater than the sin.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome and compares Adam with Christ. Through Adam sin and death entered; through Christ come forgiveness and life. Interpreters explain in various ways how the law makes sin abound: by showing it clearly, by stirring up rebellion, or both. Paul concludes that grace reigns to eternal life.
