If today your failures or your past weigh on you, remember that no guilt is greater than the grace of God. Acknowledge your sin honestly, without hiding it, and come to Jesus trusting in his forgiveness. Then live thankfully, not to earn his love, but because you have already received it.
exp.0:6:
Paul greets all the believers who live in Rome. He tells them that God loves them and that they are "called saints," that is, set apart for God. Then he wishes them "grace and peace": grace is the undeserved favor of God, and peace is the calm and reconciliation with Him. Both come from the Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, who writes this letter to a church he had not yet met in person. Before this verse he presents himself as a messenger of Christ, and he says the Romans were also called by Jesus. After greeting them, he thanks God because their faith was known in many places.

For today: your worth does not depend on your achievements, but on God's love and His calling. Today, remember that He loves you, and live at peace in His grace and His peace. Encourage another believer with that same reminder.
exp.5:22:
The explanation says that sin works like an employer that pays a wage: what one earns by working for it is death. Eternal life, by contrast, is not earned but received. The gift comes from God and is found in Christ Jesus, whom the text calls our Lord.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he reminded them that living under sin brought shame and ended in death. Now, freed and made servants of God, their path leads to a transformed life and to eternal life. Paul uses the image of two masters to show the contrast. Many understand "death" as separation from God, and others also include physical death.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's favor through effort and receive his gift with gratitude. That gratitude, in turn, encourages us to serve him in the decisions of each day.
exp.4:17:
This verse compares two men: Adam and Jesus Christ. Through the offence of Adam, guilt and condemnation reached all of humanity. In the same way, through one act of righteousness by Christ, grace is offered to all people so that they may be justified, that is, declared righteous before God, and receive life. The word "offence" means a fall or a wrong, and "unto" means "to" or "toward."

Paul is writing to believers in Rome. He wants to show that just as one man opened the door to sin and death, another, Christ, opened the door to forgiveness and life. Christians understand "all men" in different ways: some see that the offer is for everyone, and others see that it applies to those who believe. The verses that follow speak of "the many."

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness by your own efforts. Receive it with confidence and gratitude, and share it with others.
exp.8:5:
This verse says that the word of God has not failed, meaning that his promises have not come to nothing. The phrase "not as though" means "it is not that". The word "failed" means that something has fallen short or gone without being fulfilled. Paul explains that not everyone who descends from Israel (Jacob) forms the true Israel of God.

Paul speaks with sorrow for his people, since many Jews had not believed in Christ. In the verses before this one he mentions the great privileges Israel received. Someone might think that God had failed in his promises. Paul answers that God has always acted according to his promise and his calling, as the case of Isaac shows, and not only according to physical descent.

For today: do not rest on your origin, your church or your family to feel secure before God. Trust in his promise and respond to him with personal faith. You can also be confident that God keeps what he says, even when we cannot see everything at once.
exp.7:13:
This verse says that the people who are led by the Spirit of God are his children. "Led" means guided or taken by the hand, like someone following a guide along the road. It does not describe a single special moment, but a life that lets itself be directed by God day by day.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. He had been explaining that a life lived according to the flesh leads to death, and that those who, by the Spirit, put aside evil deeds live. Then he adds that we have not received a spirit of slavery and fear, but a spirit of adoption, which lets us call out to God as Father, that is, as "Daddy."

Today, before deciding something important, pray and ask God what he wants. Check your Bible and look for wise counsel. Let the Spirit correct you without fear, because it is a Father who loves you who does it.
exp.13:16:
This verse says that the kingdom of God, that is, the way God rules and lives among his people, does not depend on what one eats or drinks. What marks it is righteousness (living in an upright way), peace, and the joy that the Holy Spirit gives.

Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there were believers with different views about certain foods. Some felt free to eat anything and others did not. Paul asks that those who feel strong not wound or cause to stumble those whose conscience is more sensitive. He reminds them that Christ died for them.

Today, do not make your tastes or customs a reason to quarrel with other believers. Before arguing, ask yourself whether your attitude promotes peace and helps build up your brother or sister. Try to care for others with love.
exp.8:23:
He says that God called "vessels of mercy," and that this calling includes "us," that is, the believers. It comes not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, meaning the people of the other nations. Old wording: the phrase that was rendered "that is" simply means "that is," and "Gentiles" are the non-Jews.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were both Jews and non-Jews. He is explaining that God's promise has not failed, even though many Israelites did not believe. God always acted out of his mercy and his call, not out of family origin. He then quotes Hosea to show that God had already announced he would call a new people. Christians have debated for centuries how God's choosing and human responsibility relate here.

Today, remember that your place before God does not depend on your background, your culture, or your merits. If God has called you, live grateful and welcome with kindness those who are different from you.
exp.12:10:
Paul says it is already time to wake up from spiritual sleep. Paul explains that the full salvation is now nearer than when we first began to believe. "This" refers to living in love, as he said before.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, and he has just explained that love sums up the law. Now he gives urgency to that call: the time is short and Christ will return. Believers interpret in different ways when that final salvation will happen, but all agree that Paul asks us to live awake and alert, not distracted or spiritually asleep.

Today we can ask ourselves: in what area have I been spiritually drowsy? Perhaps it is a relationship I have neglected, or a habit I keep postponing to change. Choose one concrete thing and act today, asking God to help you love someone through actions.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that our "old man," meaning what we were before following Christ, was crucified together with Jesus. In this way the body of sin loses its power, and we no longer have to obey sin as slaves.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He had been explaining that God's grace is no excuse for continuing to sin. He uses baptism as an image: just as Christ died and rose again, the believer leaves behind the old life and walks in a new life. Some understand the body of sin as our nature dominated by sin, and others as the physical body used for evil.

For today: when old habits come back, remember that you are no longer their slave. Ask God for help and act according to your new identity in Christ.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that the peoples who did not know God spoke badly of Him, and that the cause was the conduct of those who said they were His people. "Insulted" means mocked or treated with contempt. "Gentiles" are those who were not Jews. "As it is written" points to the Scriptures of the Old Testament, probably Isaiah 52:5 and Ezekiel 36:20-23.

Paul is speaking to Jews who boasted of knowing God's law. He shows them that teaching what is right does little good if one's life contradicts it. Their failures were causing others to look badly on God. This prepares his argument that all of us need the grace of Christ.

For today: our way of living speaks of God before others. Ask Him that your actions, at work, at home and online, agree with what you say you believe.
exp.1:18:
Here Paul describes what a Jew who trusted in the law thought of himself: that he was a guide of the blind, that is, of those who do not know God, and a light for those who live in darkness, that is, in spiritual ignorance. The phrase "art confident" means that you are sure or convinced of it.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. In this passage he speaks to someone who boasts of knowing God's law but does not live by it. He is not mocking the law, which is good, but showing that knowing is not enough. The verses that follow make this clear: whoever teaches others must also obey.

For today: before correcting or advising someone, ask yourself honestly whether you practice that same thing. Let your life support your words, and teach with humility, remembering that you too need the grace of God.
exp.0:24:
It says that people exchanged the truth about God for a lie. Instead of worshipping the Creator, they honored and served created things. "Changed" is the meaning of the verse's word for exchanged; "created things" are the things that were made; "the Creator" is the one who made them. At the end, Paul breaks into praise: God is worthy of blessing forever.

Here the apostle Paul speaks, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that humanity needs the gospel, because it has rejected God even though it could have known him through creation. The verses before and after describe the consequences of that rejection: God "gave them up," that is, let them follow their own desires.

Today we can ask ourselves what good things, such as money, work or fame, we have placed in the place of God. Let us give Him first place and enjoy everything else with gratitude.
exp.13:19:
Paul asks that we not ruin what God is building in a person over a matter of food. He says that all foods are clean, but that it is wrong to eat in a way that causes another to stumble. Here "offence" means being the cause of a fall or a stumbling, not gossip.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where believers from Jewish and non-Jewish backgrounds disagreed about what to eat. Some had a freer conscience and others a more sensitive one. He reminds them that what matters most is peace and building one another up, not winning the argument.

Today, if something you do freely confuses or wounds the conscience of a brother or sister who is weaker in the faith, it is worth giving it up out of love. Care for the person before you insist on your right.
exp.10:8:
David says that the table of certain people, that is, whatever gives them pleasure and security, should become a trap for them. The verse's words "snare" and "trap" are traps for catching game; "stumblingblock" is what makes a person fall; "recompence" means a repayment or deserved punishment.

Paul quotes Psalm 69:22 to explain why many in Israel did not recognize Jesus, while a chosen remnant did. Some understand this as a judgment of God, but Paul makes clear right away that their fall is not final: God uses their stumbling to bring salvation to the Gentiles and to awaken Israel.

For today: what seems safe to us, such as our customs, achievements, or religiosity, can become a trap if it shuts us off from Christ. Let us ask God for a humble and attentive heart, one that listens to his voice today.
exp.13:18:
The explanation says that Christians should make an effort to pursue what brings peace and what helps others grow in faith. "Let us follow after" means to pursue something with determination. "Edify" means to strengthen and build up others, the way a house is built. "One another" shows that this is meant to go in both directions.

The apostle Paul writes to the church in Rome, where there was tension among believers about what to eat and which days to observe. Some were stricter and others were freer. Paul reminds them that the kingdom of God is not about food, but about righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. For that reason he asks them not to cause a fellow believer to stumble over secondary matters.

Today, before arguing over an opinion or a custom, ask yourself: "Does this bring peace and help my brother or sister grow?" Sometimes it is good to give way, in love, to take care of someone who is weaker in faith.
exp.0:31:
It says that people, although they know that God considers certain conduct worthy of death, not only continue to practice it, but also approve of those who do it. The word "knowing" means that they know or recognize it. The phrase "that they which commit such things" refers to those who practice such conduct. "Have pleasure in them that do them" means that they agree with, support, or applaud them. The phrase "worthy of death" speaks of separation from God and his judgment, not only of physical death.

The apostle Paul speaks in his letter to the Christians in Rome. In this chapter he describes how humanity, by rejecting God, sinks into sin. With the preceding list of wrongs, he shows that all of us need the gospel. Later he will say that God offers forgiveness through faith in Jesus Christ.

For today: let us watch not only what we do, but also what we applaud, share, or find amusing. Let us ask God for humility to recognize our sin and to turn to his mercy.
exp.8:30:
Paul says that the people of Israel pursued a law that could make them righteous before God, but they did not reach that righteousness. The words "followed after" and "hath not attained" are like running a race: they chased after the goal, but they never arrived at it. The Gentiles, by contrast, who were not seeking it, received it.

The apostle Paul is speaking in his letter to the Romans. He grieves over his own people and explains why many Israelites did not accept Christ. According to the following verse, the problem was that they sought righteousness through effort and works, and not through faith.

For today: we can work very hard at being good and still miss the way if we trust in our own achievements. Rest in Christ, and let your obedience be the fruit of your trust in Him, not an attempt to earn God's favor.
exp.5:0:
Paul asks a question: if God gives more grace the more we sin, should we keep on sinning so that his grace may increase? The word "continue" in the verse means to keep going, to stay in something. And "abound" means to increase or overflow. Paul answers at once with an emphatic "God forbid," that is, absolutely not!

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. In the previous chapter he said that where sin abounded, grace did much more abound. Someone might misread that as permission to sin. Paul cuts off that idea at its root, explaining that whoever belongs to Christ has died to sin.

For today: God's grace is not an excuse to live as we please, but a power that transforms us. If you have a habit today that you know displeases God, do not say "God will forgive me anyway"; instead, ask him for help to leave it, grateful for his forgiveness.
exp.0:7:
Paul begins by saying that the first thing he does is give thanks to God, whom he calls "my God," through Jesus Christ. He gives thanks for all the believers in Rome, because their faith is reported and talked about "throughout the whole world," that is, throughout the whole known world of that time. The words "first" and "concerning" mean "above all" and "because of."

Paul writes to them from afar, since he had not yet personally met this church. Before speaking of doctrine or asking for anything, he greets them with sincere gratitude. In this way he shows affection and builds a bond with them. The verses that follow say that he prays for them and wishes to visit them.

Today we can imitate him: before criticizing or asking, let us take the time to thank God for other believers. And when we see faith in someone, let us tell them, because that encourages them.
exp.0:3:
He says that Jesus was declared Son of God with power. This happened through the resurrection from the dead. "Declared" means that it was shown publicly who he was; it does not mean he began to be the Son. The words "according to the spirit of holiness" probably refer to the Holy Spirit or to the holy nature of Christ; it has been understood in both ways. "Power" means strength.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the start of the letter, he presents the gospel. He says that Jesus is a descendant of David, as the prophets promised, and also the Son of God. Paul wants them to know in whom they believe and whom he serves as an apostle.

For today: the resurrection of Jesus is the firm sign that he is who he said he was. When you doubt or feel weak, trust that he is still alive and has power. You can pray today: "Lord Jesus, you are my Lord; guide me."
exp.6:3:
It says that believers "died" to the law through the body of Christ, that is, through his death on the cross. Now they belong to another: to Jesus, who was raised. The purpose is to bear fruit for God.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He uses the example of marriage: the law releases the wife when the husband dies. In the same way, the person united to Christ in his death is freed from the law's dominion. Some explain the image in different ways, but the central idea is that we now live united to the risen Christ.

For today: do not live trying to earn God's favor through effort and fear. Belong to Christ, and let his life in you produce fruit such as love, patience, and kindness.
exp.2:23:
God declares people righteous even though they do not deserve it. Being "justified" means that God accepts us and regards us as free from guilt before Him. "Freely" means as a gift, without payment. "Redemption" is release through a payment, like when a slave is bought back. That payment was made in Christ Jesus.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just explained that everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, has sinned and falls short of the glory of God. For this reason, no one can be saved by their own merits. This verse presents the answer: God offers salvation as a gift through Jesus.

Today we can stop trying to earn God's love through effort and guilt. If you have trusted in Christ, you can come near to God with gratitude and peace, knowing that your place before Him is a gift, not a reward.
exp.0:30:
This verse follows a list of behaviors that show what life looks like when a person turns away from God. "Without understanding" describes people who lack moral sense and good judgment. "Covenantbreakers" are those who do not keep their word or their commitments. "Without natural affection" means they lack the normal love expected within the family. "Implacable" people do not forgive or seek reconciliation. "Unmerciful" people feel no compassion for someone who suffers.

Here the apostle Paul speaks, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He describes how humanity, by rejecting God, ends up damaging its relationships and its own conscience. This is the beginning of an argument: all of us need the gospel, since no one saves himself.

For today: review your close relationships. Is there someone you have not forgiven, or someone you have treated harshly? Ask God for a compassionate heart, and take one concrete step toward reconciliation today.
exp.6:12:
Paul asks whether the law, which is good, was the thing that brought him death. He answers firmly: no. It was sin that used the good commandment to produce death, and so sin was exposed for what it really is: something terrible. The phrase that appears in the verse as "exceeding sinful" means extremely sinful, very wicked to a great degree.

Paul speaks in the first person, and scholars debate whether he is describing his life before he knew Christ, his life as a believer, or a general human experience. Either way, he is defending God's law against the idea that it is evil. The law does not create sin; it brings sin to light and shows how serious it is.

For today: when God's Word confronts you and makes you uncomfortable, do not see it as an enemy. It is like a light that reveals what is wrong so that you will seek the grace of Christ and receive healing.
exp.2:11:
The explanation says that all of humanity has turned away from God's path. The phrase "together" or "all alike" describes everyone without exception. "Unprofitable" speaks of something that has spoiled and no longer serves its purpose. Paul affirms that no one, by themselves, truly does the good that God expects.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, writing to the Christians in Rome. Here he gathers several quotations from the Psalms (especially Psalm 14 and Psalm 53) to show that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin. His purpose is to prepare the way to explain that salvation comes through faith in Jesus Christ, not through one's own merits.

This verse invites us to humility. We do not have to pretend we are perfect or look down on others with pride. We can honestly acknowledge our failings and gratefully receive the grace that God offers freely in Christ.
exp.6:18:
Paul says that he does not manage to do the good he wants, and that he ends up doing the evil he does not want. It is a struggle between what his heart longs for and what he actually does.

Paul writes in the first person, explaining how God's law shows sin but does not give the strength to overcome it. Many believers think he is speaking of his life before he knew Christ; others understand that he describes the believer's constant struggle. Scholars interpret it in both ways. In the next chapter, he speaks of the freedom that the Spirit gives.

If you feel that you fail even though you want to do what is right, do not lose heart or hide it. Acknowledge your weakness before God with sincerity, ask him for help each day, and rely on his grace, not only on your own effort.
exp.5:8:
He says that Christ was raised and will never die again. Death no longer has power or authority over Him. The verse says that death "hath no more dominion" over Him, meaning it no longer rules over Him as a master would.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that whoever believes in Jesus is united with Him in His death and in His resurrection. Paul uses Christ's final victory over death as the basis for encouraging believers not to keep living under the rule of sin. What follows shows that Christ died to sin once and now lives for God.

Today we can face our struggles with hope and not with defeat. If Christ overcame death, His power also sustains us in saying no to sin. When you feel that a bad habit dominates you, remember that you belong to Christ and ask Him for strength to live for God.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that anyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. The word "call" here means to pray to him, to ask him for help and trust him. "Saved" means receiving God's salvation, his forgiveness and life with him.

The apostle Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that there is no difference between Jews and Greeks, because Jesus is Lord of all and is generous to everyone who calls on him. Paul quotes a promise from the prophet Joel to show that salvation is open to all people. He then explains that people need someone to proclaim this good news to them.

Today, if you feel far from God or unworthy, this promise is for you. You can pray simply and put your trust in Jesus. And if you already know him, think of someone you could speak to about him.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that Paul had often wanted to visit the Christians in Rome, but something kept getting in the way. "Hindered" means held back or stopped. "For which cause" refers to what he has just said: his work of preaching where Christ was not yet known.

Paul writes this letter to the Romans. He explains that his mission to proclaim the gospel in new places kept him busy in other regions. That is why he had not been able to reach Rome, where there were already believers. Now he plans to go through Rome on his way to Spain. The letter does not detail every obstacle, so it is not wise to invent them.

For today: when your plans are delayed, do not become discouraged right away. God may have you occupied with something important. Remain faithful where you are and keep alive the desire to serve and encourage others.
exp.13:7:
It says that our whole life belongs to the Lord. If we are alive, we live for him; if we die, we also die for him. In the end, whether we live or die, we are Christ's.

The word "ó" is simply "or", and "morimos" means "we die" in the sense that we reach the end of life.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements among brothers and sisters about secondary matters, such as keeping certain days or eating certain foods. He reminds them that each person, with a sincere conscience, can act for the Lord. For that reason they must not judge or look down on one another.

For today: before you criticize another believer over a secondary difference, remember that he too belongs to Christ. Ask yourself whether your own life, in the big things and in the small, is being lived for the Lord.
exp.7:31:
This verse says that God did not hold back his own Son, but gave him up to death for all of us. The phrase "did not spare" means that he did not rescue him from suffering. If God gave what was most precious to him, it makes sense that he will also give us all things along with Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been speaking about how God sustains his children in the middle of suffering and brings them to glory. With the question "if God is for us, who can be against us?" he affirms that no one can overcome the love of God. This verse is the proof of that love. Some understand "all things" to mean everything we need to reach final salvation.

When you doubt that God cares for you, look to the cross. If God gave up his Son, you can entrust your needs and your fears to him with confidence.
exp.15:9:
Paul asks that Apelles be greeted, saying he was "approved in Christ." This means his faith had been tested and had come through approved, like gold that withstands the fire. He also says to greet "them which are of Aristobulus' household," that is, those in his house, who could have been relatives or servants.

Paul writes this letter to the believers in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many brothers and sisters to show closeness and honor. We do not know more about Apelles, nor whether Aristobulus was a believer; some think only part of his household was, but this cannot be stated with certainty.

Today we can imitate Paul: recognize by name and with affection those who have remained faithful through trials. A word of gratitude to someone who has served with steadiness can greatly encourage their faith.
exp.10:26:
It says that God made a solemn promise, a covenant, with the people of Israel: that He Himself will take away their sins. The word for "take away" here is an older form of the verb, so the sense is simply that God will remove their sins. Forgiveness does not depend on human effort, but on what God committed Himself to do.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, most of whom were not of Jewish origin. He quotes the prophet Isaiah (59:20-21; 27:9) to show that God has not abandoned Israel. Christians were not to feel superior. How and when "all Israel will be saved" is understood in various ways by believers, but Paul insists that God is faithful.

For today: trust that God's forgiveness rests on His faithfulness, not on your performance. Receive it with humility, and treat others with grace, without thinking you are better than anyone.
exp.12:8:
Paul cites several of the Ten Commandments: do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not covet. He says that any other commandment is summed up in one saying: "Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself."

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. Earlier he spoke about respecting the authorities and paying what is owed. Now he says that the debt that never ends is love. He quotes the law of Moses (Leviticus 19:18) to show that loving others is at the heart of what God asks.

Before you act, ask yourself: "Is this good for my neighbour, or only for me?" Love is not only avoiding harm; it is also seeking the good of the other person in everyday life, through words, time, and concrete help.
exp.7:27:
It says that those who love God can be sure that everything that happens to them, even what is hard, God is guiding toward something good. Some understand that "all things" includes even suffering, and that this "good" refers above all to being shaped into the likeness of Christ.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of the weakness we feel, of the Spirit who prays for us, and of the sufferings of the present time. He wants to give them comfort: God has a firm purpose, which he then explains in the verses that follow.

Today, when you go through a painful situation, you do not have to pretend that it does not hurt. You can pray honestly and trust that God is still at work, even when you cannot yet see the result.
exp.11:20:
It says that we should not let evil dominate us or change us. When someone harms us, the temptation is to pay them back in kind, and in that way evil wins inside us. Instead, we are invited to overcome evil by doing good.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who lived surrounded by people who did not understand them and sometimes treated them badly. Earlier he asked them not to take revenge, but to let God do justice. He gives the example of feeding a hungry enemy. The image of "burning coals of fire" is understood in several ways: shame that leads to repentance, or God's judgment. What is clear is that the response must be kindness.

Today, if someone offends you at work, in the family, or online, do not answer with insults or cold indifference. Pray for that person and make a concrete gesture of kindness, such as helping them or speaking to them with respect.
exp.8:28:
It says that Isaiah had already announced something: if the Lord of hosts, God, had not left Israel a seed (that is, a descendant, a small remnant that survived), the people would have been destroyed like Sodom and Gomorrah.

Paul speaks here, quoting Isaiah 1:9. He is explaining why many of his people did not believe in Christ, and yet God's promise has not failed. God has always preserved a faithful remnant by his grace, not because of the people's merits.

For today: if you remain alive in faith, it is not by your own strength, but because God sustains you. Give thanks today for his mercy and trust that he cares for his own, even when they seem few.
exp.14:25:
This verse tells that the churches of Macedonia and Achaia decided, gladly, to gather an offering to help the poor believers in Jerusalem. "Offering" here means a gift of money collected from the community. The phrase "decided gladly" means they judged it good to do so, of their own free will.

Paul writes to the Romans and explains his plans: he is going to Jerusalem to bring this help, and after that he hopes to visit them on his way to Spain. Later he says that the believers of non-Jewish background felt they owed a debt to those in Jerusalem, from whom they had received the spiritual blessings of the gospel.

For today: Christian generosity springs from gratitude and willingness, not from obligation. Think of someone in your community who is in need, and give something concrete, with joy.
exp.6:14:
Paul says there is a struggle inside him: he does things he does not understand, he does not do the good he wants, and he practices exactly what he hates. "Hate" here means he strongly rejects or is repulsed by something. "Does not understand" here means his own conduct baffles him.

Paul speaks of God's law, which is good and spiritual, but which cannot give him the power to obey it. He shows sin as a force that uses the commandment to dominate the person. Christians have understood this struggle in several ways: some see Paul speaking of his life before Christ, others of his life as a believer. Both views have serious defenders.

Today we can honestly admit our struggles, without hiding them or making excuses for ourselves. Recognizing that we cannot manage alone leads us to ask God for help, who in Christ offers forgiveness and strength to change little by little.
exp.2:25:
This verse says that God showed his righteousness at the present time, that is, in the era of Christ. In this way it is made clear that God is just and, at the same time, that he is the one who declares righteous everyone who trusts in Jesus. God's declaring someone free from guilt before him is what the verse is describing.

Here the apostle Paul speaks, in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He explains that everyone has sinned and that no one is saved by their own works. God passed over the sins of the past with patience, and on the cross of Christ he showed that he had not ignored them. Paul wants us to see that forgiveness does not make God unjust.

For today: when you feel unworthy, do not try to earn forgiveness through effort. Trust in what Jesus did for you and live with gratitude and peace.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that the Gentiles, although they did not receive the law of Moses, show that the essential part of the law is written on their hearts. Their conscience confirms this, bearing witness within them. Their thoughts sometimes accuse them when they do wrong, and at other times they defend or excuse them.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, who were both Jews and Gentiles. He wants to show that no one can boast before God. The Jews had the law written down, but hearing it is not enough; it must be obeyed. The Gentiles, without that law, also have an inner sense of good and evil. Some understand that Paul speaks of Gentiles in general, and others of Gentiles who believe.

For today: do not ignore your conscience when it troubles you. Bring it to God with humility, asking him to shape it through his Word and to forgive you through Christ.
exp.11:12:
The explanation says that believers should share what they have with fellow Christians who are in need, and that they should eagerly seek to welcome others into their homes. The word "sharing" means taking part in or giving to others. "The saints" are the believers, the people of God. Pursuing hospitality means chasing after it actively, not waiting for it to come to you.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. After explaining what God has done for them in Christ, he shows them how to live a transformed life. These verses describe a practical love within the church. In that time, traveling believers depended greatly on the hospitality of other brothers and sisters.

Today you might ask yourself who near you has a need: a meal, a temporary home, companionship, or help with money. This week, take a concrete step: invite someone to your table or share something with a family that needs it.
exp.7:6:
This verse says that thinking and living according to the flesh means being against God. The "mindset" is the way of thinking, what a person wants and pursues. The "flesh" here does not mean the body, but our human nature living apart from God. "Submit" means to obey or yield. That mindset neither submits to God's law nor is able to do so on its own.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has been explaining that whoever lives according to the flesh ends in death, while whoever lives according to the Spirit finds life and peace. Then he encourages believers: God's Spirit lives in them, so they are no longer controlled by the flesh.

Today we can ask ourselves what fills our minds most each day. A practical idea is to begin the morning by asking the Spirit to guide our thoughts, and not to rely only on our own willpower.
exp.2:7:
Paul repeats a false accusation that was made against him: that he taught, "Let us do evil, that good may come." "Slandered" means falsely accused or defamed. Paul answers that those who hold that view deserve their condemnation.

Paul is explaining that God's grace is no excuse for sin. His critics twisted his message: if sin makes God's faithfulness shine more brightly, then sinning would seem good. Paul firmly rejects that reasoning. He will soon show that both Jews and Gentiles equally need God's forgiveness.

For today: grace is not permission to do wrong, but an invitation to live differently. If you ever justify yourself by saying "the end justifies it," stop and ask whether you truly honor God. A good purpose never makes a wrong action good.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that everyone will be judged by God in a fair way. Those who sinned without knowing the law of Moses (the non-Jews) will also perish, that is, they will be separated from God. And those who sinned while knowing the law (the Jews) will be judged according to that law. To perish means to be lost, to not receive salvation.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He is explaining that God shows no favoritism. The Jews might have thought that having the law would free them from judgment, and the Gentiles might have thought that without a law they had no guilt. Paul shows that no one escapes: everyone needs the mercy of God.

For today: do not use your knowledge of the Bible, your church, or your family as an excuse to feel secure, and do not think that ignoring God takes away your responsibility. Be humble, recognize your need for Christ, and live out what you already know of the truth.
exp.10:31:
It says that God left everyone, both Jews and non-Jews, shut up in disobedience, as if in a prison, so that he might show his mercy to all. "Concluded" means that God allowed or declared that all of us are unbelievers, and "unbelief" here is also understood as disobedience. In this way, no one can boast of deserving his favor.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, both Jews and Gentiles. He explains to them that the rejection of the Messiah by many Jews did not close the door to anyone, and that God continues a plan full of mercy. The verses that follow end in praise of his wisdom. Some debate whether "all" means every person or all groups; the text stresses that mercy is for both.

Today, remember that no one is saved by their own merit. This takes away pride and the attitude of judging others. If God has had mercy on you, offer it with humility and hope.
exp.13:2:
The explanation says that the one who eats everything should not look down on the one who avoids certain foods, and the one who does not eat them should not criticize the one who does. The reason is that God has already received both. To look down on someone is to treat them as if they were worth little, and to judge here means to condemn the other person.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome, where believers of Jewish background and believers of non-Jewish background lived side by side. They had differences about food and special days. Paul is not dealing with the central truths of the gospel, but with matters where people's consciences differ. That is why he asks that the one who is weaker in faith be welcomed without fighting over opinions.

Today, when another believer does something differently from you in a secondary matter, such as the kind of music or certain customs, do not look down on them or condemn them. Remember that God has accepted them too, and treat them with respect.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that sin was already in the world before God gave the law to Moses. But it explains that where there is no clear law, sin is not charged to someone's account as a formal wrong. Even so, the next verse shows that death reigned during that time.

Paul writes to the Christians in Rome. He wants to show that everyone, both before and after Moses, is under sin and death through Adam. In this way he prepares the comparison with Christ, who brings grace and life. Scholars explain in various ways how being charged with sin relates to the death of those who did not have the law.

For today: let us not downplay sin by thinking, "If no one has told me, it does not matter." Let us humbly recognize our need for Jesus and rest in his grace, which is greater than our wrongdoing.
exp.14:23:
Paul tells the Christians in Rome that, when he sets out for Spain, he will pass through their city. He hopes to see them on the way and to be helped on his journey by them, after he has enjoyed some time in their company. The words "when I take my journey" in the King James Version are the verse's own wording, so no separate explanation is needed here.

Paul writes this letter from the end of his work in the eastern part of the empire. He wants to preach where Christ is not yet known, and that is why he has Spain in mind. We do not know for certain whether he ever went there. He asks the Roman believers for support as partners in the mission, not as someone making demands.

For today: Paul joins large plans with friendship and cooperation. We can support those who serve God through prayer, practical help, or companionship, and we can let others help us too. No one serves alone.
exp.15:2:
Paul asks that they be greeted: Priscilla and Aquila, a Christian married couple. He calls them "my helpers," a word meaning fellow workers or co-laborers. He says they worked alongside him in the work of Christ Jesus. It is interesting that he names Priscilla first, which was uncommon for that time.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, and at the end he greets many people by name. According to Acts, Priscilla and Aquila were fellow tent-makers with Paul and hosted him in Corinth. The verses that follow say they risked their lives for him, although we do not know the details of when this happened. They also had a church that met in their home.

Today we can imitate this example: value and thank out loud those who serve alongside us. A message or a few words of gratitude can greatly encourage a brother or sister in the faith.
exp.15:13:
Paul sends greetings to five men: Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, and Hermes. He also greets "the brethren which are with them," that is, other believers who probably met with them. The word "Salute" in the verse is the same as "greet," meaning to send warm wishes.

Paul writes this letter to the Christians in Rome, whom he had not yet met in person. At the end he names many people, perhaps to show closeness and unity. Of these five we know almost nothing else; their names were common at that time. Some think they formed a group that met in a house, but the Bible does not make this clear.

God values every believer, even those whom almost no one remembers. Today we can imitate Paul: remembering specific names, greeting people, encouraging them, and helping those who go unnoticed feel part of the church.
exp.13:17:
This verse says that whoever serves Christ in these things, that is, in living with righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit, pleases God and also receives approval from people. "Acceptable" means well received, approved. The word "approved" in the verse above is the one to keep in mind here.

The apostle Paul writes to the Christians in Rome, where there were disagreements about which foods could be eaten. Some were judging others for it. Paul reminds them that the kingdom of God is not about food or drink, but about righteousness, peace, and joy. That is why he asks them not to cause anyone to stumble.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are fighting over secondary things. Before arguing, let us seek peace and care for the brothers and sisters who are weaker in faith. In this way we serve Christ with love and humility.
exp.0:18:
What can be known about God is plain to everyone, because God himself has made it known to them. The word "á" is an old way of writing "to," and "manifest" means clear and evident.

Paul is writing to the Christians in Rome. He has just said that the gospel shows God's righteousness, and that God's wrath is revealed against those who suppress the truth with wickedness. Here he explains why no one has an excuse: God has not hidden himself, but has made himself known, above all through creation, as the next verse says.

For today: God is not a distant mystery. When you see a sunrise, or feel your conscience, you can stop and give thanks to him. And when you speak about God with others, do it with humility, remembering that he is already speaking to them in many ways.
exp.10:35:
Everything that exists comes from God, is held together by his power, and exists for him. Nothing falls outside his work. For that reason, the right response is to give him glory forever. Those words of "forever" are the only part that needs no further comment here.

The apostle Paul is speaking in his letter to the Christians in Rome. He has just spoken of God's plan for Israel and for the nations, and he is left in awe of his wisdom. The earlier questions, which recall the prophet Isaiah and Job, show that no one advises God or can put him in debt. This verse closes that praise.

Today, when something is hard for you to understand, remember that God owes you no explanations, but he does deserve your trust. Thank him for what you have, since all of it comes from him, and offer him your work and your plans as a way of giving him glory.
exp.7:24:
It says that when we hope for something we do not yet see, we wait for it with patience. The word "but" in the verse is what connects these two ideas, and "patience" here means steady endurance, holding on without giving up. Christian hope looks toward something God has promised that has not yet been fulfilled.

Paul is writing to Christians in Rome. He has just said that all creation groans, and that we too groan as we wait for our full redemption, the completion of our bodies being made new. We live between what God has already done and what still remains. Then Paul explains that the Spirit helps us in that weakness.

For today: when a prayer takes a long time or suffering continues, you do not have to pretend that everything is fine. You can wait calmly, pray honestly, and trust that God keeps what he promises, even when you cannot yet see it.
exp.6:1:
The explanation says that a married woman is bound to her husband by the law as long as he lives. But if the husband dies, she is free from that marriage law. The word "bound" here means tied or joined, and "obligated" means she has a commitment she must keep.

Paul writes to the believers in Rome, speaking to people who know the law of Moses. He uses marriage as a simple example: the law holds a person as long as that person lives. He then explains that believers have died to the law through Christ, so that they may belong to the One who rose again. It is a comparison; some scholars discuss every detail of it, but the central idea is clear.

For today: do not spend your life trying to earn God's love through your own efforts. Belong to Christ with gratitude, and let his life in you bear fruit in love and sincere obedience.
exp.6:2:
The explanation says that a married woman, while her husband lives, commits adultery if she joins herself to another man. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law of marriage and may marry again without committing adultery. The phrase "she shall be called an adulteress" means she will be regarded as one. The word "husband" in the verse refers to the man she is married to, and the explanation's note that "rules over" means "has dominion over" is covered by the verse's wording "while her husband liveth."

Paul writes to Christians in Rome, who know the law. He uses marriage as an example: just as death ends the wife's obligation to her husband, death with Christ ends our obligation to the law. Some interpreters discuss the details of the comparison, but the central point is clear.

For today: if you belong to Christ, you do not live to earn God's favor through rules, but to bear fruit out of love for Him. Today, instead of asking yourself "what must I do to comply?", ask Him: "how can I please you with gratitude?"

sum.5: Paul teaches that whoever is united with Christ in his death and resurrection has already died to sin and now lives for God. Because of this, we should not keep sinning or let sin rule us. Instead, we should give ourselves to God to do what is right. Sin pays with death, but God gives the gift of eternal life in Christ.
sum.9: Paul longs with all his heart for Israel to be saved, but he says they have zeal for God without understanding that righteousness comes through faith in Christ, not through their own effort. He teaches that whoever confesses Jesus as Lord and believes that God raised him from the dead will be saved, whether Jew or Greek. For this reason, it is necessary that the gospel be preached and heard.
sum.10: Paul teaches that God has not rejected Israel, since there has always remained a chosen remnant by grace. Their stumbling opened the way of salvation to the Gentiles, who must be humble, like branches grafted into an olive tree. God is faithful and merciful to all, and for this reason Paul concludes by praising his wisdom.
sum.13: Paul teaches that believers should not judge or look down on one another over differences such as food or special days, because each person lives and answers to the Lord, and all of us will stand before Christ. He asks people to love their brother, not to cause him to stumble, and to pursue peace, since the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit.
sum.15: Paul commends Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchreae, and warmly greets many believers in Rome who worked for the Lord, including Priscilla and Aquila. He asks the believers to keep away from those who cause divisions and deceive people with smooth talk, and to be wise about what is good. He ends with greetings from his companions and with praise to the one wise God.
sum.0: Paul introduces himself to the Christians in Rome, thanks God for their faith, and says he wants to visit them. He affirms that the gospel is the power of God to save everyone who believes, and that the righteous will live by faith. He then explains that people rejected God, even though God could be known through creation, and so they fell into idolatry and wickedness.
sum.7: Paul teaches that those who are in Christ no longer face condemnation, because the Spirit gives them life, makes them children of God, and supports them in their weakness. Although there is suffering today, and all creation is waiting to be set free, God works all things together for good. Nothing can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
sum.4: Through believing in Christ, we are justified and have peace with God, hope, and the love of God in our hearts, even in trials. Christ died for us while we were still sinners and enemies, and in this way he reconciled us to God. Through Adam's disobedience, sin and death entered, but through Jesus's obedience, grace overflowed into eternal life.
sum.6: Paul uses the example of marriage to explain that, just as death frees a person from the husband's law, believers have died to the law through Christ so that they can serve God in a new spirit. The law is holy and good, but it reveals sin and does not give the power to overcome it. Paul describes his inner struggle and thanks God through Jesus Christ.
sum.3: Paul explains that Abraham was declared righteous because he believed God, not because of his works or because of circumcision, since the promise came before he was circumcised. In this way, Abraham is the father of all who believe, whether Jewish or not. That same faith, trusting in the God who raised Jesus from the dead, is also counted to us as righteousness.
sum.14: Paul urges those who are strong in faith to help the weak and to live in unity, following the example of Christ, who welcomed both Jews and non-Jews. He then describes how he has preached the gospel to the Gentiles and his plan to visit Rome on his way to Spain, after first taking a collection to the poor in Jerusalem. He asks for prayers.
sum.1: Paul shows that God judges with truth and without partiality, and that no one can condemn others while doing the same things themselves. God is patient, leading us toward repentance, and he will repay each person according to their deeds. Both Jews and Gentiles will be judged, because what matters is obeying from the heart, not merely knowing the law or having circumcision.
sum.2: Paul explains that God is faithful even when people fail, and that both Jews and non-Jews are under sin, so no one is saved by keeping the law. God's righteousness comes as a free gift through faith in Jesus Christ, through his redemption, for everyone who believes.
sum.8: Paul feels deep sorrow for his people, Israel, who received so many promises and who gave rise to Christ. He explains that God acts according to his promise and his mercy, not because of human merit, and that he calls both Jews and Gentiles. Israel stumbled because they sought righteousness through works rather than through faith.
sum.12: Paul teaches that people should submit to governing authorities, since God has established them to reward good and punish wrongdoing, and that everyone should pay what they owe. All of this comes down to loving your neighbor, because love fulfills the law. Since the day of salvation is near, believers should put aside the deeds of darkness and clothe themselves with Jesus Christ.
sum.11: Paul asks believers, in light of God's mercy, to offer themselves fully to Him and to renew their minds instead of following the patterns of the world. He teaches them to live with humility, to use their gifts in service to everyone as one body, and to love sincerely. He also calls them to live at peace, not to take revenge, and to overcome evil with good.
